modules.title: Hello, Rust
modules.summary: Your first programs. What fn main is, how println! prints text, and how to read the compiler's (very helpful) error messages.

steps.title: Your first program
steps.text:
A **program** is a list of instructions the computer follows from top to bottom. Rust is a *compiled* language: you write the instructions as text (the **source code**), the Rust compiler (`rustc`) checks them very carefully and translates them into machine code, and then the program runs. Every time you press **Check**, a real Rust compiler builds and runs your code.

### The shape of every Rust program

```rust
fn main() {
    println!("Hi!");
}
```

```text
Hi!
```

Piece by piece:

- `fn main()` starts a **function** called `main`. `fn` is short for *function*. Every Rust program begins running at `main`, no matter how big it is. The empty `()` say it takes no inputs.
- The curly braces `{ }` hold the function's **body**: the instructions that run, in order.
- `println!("Hi!");` prints the text `Hi!` and then ends the line ("print line"). The text goes inside double quotes.
- The `!` means `println!` is a **macro**, not a normal function. Macros are Rust code that writes more code for you; you'll meet several (`println!`, `format!`, `vec!`). For now: printing needs the `!`.
- The `;` ends the statement, like a period ends a sentence.

### Common mistakes

- **Forgetting the `!`**: `println("Hi")` makes the compiler say `` cannot find function `println` in this scope ``. It's a macro, so it's `println!`.
- **Spelling and capitals matter**: `Println!` or `printline!` don't exist.
- **Single quotes**: `'Hi'` is wrong. Text always goes in double quotes; single quotes are for one character, like `'a'`.

steps.title: Printing values with {}
steps.text:
`println!` can do more than print fixed text. Inside the string, a pair of curly braces `{}` is a **placeholder**: a hole that gets filled with a value you put after the string, separated by commas. The string with the holes is called the **format string**.

```rust
fn main() {
    println!("2 + 3 = {}", 2 + 3);
    println!("{} likes {}", "Ferris", "Rust");
}
```

```text
2 + 3 = 5
Ferris likes Rust
```

The values fill the placeholders in order: the first `{}` gets the first value, and so on. Rust checks this when it compiles: if the number of `{}` and values don't match, it's a compile error, not a surprise at run time.

### Arithmetic

Rust does the math before printing: `+` adds, `-` subtracts, `*` multiplies, `/` divides and `%` gives the remainder. With whole numbers, `/` drops the fraction: `7 / 2` is `3`. You'll see why in the Types module.

### Printing braces

To print an actual `{` or `}`, double it: `{{` and `}}`.

```rust
fn main() {
    println!("{{}} is a placeholder, and 10 / 3 = {}", 10 / 3);
}
```

```text
{} is a placeholder, and 10 / 3 = 3
```

steps.title: Comments and reading compiler errors
steps.text:
### Comments

A **comment** is a note for humans. The compiler ignores it.

```rust
fn main() {
    // A line comment runs to the end of the line.
    println!("visible"); // it can follow code, too
    /* A block comment can
       span several lines. */
}
```

```text
visible
```

Programmers also "comment out" a line to switch it off for a moment without deleting it.

### The compiler is on your side

Rust's compiler is famous for its error messages. They tell you **what** went wrong, **where** (file, line and column), and often **how to fix it**. Learning to read them is one of the most useful skills in this course. For example, this program forgets the `!`:

```rust-error
fn main() {
    println("Hi!");
}
```

```compiler
error[E0423]: cannot find function `println` in this scope
```

There's no *function* called `println`, only a macro. The full message points at the exact spot with `^^^^`, notes that ``a macro named `println` exists``, and adds ``help: use `!` to invoke the macro``. When **Check** finds a compile error, this site shows rustc's message, a short explanation in plain English, and the line it's on in the editor.

Each error has a code like `E0423`. You can look up any code in the official [Rust error index](https://doc.rust-lang.org/error_codes/error-index.html), or by running `rustc --explain E0423`.

steps.title: Cargo: how real Rust projects are built
steps.text:
On this site you press **Check** and your code is compiled for you. On your own computer (and at work) you'll use **Cargo**, Rust's build tool and package manager. Install everything with **rustup** from [rustup.rs](https://rustup.rs): it installs `rustc` (the compiler), `cargo`, and the standard library, and keeps them up to date with `rustup update`.

### A new project

```text
$ cargo new hello
    Creating binary (application) `hello` package
$ cd hello
$ cargo run
   Compiling hello v0.1.0 (/home/you/hello)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.41s
     Running `target/debug/hello`
Hello, world!
```

`cargo new` creates this:

```text
hello/
├── Cargo.toml      the project's settings: name, version, edition, dependencies
└── src/
    └── main.rs     your code, starting with fn main
```

It also starts a Git repository for the project, with a `.gitignore` file that keeps the build output out of it.

### The commands you'll use every day

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `cargo run` | build, then run the program |
| `cargo build` | build only (the program lands in `target/debug/`) |
| `cargo build --release` | build with optimizations, for speed (`target/release/`) |
| `cargo check` | check that the code compiles, without building a program: the fastest feedback |
| `cargo test` | run the project's tests |
| `cargo fmt` | format the code in the standard Rust style |
| `cargo clippy` | a linter that suggests more idiomatic, correct code |
| `cargo doc --open` | build documentation for your code and its dependencies |

Every Rust team uses `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy`; many make them part of every pull request. The **edition** in `Cargo.toml` (this site uses `2024`, the newest) picks which version of the language's rules a project uses; crates of different editions work together.

steps.title: Types: annotations and inference
steps.text:
Every value in Rust has a **type**: the kind of value it is, which decides what you can do with it. Here are the basic ones (you've already used the first and the last):

| Value | Type | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `120` | `i32` | a whole number (an **integer**) |
| `3.5` | `f64` | a number with a fraction (a **floating-point** number) |
| `true`, `false` | `bool` | a yes/no value (a **Boolean**) |
| `'R'` | `char` | one character, in single quotes |
| `"Ferris"` | `&str` | a piece of text (a **string slice**), in double quotes |

Rust is **statically typed**: every variable's type is known when the program is compiled, and it never changes. But you rarely have to write the type, because the compiler works it out from the value. That's **type inference**. When you want to, you can write it yourself with a **type annotation**: a colon and the type after the name.

```rust
fn main() {
    let lives: i32 = 3;
    let speed: f64 = 2.5;
    let is_boss: bool = false;
    let grade: char = 'A';
    let name: &str = "Ferris";
    println!("{} {} {} {} {}", lives, speed, is_boss, grade, name);
}
```

```text
3 2.5 false A Ferris
```

Without annotations, a whole number like `3` becomes an `i32` and a number with a decimal point like `2.5` becomes an `f64`. The next module covers the number types in detail (there are several sizes).

### Why annotate if the compiler can infer?

- To choose a type other than the default (you'll want bigger or non-negative integer types in the next module).
- To state your intent, so the compiler reports a mistake right where it happens.
- Some values could be several types, and the compiler needs you to pick one (you'll see this when reading numbers from input).

### The annotation is a promise

The compiler checks that the value matches the type you wrote:

```rust-error
fn main() {
    let count: i32 = "five";
    println!("{}", count);
}
```

```compiler
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:2:22
  |
2 |     let count: i32 = "five";
  |                ---   ^^^^^^ expected `i32`, found `&str`
  |                |
  |                expected due to this
```

E0308 "mismatched types" is the error you'll see most often in Rust. It always tells you what was **expected** and what was **found**.

### Common mistakes

- **`let count: i32 = 3.0;`**: `3.0` is a float, not an integer, even though it's a whole number. Write `3`.
- **Text in single quotes**: `'Ferris'` is an error. Single quotes hold exactly one `char`; text goes in double quotes.
- **Type before the name**, as in C or Java (`let i32 count`). In Rust the name comes first, then `: type`.

steps.title: Constants and naming
steps.text:
### Constants

Some values are fixed for the whole program: the maximum health, the number of seconds in a minute, a tax rate. Rust has **constants** for these, declared with `const`:

```rust
const MAX_HEALTH: i32 = 100;
const SECONDS_PER_MINUTE: i32 = 60;

fn main() {
    let minutes = 3;
    println!("max health: {}", MAX_HEALTH);
    println!("{} minutes = {} seconds", minutes, minutes * SECONDS_PER_MINUTE);
}
```

```text
max health: 100
3 minutes = 180 seconds
```

How `const` differs from `let`:

- The type annotation is **required**: `const MAX_HEALTH: i32`. Constants are often shared across a whole program, so Rust wants their type spelled out.
- A constant can never be `mut`.
- It can be declared outside any function, at the top of the file (a **global** constant), and every function in the file can use it.
- Its value must be known while compiling: numbers, text, and arithmetic on them (like `60 * 60`), but not something that only exists when the program runs.

```rust-error
const MAX_HEALTH = 100;

fn main() {
    println!("{}", MAX_HEALTH);
}
```

```compiler
error: missing type for `const` item
 --> src/main.rs:1:17
  |
1 | const MAX_HEALTH = 100;
  |                 ^ help: provide a type for the constant: `: i32`
```

Why bother? A named value explains itself (`MAX_HEALTH` versus a mysterious `100`), and when the rule changes you edit one line instead of hunting for every `100`. Unexplained numbers in code are called **magic numbers**, and code reviewers at most companies will ask you to name them.

### Naming conventions

Rust has firm naming conventions, and the compiler warns when you break them:

| Kind of name | Style | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| variables, functions | `snake_case` | `max_speed`, `player_name` |
| constants | `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` | `MAX_SPEED`, `TAX_RATE` |
| types (coming later) | `UpperCamelCase` | `Player`, `HashMap` |

```text
warning: variable `playerScore` should have a snake case name
 --> src/main.rs:2:9
  |
2 |     let playerScore = 10;
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^ help: convert the identifier to snake case: `player_score`
```

A **warning** doesn't stop the program from building, but treat warnings as things to fix: most teams make their automated checks (CI) fail on any warning. Names may contain letters, digits and `_`, but can't start with a digit.

### Unused variables and the _ prefix

If you declare a variable and never use it, rustc warns, because that's often a bug (you computed something and forgot to use it):

```text
warning: unused variable: `bonus`
 --> src/main.rs:3:9
  |
3 |     let bonus = 50;
  |         ^^^^^ help: if this is intentional, prefix it with an underscore: `_bonus`
```

Starting a name with `_` tells the compiler "I know this isn't used yet", which is handy while you're still writing the code. A lone `_` means "I don't need a name at all"; you'll meet it again in loops and patterns.

modules.summary: Rust's basic types up close. Integer sizes and what happens when they overflow, floating-point numbers, converting between types with as, true/false logic, and Unicode characters.

steps.title: Integer types and literals
steps.text:
In the last module, whole numbers were `i32`. Rust actually has a family of **integer** types. They differ in two ways: how many **bits** of memory they use (more bits, bigger range), and whether they're **signed** (can be negative, names start with `i`) or **unsigned** (zero or positive only, names start with `u`).

| Bits | Signed | Range | Unsigned | Range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | `i8` | -128 to 127 | `u8` | 0 to 255 |
| 16 | `i16` | -32,768 to 32,767 | `u16` | 0 to 65,535 |
| 32 | `i32` | about -2.1 to 2.1 billion | `u32` | 0 to about 4.3 billion |
| 64 | `i64` | about ±9.2 × 10¹⁸ | `u64` | 0 to about 1.8 × 10¹⁹ |
| 128 | `i128` | about ±1.7 × 10³⁸ | `u128` | 0 to about 3.4 × 10³⁸ |
| machine | `isize` | same as `i64` on 64-bit computers | `usize` | same as `u64` on 64-bit computers |

Every integer type knows its own limits, as the constants `MIN` and `MAX`:

```rust
fn main() {
    println!("u8:  {} to {}", u8::MIN, u8::MAX);
    println!("i8:  {} to {}", i8::MIN, i8::MAX);
    println!("i32: {} to {}", i32::MIN, i32::MAX);
    println!("u64 max: {}", u64::MAX);
}
```

```text
u8:  0 to 255
i8:  -128 to 127
i32: -2147483648 to 2147483647
u64 max: 18446744073709551615
```

`u8::MAX` means "the item called `MAX` that belongs to `u8`". The `::` is the **path separator**; you'll use it a lot.

### Which one should you use?

- `i32` is the default and a good general choice.
- Use an **unsigned** type when a negative value would be a bug: a quantity, a count, an age. The type then documents the rule and the compiler enforces it.
- `u8` for bytes (0 to 255, like the red, green and blue parts of a color).
- `i64`/`u64` when values can pass about 2 billion: money in cents, file sizes, milliseconds.
- `usize` for lengths and positions of things in memory. That's what `.len()` returns.

### Writing integer literals

A number typed into code is a **literal**, and Rust has several ways to write one:

```rust
fn main() {
    let population = 8_100_000_000_u64;
    let red = 0xff;
    let flags = 0b1010;
    let permissions = 0o755;
    let small = 200u8;
    println!("{population} {red} {flags} {permissions} {small}");
}
```

```text
8100000000 255 10 493 200
```

- `_` separates digits so they're easy to read; the compiler ignores it. `1_000_000` is one million.
- `0x` starts a **hexadecimal** number (base 16, digits 0-9 and a-f): `0xff` is 255. Common for colors and bytes.
- `0b` starts a **binary** number (base 2): `0b1010` is 10. `0o` starts an octal number (base 8), used for Unix file permissions.
- A **suffix** sets the type: `200u8` is a `u8`, `8_100_000_000_u64` a `u64`. Without the suffix, the population would be an `i32`, which can't hold 8.1 billion.

### Common mistakes

A literal that doesn't fit its type is an error:

```rust-error
fn main() {
    let level: u8 = 256;
    println!("{level}");
}
```

```compiler
error: literal out of range for `u8`
 --> src/main.rs:2:21
  |
2 |     let level: u8 = 256;
  |                     ^^^
```

- **A negative value in an unsigned type**: `let stock: u32 = -1;` gives `` error[E0600]: cannot apply unary operator `-` to type `u32` ``.
- **Mixing integer types**: if `a` is a `u32` and `b` an `i32`, `a + b` is `error[E0308]: mismatched types`. Rust never converts between number types silently; later in this module you'll learn to convert explicitly.

modules.title: Ownership
modules.summary: Where your data lives (stack and heap), who is responsible for freeing it, and why assigning a String moves it. The rules that make Rust memory-safe without a garbage collector.

steps.title: Stack and heap: where values live
steps.text:
Every value your program works with is stored somewhere in the computer's memory. To understand Rust's most famous feature, **ownership**, you first need a picture of the two places a running program keeps its data: the **stack** and the **heap**.

### The stack

The **stack** holds the local variables of the functions that are running right now. Each function call gets its own block of space, a **stack frame**, big enough for all of its variables. When the function returns, its whole frame is thrown away in one go. Making and removing frames is just moving a pointer up and down, so the stack is extremely fast.

The catch: everything on the stack must have a **size known at compile time**. An `i32` is always 4 bytes, an `f64` 8 bytes, an array `[i32; 3]` 12 bytes. The compiler lays out each frame before the program ever runs.

### The heap

What about text the user types in, or a list that grows while the program runs? Their size isn't known until run time, and it can change. That data goes on the **heap**: a big pool of memory where the program can ask for a block of any size while it runs. Asking for a block is called **allocating**. The **allocator** finds free space and hands back its address, a **pointer**. When the program is done with the block, it must give it back (**free** it) so the space can be reused.

A `String` uses both. The text lives on the heap. The `String` value itself is a small, fixed-size **handle** on the stack holding three numbers: a pointer to the text, its **length** (bytes in use) and its **capacity** (bytes reserved).

```text
fn main() {
    let lives = 3;
    let name = String::from("Ferris");
}

      STACK (main's frame)                     HEAP
     ┌───────┬──────────────────┐
     │ lives │ 3                │
     ├───────┼──────────────────┤          ┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐
     │ name  │ ptr  ────────────┼────────► │ F │ e │ r │ r │ i │ s │
     │       │ len       6      │          └───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘
     │       │ capacity  6      │
     └───────┴──────────────────┘
```

A `Vec` is built the same way: pointer, length and capacity on the stack, the elements on the heap. That's why both can grow: when they run out of capacity, they allocate a bigger block on the heap and move their contents there, while the handle on the stack keeps the same size.

You can check sizes with `std::mem::size_of::<T>()`, which tells you how many bytes a value of type `T` takes on the stack. The `::<T>` part names the type you're asking about. Since Rust 1.80, `size_of` is one of the few functions available everywhere without its full path, so you can also write just `size_of::<T>()`, as this example does.

```rust
fn main() {
    let short = String::from("hi");
    let long = String::from("a much longer piece of text");
    println!("i32: {} bytes", size_of::<i32>());
    println!("[i32; 3]: {} bytes", size_of::<[i32; 3]>());
    println!("String handle: {} bytes", size_of::<String>());
    println!("text on the heap: {} and {} bytes", short.len(), long.len());
}
```

```text
i32: 4 bytes
[i32; 3]: 12 bytes
String handle: 24 bytes
text on the heap: 2 and 27 bytes
```

The handle is 24 bytes (three 8-byte numbers on a 64-bit machine) whether the text is 2 bytes or 2 gigabytes. The text itself is somewhere else.

### Who cleans up the heap?

Stack memory cleans itself up when a function returns. Heap memory doesn't: something has to free each block, **exactly once**, **after** the last time it's used. Programming languages answer this in three ways:

| Approach | Languages | The catch |
|---|---|---|
| You free memory by hand | C, C++ (`malloc`/`free`, `new`/`delete`) | Forget it: a **memory leak**. Free twice: a **double free**. Use the memory after freeing it: a **use-after-free**. These bugs crash programs and are the classic source of security holes. |
| A **garbage collector** finds unused memory while the program runs | Java, Python, Go, JavaScript, C# | Safe, but it costs CPU time and memory, and can pause the program at moments you don't control. |
| **Ownership**: the compiler works out where to free, using rules it checks at compile time | Rust | You have to follow the rules. That's what this module teaches. |

Microsoft and Google's Chrome team have both reported that around 70% of their serious security bugs are memory-safety bugs like these. Rust's ownership rules make use-after-free and double free impossible in normal (safe) Rust, with no garbage collector and no run-time cost: the compiler inserts the code that frees memory exactly where it belongs.

### Common mistakes

- **Thinking a `String` holds its text inline.** It holds a *pointer* to the text. Copying the handle doesn't copy the text, which is exactly why the next steps matter.
- **Thinking string literals live on the heap.** `"hi"` is stored in the program's binary, read-only. `String::from("hi")` copies those bytes into a new heap block that the `String` is responsible for.
- **Mixing up length and capacity.** `.len()` is how many bytes are in use. The capacity is how many are reserved, so that pushing more text doesn't have to allocate every time.

steps.title: Moves: one owner at a time
steps.text:
Copying an integer is easy:

```rust
fn main() {
    let a = 5;
    let b = a;
    println!("a = {}, b = {}", a, b);
}
```

```text
a = 5, b = 5
```

`b` gets its own copy of the 4 bytes, and both variables can be used. Now try the same with a `String`:

```rust-error
fn main() {
    let s1 = String::from("hello");
    let s2 = s1;
    println!("{} {}", s1, s2);
}
```

```compiler
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s1`
 --> src/main.rs:4:23
  |
2 |     let s1 = String::from("hello");
  |         -- move occurs because `s1` has type `String`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
3 |     let s2 = s1;
  |              -- value moved here
4 |     println!("{} {}", s1, s2);
  |                       ^^ value borrowed here after move
```

What happened? `let s2 = s1;` copies the **handle** (pointer, length, capacity), not the heap text. If Rust stopped there, two variables would point at the same text:

```text
     s1                     s2
    ┌────────────┐         ┌────────────┐
    │ ptr ───────┼──┐   ┌──┼──── ptr    │
    │ len 5      │  │   │  │ len 5      │
    │ cap 5      │  │   │  │ cap 5      │
    └────────────┘  ▼   ▼  └────────────┘
                  ┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐
            HEAP  │ h │ e │ l │ l │ o │
                  └───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘
```

At the end of `main` both would be dropped, and the same heap block would be freed **twice**: a double free, one of the bugs that corrupt memory in C programs. Rule 2 forbids it: a value has one owner at a time. So `let s2 = s1;` **moves** ownership from `s1` to `s2`, and `s1` can't be used any more. Only `s2` will free the text.

```text
     s1  (moved out: unusable)        s2
    ┌────────────┐                   ┌────────────┐
    │ ░░░░░░░░░░ │                   │ ptr ───────┼──┐
    │ ░░░░░░░░░░ │                   │ len 5      │  │
    │ ░░░░░░░░░░ │                   │ cap 5      │  │
    └────────────┘                   └────────────┘  ▼
                                   ┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐
                             HEAP  │ h │ e │ l │ l │ o │
                                   └───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘
```

Read the error message again with that picture in mind. It names the type (`String`, which "does not implement the `Copy` trait": next step), the line where the value moved, and the line where you used it afterwards. It says "borrow" because `println!` *borrows* its arguments to print them; borrowing is the next module. The full message also suggests `.clone()`, which is one fix; step 4 covers when it's the right one.

A move is cheap: only the 24-byte handle is copied, however long the text is. Nothing on the heap is touched.

### Use the new owner

Usually the fix is to keep using the value through its new owner, or to finish with the old name before the move:

```rust
fn main() {
    let draft = String::from("Patch notes v1.2");
    println!("draft: {}", draft);       // use it before the move...
    let published = draft;              // ...ownership moves here
    println!("published: {}", published);
}
```

```text
draft: Patch notes v1.2
published: Patch notes v1.2
```

### Where moves happen

Any time a value that isn't `Copy` (like `String` and `Vec`, and most types you'll write) is handed to something else:

- assigning it: `let b = a;`
- passing it to a function (step 5)
- pushing it into a vector: `names.push(name);`
- looping over a vector with `for x in v`: the loop takes ownership of `v` and hands out its elements one by one. After the loop, `v` is gone.

```rust-error
fn main() {
    let names = vec![String::from("Ana"), String::from("Ben")];
    for name in names {
        println!("{}", name);
    }
    println!("{} names", names.len());
}
```

```compiler
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `names`
 --> src/main.rs:6:26
  |
3 |     for name in names {
  |                 ----- `names` moved due to this implicit call to `.into_iter()`
...
6 |     println!("{} names", names.len());
  |                          ^^^^^ value borrowed here after move
```

Fix it by finishing with `names` before the loop (`let count = names.len();`), or by looping over a reference with `for name in &names`, which the compiler suggests and which you'll learn in the next module.

### Reusing a moved-from variable

Moving out of a variable leaves it empty, not destroyed. If it's `mut`, you can give it a new value and use it again:

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut current = String::from("level 1");
    let finished = current;
    current = String::from("level 2");
    println!("finished {}, now playing {}", finished, current);
}
```

```text
finished level 1, now playing level 2
```

### Common mistakes

- **Using a value after moving it** (E0382). Find the "value moved here" line in the error, then use the new owner, or reorder so the old name is used first.
- **Moving inside a loop.** `let bag = item;` inside a loop moves `item` in the first round, so the next round fails with ``use of moved value: `item` `` and the note `value moved here, in previous iteration of loop`.
- **Thinking a move is expensive.** It copies three numbers. The text stays where it is.

steps.title: Copy types and clone
steps.text:
Why did `let b = a;` leave `a` usable when `a` was an integer? Because `i32` is a **`Copy` type**. Its value lives entirely on the stack and copying it is as cheap as moving it, so Rust just copies it and both variables stay valid. There's no heap block that could be freed twice. (A **trait** is a capability a type can have; you'll write your own in the traits module. `Copy` is the capability "can be duplicated by copying its bytes".)

These types are `Copy`:

- all integers (`i32`, `u8`, `usize`, ...) and floats (`f64`, `f32`)
- `bool` and `char`
- tuples and arrays made only of `Copy` types: `(i32, bool)`, `[f64; 3]`
- string literals (`&str`): copying one copies a pointer to text stored in the program, never the text itself

These are **not** `Copy`: `String`, `Vec<T>`, and anything that contains one, like `(String, i32)` or `[String; 2]`. The rule of thumb: **if a type owns heap memory, it isn't `Copy`**, because copying its handle would create two owners.

```rust
fn main() {
    let score = 1200;          // i32 is Copy
    let pos = (3, 4);          // a tuple of Copy types is Copy
    let best = score;
    let start = pos;
    println!("{} {}", score, best);
    println!("{:?} {:?}", pos, start);
}
```

```text
1200 1200
(3, 4) (3, 4)
```

One `String` inside a tuple is enough to make the whole tuple move:

```rust-error
fn main() {
    let player = (String::from("Ferris"), 100);
    let backup = player;
    println!("{:?} {:?}", player, backup);
}
```

```compiler
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `player`
  |
2 |     let player = (String::from("Ferris"), 100);
  |         ------ move occurs because `player` has type `(String, i32)`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
```

### clone: an explicit deep copy

When you really need two independent `String`s or `Vec`s, ask for one with `.clone()`. It allocates a **new** heap block and copies every byte into it:

```text
let a = String::from("hi");
let b = a.clone();

     a                              b
    ┌────────────┐                 ┌────────────┐
    │ ptr ───────┼──┐              │ ptr ───────┼──┐
    │ len 2      │  │              │ len 2      │  │
    │ cap 2      │  │              │ cap 2      │  │
    └────────────┘  ▼              └────────────┘  ▼
                  ┌───┬───┐                      ┌───┬───┐
            HEAP  │ h │ i │                      │ h │ i │
                  └───┴───┘                      └───┴───┘
```

Two owners, two heap blocks: each is freed once, by its own owner. Changing one doesn't affect the other:

```rust
fn main() {
    let defaults = vec![String::from("sound: on"), String::from("music: on")];
    let mut custom = defaults.clone();
    custom.push(String::from("subtitles: on"));
    println!("defaults: {:?}", defaults);
    println!("custom: {:?}", custom);
}
```

```text
defaults: ["sound: on", "music: on"]
custom: ["sound: on", "music: on", "subtitles: on"]
```

### What clone costs

Cloning a `String` means one allocation plus copying all of its bytes. Cloning a `Vec<String>` clones the vector **and every string in it**: here, three allocations. For a few short strings, nobody will notice. Inside a loop that runs a million times, or on the contents of a 50 MB file, you will. A move, by contrast, always copies just the 24-byte handle.

**Workplace note:** `.clone()` is the quickest way to make an ownership error go away, which is why reviewers ask "do we really need a copy here?" when they see one. Often the better answer is borrowing (next module). Clone when you truly need two independent values, for example when you'll change one and must keep the other as it was. Cloning a small string once is fine; don't feel bad about it. And `cargo clippy` warns about `.clone()` on a `Copy` type (the `clone_on_copy` lint): just write `x`.

### Common mistakes

- **Cloning to silence every error.** It compiles, but it hides a design question and costs memory and time.
- **Expecting a tuple or array with a `String` inside to be `Copy`.** It's only `Copy` if every part is.
- **Calling `.clone()` on an `i32` or `bool`.** It works, but it's noise: `Copy` types copy themselves.

steps.title: Ownership and collections
steps.text:
A `Vec` owns its elements. Pushing a `String` moves it into the vector, and when the vector is dropped, it drops every element first. Ownership forms a tree: `main` owns `roster`, `roster` owns its strings, and each string owns its text.

```text
  STACK              HEAP: roster's buffer             HEAP: each string's text
  roster            ┌──────────────────────┐
 ┌────────────┐     │ [0] ptr ─────────────┼─────────► "Ana"
 │ ptr ───────┼───► │     len 3   cap 3    │
 │ len 2      │     ├──────────────────────┤
 │ cap 4      │     │ [1] ptr ─────────────┼─────────► "Bartholomew"
 └────────────┘     │     len 11  cap 11   │
                    └──────────────────────┘
```

When `roster` goes out of scope, the whole tree is freed, each block exactly once, without a line of code from you.

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut roster: Vec<String> = Vec::new();
    let name = String::from("Ana");
    roster.push(name);                          // name moves into the Vec
    roster.push(String::from("Bartholomew"));
    println!("{} players: {:?}", roster.len(), roster);
}
```

```text
2 players: ["Ana", "Bartholomew"]
```

`Vec::new()` creates an empty vector, like `String::new()` does for text. The annotation `Vec<String>` says what it will hold (Rust could also work that out from the first `push`).

### You can't move out of an index

Taking an element by index is fine for `Copy` types: `let first = scores[0];` copies the number. With `String`s it doesn't compile:

```rust-error
fn main() {
    let names = vec![String::from("Ana"), String::from("Ben")];
    let first = names[0];
    println!("{} {}", first, names.len());
}
```

```compiler
error[E0507]: cannot move out of index of `Vec<String>`
 --> src/main.rs:3:17
  |
3 |     let first = names[0];
  |                 ^^^^^^^^ move occurs because value has type `String`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
  |
help: consider borrowing here
  |
3 |     let first = &names[0];
  |                 +
help: consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable
  |
3 |     let first = names[0].clone();
  |                         ++++++++
```

Why? Moving `names[0]` out would leave a hole: the vector would still believe it owns a string in slot 0 and would free it again when it's dropped. Rust refuses. The compiler's two suggestions are the real options:

- `names[0].clone()`: make your own copy; the vector keeps its string.
- `&names[0]`: borrow it without copying (next module).

And if you're done with the whole vector, a `for` loop moves every element out of it, one by one. That's allowed because the vector is used up as a whole:

```rust
fn main() {
    let names = vec![String::from("Ana"), String::from("Ben")];
    let captain = names[0].clone();     // our own copy
    for name in names {                 // moves each String out; names is gone after
        println!("player: {}", name);
    }
    println!("captain: {}", captain);
}
```

```text
player: Ana
player: Ben
captain: Ana
```

### Move, copy or clone?

| Situation | What to do |
|---|---|
| The value is a small `Copy` type (numbers, `bool`, `char`) | Nothing: it's copied automatically |
| You're done with the value and something else should own it now | **Move** it |
| You need two independent values that will change separately | **Clone** |
| Something only needs to read the value for a moment | **Borrow** it (next module) |

### Why this is worth it

Look at what these rules rule out, with no garbage collector and no run-time checks:

- **Double free**: a value has one owner, so its memory is freed once.
- **Use after free**: memory is freed only when its owner's scope ends, and using a moved-from variable doesn't compile.
- **Forgotten frees**: every value is dropped when its owner goes out of scope, so you can't leak memory by forgetting a `free`.
- **Data races** (two threads changing the same data at once): the one-owner idea, extended by the borrowing rules of the next module, stops them at compile time. You'll see it in the threads module.

C++ has the same idea in `std::unique_ptr` and move semantics, but its compiler lets you keep using a moved-from object. Rust checks it.

### Common mistakes

- **`let x = v[i];` with a `Vec<String>`** (E0507): clone it, or borrow it.
- **Using a `String` after pushing it into a vector** (E0382): use it before the push, or reach it through the vector afterwards (`println!("{}", v[0])` only borrows it, which is fine).
- **Looping with `for x in v` and then using `v`** (E0382).

modules.title: Borrowing
modules.summary: Use a value without taking ownership of it. References (&T and &mut T), the "many readers or one writer" rule, and how the borrow checker makes dangling pointers and data races impossible.

steps.title: References: borrowing a value
steps.text:
The ownership module ended with an awkward pattern: to let a function look at a `String`, you had to move it in and get it back in a tuple. Real Rust code almost never does that. Instead, it lends the function a **reference**.

A **reference** is a pointer to a value that someone else owns. You make one with `&`: `&msg` means "a reference to `msg`". The type of a reference to a `String` is `&String`. Making a reference is called **borrowing**: you get to use the value, but you don't own it, so you never drop it, and the owner still has it afterwards.

```rust
fn char_count(text: &String) -> usize {   // borrows a String
    text.chars().count()
}                                          // text goes away, but it owned nothing: nothing is dropped

fn main() {
    let msg = String::from("good game");
    let n = char_count(&msg);              // lend msg to the function
    println!("'{}' has {} characters", msg, n);   // msg is still ours
}
```

```text
'good game' has 9 characters
```

Compare it with the tuple version from the ownership module: no giving back, no shadowing. In memory, the reference is just one more pointer, pointing at the owner:

```text
   char_count's frame          main's frame
   text                        msg
  ┌────────────┐              ┌────────────┐          HEAP
  │ ptr ───────┼────────────► │ ptr ───────┼─────► ┌───┬───┬───┬─ ─ ─┬───┐
  └────────────┘              │ len 9      │       │ g │ o │ o │ ... │ e │
                              │ cap 9      │       └───┴───┴───┴─ ─ ─┴───┘
                              └────────────┘
```

When `char_count` returns, `text` disappears. It was only a borrow, so the `String` isn't dropped: `msg` is still its owner.

### Reading through a reference

Method calls and `println!` work through references automatically: `text.chars()`, `text.len()` and `println!("{}", text)` all reach the `String` behind the reference. You don't need any extra syntax to *read* through a `&`.

You can borrow in a `let` and in a `for` loop too. `for x in &v` loops over a vector **without moving it**: each `x` is a reference to one element.

```rust
fn main() {
    let names = vec![String::from("Ana"), String::from("Ben")];
    for name in &names {              // borrow the vector: name is a &String
        println!("hello, {}", name);
    }
    println!("{} names, still ours", names.len());
    let first = &names[0];            // borrow one element: no clone needed
    println!("first: {}", first);
}
```

```text
hello, Ana
hello, Ben
2 names, still ours
first: Ana
```

Those are exactly the fixes the compiler suggested for the loop and index errors in the ownership module. With a `Vec<i32>` or `Vec<f64>`, each `x` in `for x in &v` is a `&i32` or `&f64`, and arithmetic accepts those directly: `sum += x` works.

You've been using one kind of reference since your first program: string literals. Their type, `&str`, is a reference to text stored in the program itself. The slices module covers `&str` properly; for now, it's the type to write for a parameter that receives a string literal.

### Common mistakes

- **Passing the value instead of a reference.** If the function takes `&String` and you pass `msg`, the types don't match:

```rust-error
fn char_count(text: &String) -> usize {
    text.chars().count()
}

fn main() {
    let msg = String::from("gg");
    println!("{}", char_count(msg));
}
```

```compiler
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:7:31
  |
7 |     println!("{}", char_count(msg));
  |                    ---------- ^^^ expected `&String`, found `String`
  |
help: consider borrowing here
  |
7 |     println!("{}", char_count(&msg));
  |                               +
```

- **Trying to change a value through a `&` reference.** Plain references are read-only. The next step shows how to lend something for changing.
- **Taking ownership when you only need to read.** If a function only looks at a value, its parameter should be a reference.

modules.title: Slices
modules.summary: Borrow part of a string, array or vector without copying it. String slices (&str), array and vector slices (&[T] and &mut [T]), and why &str and &[T] are the parameter types experienced Rust programmers reach for.

steps.title: String slices
steps.text:
You often need part of a string: the first word of a command, the domain of an email address, the date at the start of a log line. Copying that part into a new `String` would work, but it costs an allocation every time. A **slice** lets you refer to part of a string without copying anything.

`&s[start..end]` is a **string slice**: a reference to the bytes of `s` from index `start` up to, but **not including**, `end`. Its type is `&str`.

```rust
fn main() {
    let line = String::from("2024-05-17 ERROR disk full");
    let date = &line[0..10];
    let level = &line[11..16];
    let message = &line[17..];
    println!("date: {}", date);
    println!("level: {}", level);
    println!("message: {}", message);
}
```

```text
date: 2024-05-17
level: ERROR
message: disk full
```

A slice is a reference made of two numbers: a pointer to its first byte and a length. (It's sometimes called a **fat pointer**, because it's twice the size of a plain reference.) It points straight into the `String`'s heap text:

```text
                                       0         1         2
                                       01234567890123456789012345
 line: String  ┌────────────┐
               │ ptr ───────┼───────►  2024-05-17 ERROR disk full   (heap)
               │ len 26     │          ▲          ▲
               │ cap 26     │          │          │
               └────────────┘          │          │
 date: &str    ┌────────────┐          │          │
               │ ptr ───────┼──────────┘          │
               │ len 10     │                     │
               └────────────┘                     │
 level: &str   ┌────────────┐                     │
               │ ptr ───────┼─────────────────────┘
               │ len 5      │
               └────────────┘
```

Nothing was copied: `date` and `level` **borrow** from `line`, with all the borrowing rules you know. While they're in use, `line` can't be changed or moved.

### Range shorthand

| You write | You get |
|---|---|
| `&s[2..5]` | bytes 2, 3 and 4 |
| `&s[..5]` | from the start up to (not including) 5 |
| `&s[6..]` | from byte 6 to the end |
| `&s[..]` | the whole string |
| `&s[2..=4]` | bytes 2 to 4, including 4 |

It's the same range syntax as in `for` loops.

### Indexes count bytes, not characters

Slice indexes are **byte** positions. For plain ASCII text (English letters, digits, common punctuation), one character is one byte, so it's what you'd expect. But characters like `é`, `ü` or `🦀` take 2 to 4 bytes in UTF-8, and a slice must start and end on a character boundary. If it doesn't, the program panics:

```rust
fn main() {
    let word = String::from("héllo");
    println!("{} bytes", word.len());
    println!("{}", &word[0..2]);
}
```

```text
6 bytes
```

The panic message explains it: `end byte index 2 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 1..3 of string)`. A slice past the end panics too (`&line[0..50]` on a 26-byte string), just like an array index out of bounds.

This is also why `s[0]` doesn't compile for strings: ``error[E0277]: the type `str` cannot be indexed by `{integer}` ``. Byte 0 might be only part of a character. The strings module shows how to walk through characters properly.

### Common mistakes

- **Off by one**: `end` is exclusive. `&s[0..4]` is 4 bytes: indexes 0, 1, 2 and 3.
- **Slicing user text at fixed byte positions.** It works for ASCII but panics on accents or emoji.
- **Expecting a slice to be a `String`.** `&s[1..3]` is a `&str`. If you need an owned copy, call `.to_string()` on it. Assigning it to a `String` variable directly gives ``error[E0308]: mismatched types`` (``expected `String`, found `&str` ``).

steps.title: &str: the type for text parameters
steps.text:
Now you can see what string literals really are. A literal like `"hello"` is stored in the program's binary, and the value you get is a **slice** pointing at it: that's why its type is `&str`, and why it's read-only. (Its full type is `&'static str`: a borrow that's valid for the whole run of the program. More on that in the lifetimes module.)

So text comes in three shapes: an owned `String`, a slice of a `String`, and a literal. A function that takes `&String` only accepts the first. A function that takes **`&str`** accepts all three, because Rust automatically turns a `&String` into a `&str` covering the whole text. This automatic conversion is called **deref coercion**.

```rust
fn shout(text: &str) -> String {
    text.to_uppercase()
}

fn main() {
    let owned = String::from("ferris wins");
    println!("{}", shout(&owned));        // &String becomes &str automatically
    println!("{}", shout(&owned[7..]));   // a slice of it
    println!("{}", shout("gg"));          // a literal
}
```

```text
FERRIS WINS
WINS
GG
```

With a `&String` parameter, the literal doesn't fit:

```rust-error
fn shout(text: &String) -> String {
    text.to_uppercase()
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", shout("gg"));
}
```

```compiler
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:6:26
  |
6 |     println!("{}", shout("gg"));
  |                    ----- ^^^^ expected `&String`, found `&str`
```

### Prefer &str over &String

**Workplace note:** for a parameter that only reads text, write `&str`. It accepts more kinds of argument and loses nothing: every method that reads text (`len`, `chars`, `contains`, `to_uppercase`, `trim`, ...) is a `str` method, which `String` just makes available. Clippy flags `&String` parameters with its `ptr_arg` lint ("writing `&String` instead of `&str` involves a new object where a slice will do"). Take an owned `String` only when the function keeps the text, for example to store it in a vector.

| | `String` | `&str` |
|---|---|---|
| Owns its text? | yes | no, borrows it |
| Can grow or change? | yes (if `mut`) | no |
| Where the text is | its own heap block | anywhere: a `String`'s heap block, or the program's binary |
| Size of the value | 24 bytes (pointer, length, capacity) | 16 bytes (pointer, length) |
| Get the other one | `&s`, `&s[..]` or `s.as_str()` | `s.to_string()` or `String::from(s)` |

### Methods that return slices

Several `str` methods hand you slices of the original text instead of new strings. `trim()` returns the part without the spaces at both ends, as a `&str` pointing into the original:

```rust
fn main() {
    let input = String::from("   add milk   ");
    let cleaned: &str = input.trim();      // a slice of input: nothing copied
    println!("[{}] {} bytes", input, input.len());
    println!("[{}] {} bytes", cleaned, cleaned.len());
}
```

```text
[   add milk   ] 14 bytes
[add milk] 8 bytes
```

`split_whitespace()`, which you used for reading input, works the same way: each word it gives you is a `&str` slice of the original line. No copies.

### Common mistakes

- **`&String` parameters.** They work, but they force every caller to have a `String`. Use `&str`.
- **Trying to change a `&str`.** It's a read-only view. To build or change text, use a `String`.
- **Returning a `&str` that points into a `String` created inside the function** (E0515 from the borrowing module). Return the `String`.

steps.title: Array and Vec slices: &[T]
steps.text:
Slices aren't only for text. `&v[1..3]` is a slice of a vector or array: its type is `&[T]` (for example `&[i32]`), a pointer to the first element plus a count of elements.

```rust
fn main() {
    let temps = vec![14, 17, 21, 19, 16, 12, 10];
    let weekdays = &temps[..5];
    let weekend = &temps[5..];
    println!("weekdays {:?}, weekend {:?}", weekdays, weekend);
    println!("{} + {} days", weekdays.len(), weekend.len());
}
```

```text
weekdays [14, 17, 21, 19, 16], weekend [12, 10]
5 + 2 days
```

```text
 temps: Vec<i32>  ┌────────────┐
                  │ ptr ───────┼───────►  [14, 17, 21, 19, 16, 12, 10]   (heap)
                  │ len 7      │           ▲                   ▲
                  │ cap 7      │           │                   │
                  └────────────┘           │                   │
 weekdays: &[i32] ┌────────────┐           │                   │
                  │ ptr ───────┼───────────┘                   │
                  │ len 5      │                               │
                  └────────────┘                               │
 weekend: &[i32]  ┌────────────┐                               │
                  │ ptr ───────┼───────────────────────────────┘
                  │ len 2      │
                  └────────────┘
```

### Functions that take &[T]

A `&[T]` parameter accepts a vector, an array, or any part of either. A `&Vec<T>` turns into a `&[T]` automatically, just like `&String` turns into `&str`:

```rust
fn total(values: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    let mut sum = 0;
    for v in values {
        sum += v;
    }
    sum
}

fn main() {
    let week = vec![3, 5, 2, 8, 6, 1, 0];
    let fixed = [10, 20, 30];
    println!("{}", total(&week));         // &Vec<i32> becomes &[i32]
    println!("{}", total(&week[..5]));    // part of it
    println!("{}", total(&fixed));        // an array
    println!("{}", total(&[]));           // an empty slice
}
```

```text
25
24
60
0
```

**Workplace note:** it's the same advice as for text: **prefer `&[T]` over `&Vec<T>`** for parameters (clippy's `ptr_arg` lint again). `&str` is to `String` what `&[T]` is to `Vec<T>`: a borrowed view that doesn't care who owns the data.

What you can do with a `&[T]`:

- `.len()` and `.is_empty()`
- index it, `s[i]`, and slice it again, `&s[a..b]`
- loop over it: `for x in s` gives a `&T` for each element
- `s.contains(&x)`: is `x` in it?
- `s.split_at(i)`: two slices, before and after `i`

```rust
fn main() {
    let scores = [88, 92, 75, 64, 99, 81];
    let (first_half, second_half) = scores.split_at(3);
    println!("{:?} | {:?}", first_half, second_half);
    println!("has a 99: {}", scores.contains(&99));
}
```

```text
[88, 92, 75] | [64, 99, 81]
has a 99: true
```

### Common mistakes

- **`&Vec<T>` parameters.** They work, but callers with an array or a part of a vector can't use them. Take `&[T]`.
- **Passing the vector instead of a reference**: ``error[E0308]: mismatched types`` (``expected `&[i32]`, found `Vec<{integer}>` ``) with the help `consider borrowing here`.
- **Moving out of a slice**: `let first = names[0];` with a `&[String]` is ``error[E0508]: cannot move out of type `[String]`, a non-copy slice``. As with vectors, borrow (`&names[0]`) or clone.
- **Out-of-range slices panic**, like out-of-range indexes: `&v[3..10]` on a 5-element vector.

steps.title: Nested enums and ignoring parts
steps.text:
Patterns nest exactly as deep as your data does. An enum variant can hold a struct-like set of fields, and those fields can hold other enums; one pattern can look at all of it.

```rust
enum Button {
    Left,
    Right,
}

enum Event {
    Key(char),
    Click { x: i32, y: i32, button: Button },
    Scroll(i32),
    Quit,
}

fn handle(event: &Event) -> String {
    match event {
        Event::Key('q') | Event::Quit => String::from("quit"),
        Event::Key(c @ '0'..='9') => format!("digit {c}"),
        Event::Key(c) => format!("key {c}"),
        Event::Click { button: Button::Right, .. } => String::from("open menu"),
        Event::Click { x, y, button: Button::Left } => format!("left click at ({x}, {y})"),
        Event::Scroll(0) => String::from("no scroll"),
        Event::Scroll(n) if *n > 0 => format!("scroll down {n}"),
        Event::Scroll(n) => format!("scroll up {}", -n),
    }
}

fn main() {
    let events = [
        Event::Key('7'),
        Event::Key('w'),
        Event::Click { x: 10, y: 20, button: Button::Left },
        Event::Click { x: 5, y: 5, button: Button::Right },
        Event::Scroll(-3),
        Event::Scroll(4),
        Event::Key('q'),
        Event::Quit,
    ];
    for e in &events {
        println!("{}", handle(e));
    }
}
```

```text
digit 7
key w
left click at (10, 20)
open menu
scroll up 3
scroll down 4
quit
quit
```

Piece by piece:

- `Event::Key('q') | Event::Quit` combines a variant with a literal inside it and another variant, with `|`.
- `Event::Click { button: Button::Right, .. }` looks *inside* the click at its `button` field and checks it's `Button::Right`. The `..` ignores `x` and `y`.
- `Event::Click { x, y, button: Button::Left }` binds `x` and `y` and requires a left button.
- `Event::Scroll(n) if *n > 0`: since `handle` takes `&Event`, `n` is a `&i32`. Comparing needs the number itself, so the guard says `*n`. Printing works on the reference directly.
- The compiler checks the whole nested structure for exhaustiveness: remove the `Button::Left` arm and it tells you that `&Event::Click { button: Button::Left, .. }` isn't covered (with a `&`, because `handle` matches on a reference).

### `_`, `_name` and `..`

| Pattern | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `_` | match one value, don't bind it (nothing is moved or borrowed) |
| `_name` | bind the value (it **is** moved or borrowed) but don't warn if it's unused |
| `..` | skip all remaining fields or elements |

### Common mistake: moving out while matching

Matching on an owned value with a binding moves the data out of it:

```rust-error
fn main() {
    let name: Option<String> = Some(String::from("Ferris"));
    match name {
        Some(n) => println!("hi {n}"),
        None => println!("nobody"),
    }
    println!("{:?}", name);
}
```

```compiler
error[E0382]: borrow of partially moved value: `name`
```

`Some(n)` moved the String into `n`, so `name` is no longer whole. Match on a reference instead (`match &name`), and `n` becomes a `&String`. If you don't need the value at all, `Some(_)` doesn't move anything.

steps.title: Monomorphization: generics cost nothing at run time
steps.text:
How can one `largest` function work on `i32`s, `f64`s and `char`s, which have different sizes and are compared by different machine instructions? The compiler doesn't keep one flexible version. For every concrete type you actually use, it generates a separate copy of the generic code with `T` filled in, as if you had written `largest_i32`, `largest_f64` and `largest_char` yourself. This is called **monomorphization** ("making into a single form").

You can watch it happen. `std::any::type_name::<T>()` returns the name of whatever `T` is in the copy that's running:

```rust
fn describe<T: std::fmt::Debug>(value: T) -> String {
    format!("{} = {:?}", std::any::type_name::<T>(), value)
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", describe(42));
    println!("{}", describe(2.5));
    println!("{}", describe('z'));
    println!("{}", describe("crab"));
    println!("{}", describe(7u8));
    println!("{}", describe::<i64>(7));
}
```

```text
i32 = 42
f64 = 2.5
char = 'z'
&str = "crab"
u8 = 7
i64 = 7
```

This program contains six versions of `describe`: for `i32`, `f64`, `char`, `&str`, `u8` and `i64`. (`std::fmt::Debug` is written out in full here instead of with a `use` line; both work.)

### Zero-cost abstraction

Because each copy is specialized, generic code runs exactly as fast as the hand-written versions would: no checking types at run time, no extra indirection. Rust people call this a **zero-cost abstraction**: you pay nothing at run time for writing the code once.

The cost is paid at compile time instead: every copy has to be compiled, and the program file gets bigger. In large projects heavy generic code can noticeably slow down builds. The alternative is **dynamic dispatch**, which you've already met in `Box<dyn Error>`: one copy of the code, and a small run-time lookup to find the right method. Module 25 compares the two.

### The turbofish: ::<>

Usually the compiler infers `T` from the arguments. When it can't, or when you want a different type, write it explicitly with `::<Type>`, nicknamed the **turbofish**:

- `describe::<i64>(7)`: without it, `7` would be an `i32`.
- `"42".parse::<u32>()`: `parse` can produce many types, and nothing else says which.
- `Vec::<String>::new()`: an empty `Vec` has no elements to infer from.
- `std::mem::size_of::<u64>()`: a function with a type parameter and no arguments at all.

### Common mistakes

- **Nothing to infer the type from.** `parse` needs to know its target type:

```rust-error
fn main() {
    let n = "42".parse().unwrap();
    println!("{n}");
}
```

```compiler
error[E0284]: type annotations needed
```

Fix it with `"42".parse::<u32>()` or `let n: u32 = ...`.

- **Thinking generics are slow.** It's the opposite: generic code is specialized for each type. If you hear "use `dyn` instead of generics for speed", it's backwards; `dyn` trades a little speed for less compiled code.
- **The turbofish on the wrong name.** It goes right after the generic function or type: `parse::<u32>()`, not `parse()::<u32>`.

(The `(u8, u32)` tuple takes 8 bytes, not 5: the compiler adds padding so the `u32` sits at a position divisible by 4, where the processor reads it fastest.)

steps.title: Deriving the standard traits
steps.text:
Many standard traits have one obvious implementation: compare the fields one by one, copy every field, print every field. For those, `#[derive(...)]` writes the `impl` for you. You've used `#[derive(Debug)]` since the structs module; here's the whole family.

| Derive | What you get | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| `Debug` | `{:?}` and `{:#?}` | every field is `Debug` |
| `Clone` | `.clone()`, a deep copy | every field is `Clone` |
| `Copy` | values are copied instead of moved | `Clone`, and every field is `Copy` (no `String`, no `Vec`) |
| `PartialEq` | `==` and `!=`, field by field | every field is `PartialEq` |
| `Eq` | a promise that `x == x` is always true | `PartialEq`; not possible with `f64` fields (NaN != NaN) |
| `Hash` | can be a `HashMap` key or in a `HashSet` | usually derived together with `Eq` |
| `PartialOrd` | `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` | `PartialEq` |
| `Ord` | `.sort()`, `.max()`, `BTreeMap` keys | `Eq` and `PartialOrd` |
| `Default` | `Type::default()`: zeros, `false`, empty strings and vectors | every field is `Default` |

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, PartialOrd, Ord)]
enum Priority {
    Low,
    Medium,
    High,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
struct Ticket {
    priority: Priority,
    id: u32,
}

#[derive(Debug, Default)]
struct Settings {
    volume: u8,
    muted: bool,
    nickname: String,
}

fn main() {
    let mut tickets = vec![
        Ticket { priority: Priority::High, id: 7 },
        Ticket { priority: Priority::Low, id: 3 },
        Ticket { priority: Priority::High, id: 2 },
    ];
    tickets.sort();
    for t in &tickets {
        println!("{:?} #{}", t.priority, t.id);
    }

    let p = Priority::Medium;
    let q = p; // Copy: p is still usable
    println!("{} {}", p == q, Priority::High > Priority::Low);
    let s = Settings::default();
    println!("volume {}, muted {}, nickname {:?}", s.volume, s.muted, s.nickname);
}
```

```text
Low #3
High #2
High #7
true true
volume 0, muted false, nickname ""
```

How derived comparisons work:

- **Structs** compare field by field **in the order the fields are written**: first `priority`, and only if those are equal, `id`. That's why the two High tickets end up sorted by id. Reordering the fields changes the sort order.
- **Enums** compare by the order the variants are written: `Low < Medium < High`. Put variants in a meaningful order and sorting comes for free.

### Which ones should you derive?

Derive `Debug` on almost everything: error messages and `dbg!` need it, and tests need it for `assert_eq!`. For small value types (ids, coordinates, enums without data), `Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash` is a common set. Libraries derive every standard trait that makes sense for a type, because users of the library can't add them later (the orphan rule). Don't derive what doesn't make sense: `Copy` on a big struct hides expensive copies, and `Default` for a type with no sensible empty value invites bugs.

### Common mistakes

- **`Copy` with a `String` field.** A `String` owns heap memory, so it can't be copied bit by bit:

```rust-error
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Player {
    name: String,
    hp: u32,
}

fn main() {}
```

```compiler
error[E0204]: the trait `Copy` cannot be implemented for this type
```

- **`Eq` or `Ord` with an `f64` field**: ``error[E0277]: the trait bound `f64: Eq` is not satisfied``. Floats only have `PartialEq`/`PartialOrd`. Store cents as an integer, or compare floats by hand.
- **Deriving `Copy` without `Clone`, or `Ord` without `PartialOrd` and `Eq`.** Each needs the traits listed in its "Needs" column. The error names the missing one.
- **Expecting `derive(Display)`.** It doesn't exist; there's no single obvious way to show a type to users. Write it by hand (previous step).

steps.title: Reading lifetime errors
steps.text:
Lifetime errors look scary but come in a handful of shapes, and each shape has a short list of fixes. Here's the field guide.

| Error | What it means | Usual fixes |
|---|---|---|
| `E0106` missing lifetime specifier | A signature or struct returns/holds a reference, and elision can't tell where from. | Add `'a` to tie the output to the right inputs; or return owned data; or `'static` for literals. |
| `E0597` `x` does not live long enough | A value is dropped while a reference to it is still used later. | Move the value to an outer scope; use the reference earlier; own the data. |
| `E0515` cannot return reference to local variable | A function returns a reference to something it created. | Return the owned value (`String`, `Vec`). |
| `E0716` temporary value dropped while borrowed | You borrowed from a value that was never stored in a variable. | Store it in a `let` first. |
| lifetime may not live long enough | A function's body returns a reference with a different lifetime than its signature promised. | Fix the signature (often rule 3 guessed `self`), or return what it promises. |
| `E0499` / `E0502` borrow conflicts | Two borrows overlap (borrowing module). With methods: often a result tied to `&mut self` that should be tied to `'a`. | Shorter borrows; return `&'a T` from the data, not from `self`. |

The temporary one deserves an example, because it surprises everyone once:

```rust-error
fn main() {
    let label = format!("v{}", 2).as_str();
    println!("{label}");
}
```

```compiler
error[E0716]: temporary value dropped while borrowed
 --> src/main.rs:2:17
  |
2 |     let label = format!("v{}", 2).as_str();
  |                 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^         - temporary value is freed at the end of this statement
  |                 |
  |                 creates a temporary value which is freed while still in use
3 |     println!("{label}");
  |                ----- borrow later used here
  |
  = note: consider using a `let` binding to create a longer lived value
```

The `String` from `format!` has no owner variable, so it's dropped at the `;`. The fix is in the note: give it an owner first (or just use the `String`).

```rust
fn main() {
    let owned = format!("v{}", 2);
    let label = owned.as_str();
    println!("{label}");
}
```

```text
v2
```

### A method for any lifetime error

1. **Find the value** the error is about (the name in backticks).
2. **Find where it's dropped**: the label `dropped here while still borrowed`, or the end of a function for E0515.
3. **Find the late use**: `borrow later used here`.
4. **Pick a fix**: make the owner live longer, end the use sooner, own the data, or (for signatures) describe the real relationship with `'a`.

Resist adding annotations at random until it compiles. Each error describes a real dangling reference that would have crashed or corrupted data in C. Once you see *which* value would dangle, the fix is usually one line.

steps.title: Closures at work: sorting, filtering, defaults
steps.text:
Most closures you'll write at work are tiny arguments to standard library methods. You've used several of these methods already; now you know what they take.

```rust
struct Ticket {
    id: u32,
    title: String,
    priority: u8,
    open: bool,
}

fn main() {
    let mut tickets = vec![
        Ticket { id: 7, title: String::from("Login fails"), priority: 1, open: true },
        Ticket { id: 3, title: String::from("Typo on homepage"), priority: 3, open: true },
        Ticket { id: 9, title: String::from("Old bug"), priority: 2, open: false },
        Ticket { id: 4, title: String::from("Slow search"), priority: 1, open: true },
    ];

    tickets.retain(|t| t.open);                  // keep only open tickets
    tickets.sort_by_key(|t| (t.priority, t.id)); // by priority, then by id

    for t in &tickets {
        println!("#{} [P{}] {}", t.id, t.priority, t.title);
    }

    let top = tickets.first().map(|t| t.title.to_uppercase());
    println!("{}", top.unwrap_or_else(|| String::from("nothing to do")));
}
```

```text
#4 [P1] Slow search
#7 [P1] Login fails
#3 [P3] Typo on homepage
SLOW SEARCH
```

| Method | The closure gets | and returns | Bound |
|---|---|---|---|
| `v.retain(f)` | `&T` | `bool`: keep this element? | `FnMut` |
| `v.sort_by_key(f)` | `&T` | a key to sort by (anything `Ord`: numbers, tuples, `String`s) | `FnMut` |
| `v.sort_by(f)` | `&T, &T` | an `Ordering`, usually from `a.cmp(b)` | `FnMut` |
| `opt.map(f)` | the value inside `Some` | the new value | `FnOnce` |
| `opt.unwrap_or_else(f)` | nothing | the fallback value | `FnOnce` |
| `map.entry(k).or_insert_with(f)` | nothing | the value to insert | `FnOnce` |

Tricks worth knowing:

- **Several sort keys**: a tuple key `(t.priority, t.id)` sorts by the first field, then breaks ties with the second.
- **Descending order**: swap `a` and `b`: `v.sort_by(|a, b| b.score.cmp(&a.score))`.
- **Combining comparisons**: `Ordering` has `.then(...)`: `b.score.cmp(&a.score).then(a.name.cmp(&b.name))` means "highest score first, and for equal scores, by name".
- **Lazy defaults**: `unwrap_or(expensive())` always runs `expensive()`; `unwrap_or_else(|| expensive())` only runs it when the value is missing. Clippy's `or_fun_call` lint points this out (it's off by default; turn on the `clippy::nursery` group to get it).
- **Function names instead of closures**: when a closure only calls a function, pass the function itself: `map.entry(key).or_insert_with(Vec::new)` instead of `|| Vec::new()`. Clippy's `redundant_closure` lint suggests this.

### Common mistakes

- **A sort key that borrows from the element.** `sort_by_key` can't return a reference into the elements it's moving around:

```rust-error
struct Player {
    name: String,
    score: u32,
}

fn main() {
    let mut players = vec![
        Player { name: String::from("Zed"), score: 3 },
        Player { name: String::from("Amy"), score: 5 },
    ];
    players.sort_by_key(|p| &p.name);
    println!("{} {}", players[0].name, players[0].score);
}
```

```compiler
error: lifetime may not live long enough
```

Use `players.sort_by(|a, b| a.name.cmp(&b.name))` instead (no copies), or `sort_by_key(|p| p.name.clone())` (allocates a String per comparison).

- **Sorting by an `f64` key.** Floats aren't `Ord` (what's the order of `NaN`?), so `sort_by_key(|i| i.price)` fails with ``the trait bound `f64: Ord` is not satisfied``. Use `sort_by(|a, b| a.price.total_cmp(&b.price))`: `total_cmp` gives floats a complete order.

hints: `players.retain(|p| p.score >= min_score);` keeps the good ones.

steps.title: Combining iterators: enumerate, zip, chain, flat_map, windows
steps.task: Write `fn number_lines(lines: &[&str]) -> Vec<String>` that returns `"N: line"` for every line that isn't blank, where `N` is the line's number in the original list (starting at 1). Blank lines (empty, or only spaces) are skipped but still **count** for the numbering. For example `["fn main() {", "", "}"]` gives `["1: fn main() {", "3: }"]`. No loops.
steps.solution:
fn number_lines(lines: &[&str]) -> Vec<String> {
    lines
        .iter()
        .enumerate()
        .filter(|(_, line)| !line.trim().is_empty())
        .map(|(i, line)| format!("{}: {line}", i + 1))
        .collect()
}
hints: `enumerate` has to come **before** the `filter`, so the numbers belong to the original positions.
`.enumerate().filter(|(_, line)| !line.trim().is_empty()).map(|(i, line)| format!("{}: {line}", i + 1))`

require.message: Number the lines with `.enumerate()`.

forbid.message: Use `enumerate`, `filter`, `map` and `collect`, no loops.

steps.title: Cargo: dependencies, versions, features, workspaces
steps.text:
Real projects stand on other people's code. **crates.io** is Rust's public registry of crates, and **Cargo** downloads, builds and links them for you. You list what you need in `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[package]
name = "inventory"
version = "0.3.1"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
regex = "1.11"
itertools = "0.14"
```

- `cargo add regex` adds the line for you (with the newest version); `cargo remove regex` takes it out.
- On the first build, Cargo picks exact versions and writes them to **Cargo.lock**, so every build (yours, your teammates', CI's) uses the same code. Commit `Cargo.lock`. `cargo update` moves to newer compatible versions on purpose.
- In code, a dependency's crate name is the start of a path, like `std`: `use regex::Regex;`. Dashes become underscores: package `serde_json` is `serde_json::`, package `my-utils` would be `my_utils::`.

This site's compiler has a few popular crates available, as if they were in your `Cargo.toml` (serde, serde_json, anyhow, thiserror, tokio, regex, itertools, rayon, chrono). For example, `itertools` adds extra iterator methods:

```rust
use itertools::Itertools;

fn main() {
    let scores = vec![30, 10, 20, 10];
    let line = scores.iter().sorted().dedup().join(" < ");
    println!("{line}");
}
```

```text
10 < 20 < 30
```

`use itertools::Itertools;` brings a **trait** into scope. A trait's methods can only be called where the trait is in scope; that's why crates offer preludes, and why forgetting the `use` gives "no method named `sorted` found".

### Semantic versioning

Crate versions are **MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH**, and the numbers carry a promise (**semver**):

- **PATCH** (1.4.2 to 1.4.3): bug fixes only.
- **MINOR** (1.4.2 to 1.5.0): new features, nothing breaks.
- **MAJOR** (1.4.2 to 2.0.0): breaking changes; your code may need updating.
- Before 1.0, the first non-zero number acts as the major: 0.14 to 0.15 may break things.

In `Cargo.toml`, `regex = "1.11"` doesn't mean exactly 1.11. It's a **caret requirement** (`^1.11`): any version that semver says is compatible.

| Requirement | Allows |
|---|---|
| `"1.11.2"` (same as `"^1.11.2"`) | `>= 1.11.2` and `< 2.0.0` |
| `"0.14"` | `>= 0.14.0` and `< 0.15.0` |
| `"0.0.3"` | exactly `0.0.3` |
| `"~1.11.2"` (tilde) | `>= 1.11.2` and `< 1.12.0` |
| `"=1.11.2"` | exactly `1.11.2` (rarely a good idea) |

Cargo uses **one** version per semver-compatible range in a build: if two of your dependencies need `regex 1.9` and `regex 1.11`, both get the newest 1.x. Incompatible majors (`1.x` and `2.x`) can live side by side. As a **library author**, the promise is on you: removing a `pub` item, changing a public function's signature or adding a field to a public struct whose fields are all `pub` (users build it with a struct literal, which now misses a field) is a breaking change that needs a new major version. `cargo-semver-checks` can catch these before you publish.

### Features

**Features** are optional parts of a crate that you switch on. `serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }` turns on serde's derive macros. Your own crate can define features too:

```toml
[features]
default = ["color"]          # on unless the user opts out
color = []                   # a plain on/off switch
json = ["dep:serde_json"]    # turning it on pulls in an optional dependency

[dependencies]
serde_json = { version = "1", optional = true }
```

```rust
#[cfg(feature = "json")]
pub fn to_json(report: &Report) -> String {
    serde_json::to_string(report).unwrap()
}
```

Code under `#[cfg(feature = "json")]` is compiled only when the feature is on: `cargo build --features json`, or `--no-default-features` to turn off the defaults. Features should be **additive**: turning one on may add things, never break or remove them, because Cargo merges the features everybody in the build asks for.

Other dependency sections: `[dev-dependencies]` are only for tests, examples and benchmarks; `[build-dependencies]` are for build scripts.

### Workspaces

A **workspace** is several related packages developed together: one shared `Cargo.lock`, one `target/` folder, one command to build or test everything.

```text
shop/
├── Cargo.toml          the workspace
├── shop-core/          library: domain logic
│   ├── Cargo.toml
│   └── src/lib.rs
└── shop-cli/           binary: the command-line tool
    ├── Cargo.toml
    └── src/main.rs
```

```toml
# shop/Cargo.toml
[workspace]
members = ["shop-core", "shop-cli"]
resolver = "3"

[workspace.dependencies]
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
```

```toml
# shop-cli/Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "shop-cli"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
shop-core = { path = "../shop-core" }
serde = { workspace = true }
```

`cargo build` at the top builds every member; `cargo test -p shop-core` tests one package; `cargo run -p shop-cli` runs the tool. In `shop-cli`'s code, the library is `shop_core::`. Most company codebases with more than one crate are workspaces.

### Publishing on crates.io

1. Add metadata to `[package]`: `description`, `license` (often `"MIT OR Apache-2.0"`), `repository`, and optionally `readme`, `keywords`, `categories`.
2. Document the public API with `///` comments: docs.rs builds and hosts the documentation of every published crate.
3. `cargo login` with an API token from your crates.io account.
4. `cargo publish --dry-run` to check, then `cargo publish`.
5. A published version is **permanent**: it can't be overwritten or deleted. To fix a mistake, publish a new version. `cargo yank --version 1.0.1` stops new projects from choosing a broken version, while existing `Cargo.lock`s keep working.

Most code at work is never published. Teams depend on internal crates through workspaces, `path` dependencies, git dependencies (`my-lib = { git = "https://..." }`) or a private registry.

steps.title: Tests that catch bugs
steps.text:
A test suite is only as good as the bugs it would catch. Here's a classic: in the Gregorian calendar, a year is a **leap year** if it's divisible by 4, *except* years divisible by 100, *except again* years divisible by 400. So 2024 is a leap year, 1900 isn't, and 2000 is.

Suppose someone forgot the century rules:

```rust
fn is_leap_year(year: u32) -> bool {
    year % 4 == 0 // bug: ignores the 100 and 400 rules
}

fn main() {
    // "typical" checks, the kind people write first
    for (year, expected) in [(2024, true), (2023, false), (2020, true)] {
        println!("{year}: expected {expected}, got {}", is_leap_year(year));
    }
    println!("1900: got {} (should be false)", is_leap_year(1900));
}
```

```text
2024: expected true, got true
2023: expected false, got false
2020: expected true, got true
1900: got true (should be false)
```

Every "typical" check passes, and the bug sails through. Tests that only use ordinary inputs prove very little.

### Think in rules and boundaries

Good tests come from reading the specification and asking "what would a wrong implementation get wrong?":

- **One test per rule.** The leap year rules need at least: a normal leap year (2024), a normal non-leap year (2023), a century that isn't a leap year (1900) and a century that is (2000).
- **Boundaries.** Off-by-one errors live at the edges: if adults are 18 and over, test 17 *and* 18. For `<` versus `<=`, the boundary value itself is the one that tells them apart.
- **Special inputs.** Empty strings and slices, zero, negative numbers, the maximum value, non-ASCII text.

### Mutation testing

How do you know your tests are good enough? Break the code on purpose and see if a test notices. Each broken copy is a **mutant**; a mutant your tests don't notice has **survived**, and it points at a missing test. That's what this site does with the planted bugs in each exercise, and at work the tool `cargo-mutants` does it automatically for a whole project (it flips `<` to `<=`, replaces function bodies with default values, and so on).

### Common mistakes

- **Testing the implementation instead of the rules**: copying the formula into the test (`assert_eq!(is_leap_year(y), y % 4 == 0)`) repeats the bug instead of catching it. Write expected values you worked out by hand.
- **One giant test.** Small tests with clear names tell you which rule broke.
- **Chasing 100% coverage.** Running every line isn't the same as checking every rule: a test can execute code without asserting anything useful about it.
