steps.title: Undefined behavior and Miri
steps.text:
**Undefined behavior** (UB) is what happens when unsafe code breaks one of Rust's rules. The name is literal: the language makes **no promise** about what the program does next. The optimizer assumes UB never happens and rearranges code based on that assumption, so a program with UB can:

- work perfectly in a debug build and fail in release,
- work today and break after a compiler update,
- corrupt unrelated data, which then crashes somewhere far away from the bug,
- turn into a security hole (most memory-safety CVEs in C and C++ are UB).

That's why "I ran it and it worked" proves nothing about unsafe code.

### The rules unsafe code must keep

The most common ways to cause UB:

| UB | Example |
|---|---|
| dangling, null or misaligned pointer dereference | using a pointer to a dropped local; reading a `u32` from an odd address |
| out-of-bounds access | `get_unchecked(len)`, `ptr.add(i)` past the end |
| breaking the aliasing rules | two live `&mut` to the same value, or writing through a pointer while a `&` to it is in use |
| invalid values | a `bool` that's not 0 or 1, a `char` that isn't a Unicode scalar value, an enum with no matching variant, a null `&T` |
| reading uninitialized memory | reading a `MaybeUninit` before writing it |
| data races | two threads writing a `static mut` |
| wrong FFI signature | declaring a C function with the wrong types |

### Debug builds catch a few

Debug builds (like this site's) check some of std's unsafe preconditions at runtime and **abort** if they're violated:

```rust
fn main() {
    let v = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let x = unsafe { *v.get_unchecked(10) };
    println!("{x}");
}
```

```text
thread 'main' (4242) panicked at src/main.rs:3:25:
unsafe precondition(s) violated: slice::get_unchecked requires that the index is within the slice

This indicates a bug in the program. This Undefined Behavior check is optional, and cannot be relied on for safety.
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
thread caused non-unwinding panic. aborting.
```

Similar checks catch misaligned pointer reads and invalid `char` and enum values. Read the warning in the message again ("optional, and cannot be relied on"): release builds remove these checks, and many kinds of UB are never checked at all. They're a safety net, not a guarantee.

### Miri: the UB detector

**Miri** is an interpreter for Rust's compiled intermediate code that checks **every** memory access against Rust's rules. It catches out-of-bounds and use-after-free accesses, invalid values, aliasing violations, data races and memory leaks, and tells you exactly where:

```text
$ rustup +nightly component add miri
$ cargo +nightly miri test
error: Undefined Behavior: constructing invalid value: encountered 0x02, but expected a boolean
 --> src/lib.rs:8:20
  |
8 |     let b: bool = unsafe { std::mem::transmute::<u8, bool>(raw) };
  |                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ Undefined Behavior occurred here
```

Run it on the tests of any module that contains unsafe code, ideally in CI. It's slow (often 100 times slower than a normal run) and can't run most calls into C, so keep those tests small. The Rust Playground has it under **Tools > Miri**. For FFI-heavy code, sanitizers like AddressSanitizer fill the gap.

### Fixing UB

The best fix is usually to **remove** the unsafe code: almost every unchecked operation has a checked, safe twin.

```rust
fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", char::from_u32(0x41));
    println!("{:?}", char::from_u32(0xD800));
    let v = [1, 2, 3];
    println!("{:?} {:?}", v.get(1), v.get(10));
    let raw: Vec<u8> = vec![0xff, 0xfe];
    println!("{}", String::from_utf8(raw).is_err());
}
```

```text
Some('A')
None
Some(2) None
true
```

When you must keep the unsafe call (measured performance, FFI), add the check that makes the `SAFETY` comment **true**.

modules.title: Performance
modules.summary: Honest, measured performance work. Pick the right algorithm and collection first, then cut needless clones and allocations, lean on zero-cost iterators and Cow, and learn the release builds, benchmarks and profilers that tell you where the time really goes.

steps.title: Measure first, and fix the algorithm first
steps.text:
Rust is fast by default, and most code is fast enough as written. When something **is** slow, the time almost always goes to a few hot spots, and the biggest wins come from doing **less work**, not from clever tricks. The order teams follow: make it work, make it right, then measure, and only then make it fast.

### Debug versus release

`cargo run` and `cargo build` make a **debug build**: no optimizations, plus extra checks like integer overflow. It compiles quickly and is great for development, but it's often 10 to 100 times slower than a **release build**:

```text
$ cargo build --release
$ ./target/release/report big_input.txt
```

Never judge speed from a debug build, and never benchmark one. Release builds can be tuned in `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[profile.release]
lto = true            # optimize across crates: slower to build, often a bit faster to run
codegen-units = 1     # fewer parallel compile units: better optimization, slower builds
debug = true          # keep symbols so profilers can show function names
```

This site runs debug builds, so its tests can't measure fine-grained speed. Instead, the exercises in this module check what matters most: the **amount of work**. Tests use inputs big enough that a quadratic solution runs past the 2-second time limit, while a linear one finishes in milliseconds, even unoptimized. Other exercises check for allocations and clones with rules.

### Big-O beats micro-optimization

**Big-O** describes how the work grows with the input size `n`. For `n = 100_000`:

| Complexity | Example | Steps for 100,000 items |
|---|---|---|
| O(1) | `HashSet::contains`, `Vec` index | 1 |
| O(log n) | `binary_search` on a sorted Vec | about 17 |
| O(n) | one pass over the data | 100,000 |
| O(n log n) | sorting | about 1.7 million |
| O(n²) | a loop inside a loop | 10,000,000,000 |

No compiler flag turns ten billion steps into a hundred thousand. The most common O(n²) at work hides in one innocent line: **`Vec::contains` inside a loop**.

```rust
use std::collections::HashSet;

// O(n * m): for every wanted id, scan the whole stock list.
fn missing_slow(wanted: &[u32], in_stock: &[u32]) -> Vec<u32> {
    wanted.iter().filter(|id| !in_stock.contains(id)).copied().collect()
}

// O(n + m): build a set once, then each lookup is O(1).
fn missing_fast(wanted: &[u32], in_stock: &[u32]) -> Vec<u32> {
    let stock: HashSet<u32> = in_stock.iter().copied().collect();
    wanted.iter().filter(|id| !stock.contains(id)).copied().collect()
}

fn main() {
    let wanted = [3, 8, 15, 42];
    let in_stock = [42, 8, 7];
    println!("{:?}", missing_slow(&wanted, &in_stock));
    println!("{:?}", missing_fast(&wanted, &in_stock));
}
```

```text
[3, 15]
[3, 15]
```

Same answer. With 100,000 orders and 100,000 stock items, the slow version does ten billion comparisons; the fast one does about 200,000 hash operations. For a dozen items, though, the `Vec` is fine (hashing has a cost too). Big-O matters when `n` can grow.

### Choosing a collection

| You need | Use | Cost per operation |
|---|---|---|
| "is X in here?" many times | `HashSet` / `HashMap` | O(1) on average |
| keys in sorted order, or ranges | `BTreeMap` / `BTreeSet` | O(log n) |
| many searches in data that rarely changes | sort once, then `binary_search` | O(log n) per search |
| a queue (push at the back, pop at the front) | `VecDeque` | O(1); `Vec::remove(0)` is O(n) |
| counting things | `HashMap` with `entry` | O(1) per item |

### Common mistakes

- **Optimizing without measuring**: you'll speed up code that wasn't slow and make it harder to read.
- **Sorting inside a loop**, or calling `.contains` on a `Vec` inside a loop: each turns a linear job into a quadratic one.
- **Reaching for a `HashMap` for five items**: a small `Vec` or array is simpler and often faster.

steps.title: Benchmarks and profilers
steps.text:
Guessing where a program spends its time is famously unreliable, even for experts. Two tools replace guessing: **profilers** tell you *where* the time goes, and **benchmarks** tell you *how much* a change helped.

### Benchmarks with criterion

**criterion** is the standard benchmarking crate. It runs your code many times, warms up first, and uses statistics to tell real changes from noise:

```toml
# Cargo.toml
[dev-dependencies]
criterion = "0.5"   # check crates.io for the current version

[[bench]]
name = "word_count"
harness = false
```

```rust
// benches/word_count.rs
use criterion::{criterion_group, criterion_main, Criterion};
use std::hint::black_box;
use my_app::count_words;

fn bench_count_words(c: &mut Criterion) {
    let text = std::fs::read_to_string("benches/sample.txt").unwrap();
    c.bench_function("count_words 1 MB", |b| {
        b.iter(|| count_words(black_box(&text)))
    });
}

criterion_group!(benches, bench_count_words);
criterion_main!(benches);
```

```text
$ cargo bench
count_words 1 MB        time:   [2.8131 ms 2.8297 ms 2.8476 ms]
                        change: [-41.205% -40.731% -40.249%] (p = 0.00 < 0.05)
                        Performance has improved.
```

- `cargo bench` always builds with optimizations.
- **`std::hint::black_box`** hides a value from the optimizer. Without it, the compiler may notice the result is unused and delete the work you meant to measure.
- The three times are a confidence interval; the `change` line compares with the previous run.
- Benchmark with **realistic input**. A function that's fastest on 10 items may be slowest on 10 million.

A hand-rolled `Instant::now()` timing loop is fine for a rough idea, in a release build, but it won't tell you whether a 3% difference is real.

### Profilers: where does the time go?

A **sampling profiler** interrupts the program thousands of times per second and records which function was running. On Linux:

```text
$ cargo build --release            # with debug = true in [profile.release]
$ perf record -g ./target/release/report big_input.txt
$ perf report                      # functions sorted by share of samples
```

**Flamegraphs** draw the same data as a picture. `cargo install flamegraph`, then `cargo flamegraph --bin report -- big_input.txt` writes `flamegraph.svg` (it builds in release mode by default). How to read one:

- Each box is a function; the boxes on top of it are the functions it called.
- **Width** is the share of samples, so wide boxes are where the time goes. The x-axis is **not** time order.
- Look for wide plateaus near the top: a function that is wide itself, not just because of what it calls.

`samply` is a cross-platform alternative that opens results in the Firefox profiler; macOS has Instruments. For memory, `heaptrack` and the `dhat` crate show who allocates.

### The workflow

1. Reproduce the slowness with realistic input, in a **release** build.
2. Profile. Find the widest box.
3. Fix that one thing (usually an algorithm, a collection, or an allocation in a loop).
4. Benchmark before and after, and keep the benchmark so a later change can't quietly undo it.

### A real hot spot

Suppose a flamegraph of a text tool looks like this (one line per stack level, with its share of samples):

```text
main                                 100%
└─ count_vowels                       98%
   └─ core::iter::Iterator::nth       96%   <- almost all the time
```

and `count_vowels` is:

```rust
fn count_vowels(text: &str) -> usize {
    let mut count = 0;
    for i in 0..text.chars().count() {
        let c = text.chars().nth(i).unwrap(); // walks from the start every time
        if "aeiouAEIOU".contains(c) {
            count += 1;
        }
    }
    count
}
```

Strings are UTF-8, so finding the `i`-th character means walking from the start: `nth(i)` is O(i), and the loop makes the whole function O(n²). The profile points straight at it; no amount of compiler tuning would.
steps.task: Fix `count_vowels` so it walks the characters once (O(n)), without `nth`. The tests include a 100,000-character string.
hints: `text.chars()` already gives every character in order; you don't need the index at all.

modules.title: Building Command-Line Tools
modules.summary: Write real command-line programs. Arguments and flags, exit codes and stderr, reading files and standard input, and the Config/run structure every Rust CLI uses, plus how clap does the parsing for you.

steps.title: Command-line arguments
steps.text:
Rust is a favorite for command-line tools (`ripgrep`, `fd`, `bat`, `uv` and Cargo itself are written in it): they start instantly, ship as one file, and don't crash on odd input. A command-line tool gets its instructions as **arguments**: the words typed after its name.

```text
$ grep -n error app.log
       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^  three arguments: "-n", "error", "app.log"
```

The shell splits the line into words (quotes keep spaces together: `"big world"` is one argument) and the program receives them as a list of strings. In Rust that list comes from `std::env::args()`:

```rust
use std::env;

fn main() {
    let args: Vec<String> = env::args().skip(1).collect();
    println!("got {} arguments", args.len());
    for (i, arg) in args.iter().enumerate() {
        println!("{i}: {arg}");
    }
}
```

```text
got 0 arguments
```

The example above ran without arguments. With Cargo, everything after `--` goes to your program (before it, the arguments are for Cargo itself):

```text
$ cargo run -- hello "big world" 42
got 3 arguments
0: hello
1: big world
2: 42
```

Piece by piece:

- `env::args()` returns an **iterator** of `String`s. The **first item is the program's own path** (like `target/debug/greet`), which is why we `skip(1)`.
- `collect()` gathers the rest into a `Vec<String>` you can index, count and pass around.
- Arguments are always text. `"42"` is a `String`; to use it as a number you `parse` it, and handle the error when it isn't one.
- `env::args()` panics if an argument isn't valid Unicode (rare; possible with odd file names on Linux). Tools that must accept any file name use `env::args_os()`, which yields `OsString`s.

### Common mistakes

**Indexing without checking.** `args[1]` panics when the user gave no arguments, the most common way a CLI crashes:

```rust
fn main() {
    let args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().collect();
    let name = &args[1];
    println!("Hello, {name}!");
}
```

```text
thread 'main' (4242) panicked at src/main.rs:3:21:
index out of bounds: the len is 1 but the index is 1
```

Ask for an `Option` instead and handle the `None`, usually by printing a **usage** line that shows how to call the tool:

```rust
fn main() {
    match std::env::args().nth(1) {
        Some(name) => println!("Hello, {name}!"),
        None => println!("usage: greet <name>"),
    }
}
```

```text
usage: greet <name>
```

- **Forgetting `skip(1)`**: the program's path shows up as the first "real" argument.
- **Printing `args[0]`** in messages: it's a full path that differs between machines. Write the tool's name yourself (`usage: greet ...`).

steps.title: Exit codes and stderr
steps.text:
Every program ends with an **exit code**, a small number it hands back to whoever started it. `0` means success, anything else means failure. Humans rarely see it, but everything else does: shell scripts (`mytool && deploy`), CI pipelines (a non-zero code fails the build), and other programs. A tool that prints "error" but exits with 0 tells the script everything went fine.

```text
$ grep crab notes.txt; echo "exit code: $?"
the crab sleeps
exit code: 0
$ grep lobster notes.txt; echo "exit code: $?"
exit code: 1
$ grep lobster missing.txt; echo "exit code: $?"
grep: missing.txt: No such file or directory
exit code: 2
```

Common conventions: `0` success, `1` a general failure (or "nothing found", for search tools), `2` the tool was called wrong (bad arguments). Codes go from 0 to 255.

### Returning an exit code from main

```rust
use std::process::ExitCode;

fn main() -> ExitCode {
    let words = ["alpha", "beta", "gamma"];
    for w in words {
        println!("{w}");
    }
    eprintln!("debug: printed {} words", words.len());
    ExitCode::SUCCESS
}
```

```text
alpha
beta
gamma
```

- `fn main() -> ExitCode` lets `main` choose the code: `ExitCode::SUCCESS` (0), `ExitCode::FAILURE` (1), or any `u8` with `ExitCode::from(2)`.
- The `debug:` line isn't in the output above because `eprintln!` writes to **standard error** (stderr), a second output stream. Messages for humans (errors, warnings, progress) go to stderr; the tool's real **results** go to stdout. That way `mytool > results.txt` puts only results in the file while errors still appear on screen, and a pipe like `mytool | sort` doesn't sort your error messages.

Here is a typical `main` for a tool that can be called wrong:

```rust
use std::process::ExitCode;

fn main() -> ExitCode {
    let args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().skip(1).collect();
    if args.is_empty() {
        eprintln!("usage: shout <word>...");
        return ExitCode::from(2);
    }
    println!("{}", args.join(" ").to_uppercase());
    ExitCode::SUCCESS
}
```

```text
$ shout hello crab
HELLO CRAB
$ shout; echo $?
usage: shout <word>...
2
```

### `std::process::exit`

`std::process::exit(2)` ends the program immediately from anywhere. It's handy in small tools, but it doesn't return: values in scope are never dropped (their `Drop` code doesn't run), and a function that might call it is hard to test. Prefer returning `ExitCode` (or a `Result`) up to `main`, and keep `exit` for the top level.

(Recall from the last module: a `main` that returns `Err` exits with 1, and a panic exits with 101.)

### Common mistakes

- **Errors on stdout** with `println!`: they end up in the output file or the next program in the pipe.
- **Exiting with 0 after an error.** Check: does `mytool bad-input && echo ok` print `ok`? It shouldn't.
- **`exit(256)`**: codes are taken modulo 256 on Unix, so 256 becomes 0, which means success. `ExitCode::from` takes a `u8`, which avoids that.

modules.title: Web Services and JSON APIs
modules.summary: How HTTP APIs work and how to build one in Rust. Requests and responses, routing, JSON with serde, errors as status codes, shared state, and testing handlers, then the same API in axum.

steps.title: HTTP in one page
steps.text:
A **web API** is a program that waits for **requests** over the network and sends back **responses**, using the **HTTP** protocol. Your browser, a phone app, `curl` and other services are the **clients**; your program is the **server**. Underneath every framework, HTTP/1.1 is just text. A client that creates a score sends:

```text
POST /scores HTTP/1.1                 <- request line: method, path, version
Host: arena.dev                       <- headers, one "Name: value" per line
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 26
                                      <- an empty line ends the headers
{"player":"ana","score":7}            <- the body (optional)
```

and the server answers:

```text
HTTP/1.1 201 Created                  <- status line: version, status code, reason
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 34

{"id":12,"player":"ana","score":7}
```

Lines end with `\r\n` (carriage return + newline), and the blank line is `\r\n\r\n`.

### Methods say what to do

| Method | Meaning | Body? |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | read a resource; never changes anything | no |
| `POST` | create something new (or trigger an action) | yes |
| `PUT` | replace a resource completely | yes |
| `PATCH` | change some fields of a resource | yes |
| `DELETE` | remove a resource | no |

The **path** names the resource: `/scores` is the collection, `/scores/12` one item in it.

### Status codes say how it went

| Code | Name | When |
|---|---|---|
| 200 | OK | it worked, here's the result |
| 201 | Created | a POST created something |
| 204 | No Content | it worked, nothing to send back (typical for DELETE) |
| 400 | Bad Request | the request is malformed (bad JSON, bad id) |
| 404 | Not Found | no such resource or path |
| 405 | Method Not Allowed | the path exists, but not with that method |
| 409 | Conflict | clashes with current state (duplicate name, not enough money) |
| 422 | Unprocessable Content | well-formed, but the data breaks a rule |
| 500 | Internal Server Error | the server's fault |

The first digit is what clients check first: **2xx** success, **4xx** the client's mistake, **5xx** the server's.

### Modeling it in Rust

Frameworks (like axum, at the end of this module) parse the text for you, but knowing what's underneath makes you much better at debugging (`curl -v` shows exactly this text). Here is the core of a request parser:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Method {
    Get,
    Post,
}

struct Request {
    method: Method,
    path: String,
    body: String,
}

fn parse_request(raw: &str) -> Option<Request> {
    let (head, body) = raw.split_once("\r\n\r\n")?;
    let request_line = head.split("\r\n").next()?;
    let mut parts = request_line.split(' ');
    let method = match parts.next()? {
        "GET" => Method::Get,
        "POST" => Method::Post,
        _ => return None,
    };
    let path = parts.next()?.to_string();
    Some(Request { method, path, body: body.to_string() })
}

fn main() {
    let raw = "POST /scores HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: arena.dev\r\nContent-Type: application/json\r\n\r\n{\"player\":\"ana\",\"score\":7}";
    if let Some(req) = parse_request(raw) {
        println!("{:?} {} body={}", req.method, req.path, req.body);
    }
    let get = parse_request("GET /scores/12 HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: arena.dev\r\n\r\n").unwrap();
    println!("{:?} {} body is empty: {}", get.method, get.path, get.body.is_empty());
    println!("{}", parse_request("BREW /coffee HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n").is_none());
}
```

```text
Post /scores body={"player":"ana","score":7}
Get /scores/12 body is empty: true
true
```

- `split_once("\r\n\r\n")` separates the head from the body at the first blank line; `?` returns `None` if there isn't one.
- The first line of the head is the request line; the rest are headers (ignored here).
- An **enum for the method** means the rest of the program can't see a misspelled `"GETT"`: invalid methods are rejected at the edge, once.

### Common mistakes

- **Splitting on `\n` only.** HTTP uses `\r\n`; splitting on `\n` leaves a `\r` at the end of every line and `"HTTP/1.1\r" != "HTTP/1.1"`.
- **Treating methods as case-insensitive.** `get` is not a valid method; methods are case-sensitive (header *names*, on the other hand, are case-insensitive).
- **Counting characters for `Content-Length`.** It's the number of **bytes** of the body: `"é"` is 2 bytes, so use `.len()`, not `.chars().count()`.

`status` is a `match self` with one arm per variant; `into_response` builds `json!({ "error": self.to_string() })` with `self.status()`.

steps.title: Shared state: an in-memory store
steps.task:
Write `handle` for an inventory API. The types and helpers are ready; the routes are:
- `GET /items`: `200`, a JSON array of all items in id order
- `POST /items` with `{"name": "mug", "qty": 3}`: `201` and the new item (ids start at 1); a body that doesn't parse: `400` `{"error":"invalid JSON"}`
- `GET /items/{id}`: `200` and the item, or `404` `{"error":"item 7 not found"}`
- `DELETE /items/{id}`: `204` with an empty body, or the same `404`
- an id that isn't a number: `400` `{"error":"bad id"}`; a known path with another method: `405` `{"error":"method not allowed"}`; anything else: `404` `{"error":"not found"}`
hints: Write one small function per route (`list_items`, `create_item`, `get_item`, `delete_item`) and route to them with `match (req.method, segments.as_slice())`.
In `create_item`, parse the body **before** locking. Then, under one lock: bump `next_id`, build the Item, insert a clone, return it with 201.
`store.items.values().collect::<Vec<&Item>>()` serializes as a JSON array in id order (BTreeMap). `items.remove(&id)` returns `Some` if it existed.

steps.title: Testing handlers
steps.task: This time you write the tests. The handler below quotes a price for a shopping cart. Its rules: only `POST /quote` exists (another method on `/quote` is `405`, other paths `404`); the body is `{"cents": <cart total>, "code": <optional discount code>}`, and one that doesn't parse is `400`; no code means the full price; `CRAB10` takes 10% off; `HALF` halves the price but only for carts of **at least** 2000 cents (below that: `422`); any other code is `422`. Success is `200` with `{"total": <cents>}`. Write at least 4 tests that pin down these rules. Hidden broken versions of the handler (a wrong discount, an off-by-one boundary, wrong status codes) must each make at least one of your tests fail.
hints: Start with the happy paths: `let r = post(r#"{"cents": 1000, "code": "CRAB10"}"#);` then check `r.status` and `body_json(&r)["total"]`.
Boundaries catch off-by-one bugs: test HALF with exactly 2000 cents (works) and 1999 (422).
Don't forget the error paths: an unknown code, a body that isn't JSON, `Method::Get` on `/quote`, and another path.

steps.title: The same API in axum
steps.task:
Build axum's `IntoResponse` idea. Implement `IntoResponse` for:
- `&'static str`: status 200, content type `text/plain`, the text as the body
- `(u16, &'static str)`: that status, `text/plain`
- `Json<T>` where `T: Serialize`: status 200, `application/json`, the value serialized
- `(u16, Json<T>)`: that status, `application/json`
- `Result<T, E>` where both `T` and `E` implement `IntoResponse`: whichever one it holds

Then any handler that returns one of these, like `fn score() -> Result<Json<Score>, (u16, &'static str)>`, can be turned into a `Response`, exactly like in axum.
hints: Each case is its own impl block: `impl IntoResponse for &'static str { fn into_response(self) -> Response { ... } }`.
Generic impls carry their bounds: `impl<T: Serialize> IntoResponse for Json<T>` and `impl<T: IntoResponse, E: IntoResponse> IntoResponse for Result<T, E>`.
The tuple impls can reuse the others: `let mut r = self.1.into_response(); r.status = self.0; r`.

modules.summary: The patterns experienced Rust developers reach for, and the ones reviewers ask for. Builders, newtypes, state machines, conversions, RAII guards and returned iterators, ending with a real code-review refactor.

steps.title: Constructors, Default and builders
steps.task: Write a builder for `Server`. `Server::builder()` returns a `ServerBuilder` with defaults host `127.0.0.1`, port `8080`, workers `4`, tls `false`. `build(self)` checks `self.port == 0`, then `!(1..=64).contains(&self.workers)`, then moves the fields into a `Server`.

steps.title: Newtypes: give plain values a meaning
steps.task: Write `Cents`, a money type. `Cents::parse(s)` accepts dollar amounts like `"12.34"`, `"12.3"`, `"5"` or `"$5"` (an optional leading `$`) and returns the amount in cents. Anything else (empty, a minus sign, no digit before the `.`, more than two decimals, letters) is `Err(format!("invalid amount {s:?}"))`. Implement `Add` so two `Cents` can be added, and `Display` so `Cents(1234)` prints `$12.34`.
hints: Strip an optional `$` with `strip_prefix('$').unwrap_or(s)`, then `split_once('.')` into whole and fraction (no dot means an empty fraction).
Check that the whole part is non-empty, both parts are only ASCII digits, and the fraction has at most 2 digits. Pad the fraction to 2 digits (`format!("{frac:0<2}")`) before parsing it.
`Display`: `write!(f, "${}.{:02}", self.0 / 100, self.0 % 100)`; `Add`: `type Output = Cents;` and `Cents(self.0 + other.0)`.

steps.title: Make invalid states unrepresentable
steps.task:
Write a payment state machine. `Payment::next(self, event)` returns the new state or an error string. Allowed transitions:
- `Pending` + `Authorize(code)` becomes `Authorized { amount, auth_code: code }`
- `Pending` or `Authorized` + `Decline(reason)` becomes `Failed { reason }`
- `Authorized` + `Capture` becomes `Captured { amount }`
- `Captured` + `Refund` becomes `Refunded { amount }`

Anything else is `Err(format!("cannot {event:?} a {} payment", state.name()))`, where `name()` returns `pending`, `authorized`, `captured`, `refunded` or `failed`.
hints: `name` is a `match self` with `{ .. }` patterns, one arm per variant.
In `next`, `match (self, event)`: `(Payment::Pending { amount }, Event::Authorize(code)) => Ok(Payment::Authorized { amount, auth_code: code })` and so on.
Combine states with `|`: `(Payment::Pending { .. } | Payment::Authorized { .. }, Event::Decline(reason))`. The last arm `(state, event) => Err(...)` catches the rest.

steps.task: Tags on articles. Implement `From<&str> for Tag` (trim and lowercase the text) and `From<Tag> for String`. Write `fn normalize_all<S: AsRef<str>>(items: &[S]) -> Vec<Tag>` (works for `&[&str]` and `&[String]`), and give `Article` a constructor `new(title: impl Into<String>)` and a chainable `with_tag(mut self, tag: impl Into<Tag>) -> Self`.

steps.title: RAII guards and Drop
steps.task: Count active work with a guard. `Tracker::enter(&self)` increments `active`, updates `peak` (the highest `active` ever seen) and returns an `ActiveGuard`; dropping the guard decrements `active`. The fields are `Cell<u32>` so they can change through `&self` (interior mutability, from the smart pointers module).

steps.title: Returning iterators
steps.task: Give `Log` three methods that return iterators (no `Vec` in their return types): `errors()` yields the lines that start with `ERROR`; `with_level(level)` yields the **message part** of the lines that start with exactly that level followed by a space, so `with_level("WARN")` on `WARN disk 91%` yields `disk 91%` (and skips `WARNING ...`); `numbered()` yields `(line_number, line)` pairs counting from 1.

`numbered`: `self.lines.iter().enumerate().map(|(i, l)| (i + 1, l.as_str()))`.

modules.title: Debugging, Docs and Tooling
modules.summary: The tools around the code. Debug with dbg! and eprintln!, read panics and backtraces, use a debugger and logging, document with rustdoc, satisfy clippy and rustfmt, and wire it all into CI.

steps.title: dbg! and eprintln!: print debugging done right
steps.text:
When code does something unexpected, the quickest tool is still printing values. Rust has two macros made for it.

### dbg!

`dbg!(expression)` prints the file, line and column, the expression's source text, and its value (pretty-printed with `{:#?}`), then **returns the value**. So you can wrap any expression in place without restructuring your code:

```rust
fn average(scores: &[u32]) -> u32 {
    let total: u32 = dbg!(scores.iter().sum());
    dbg!(total / scores.len() as u32)
}

fn main() {
    let avg = average(&[70, 85, 90]);
    eprintln!("debug: average is {avg}");
    println!("average: {avg}");
}
```

```text
average: 81
```

The program's normal output is that one line. The debug lines went somewhere else, to the terminal's error stream:

```text
[src/main.rs:2:22] scores.iter().sum() = 245
[src/main.rs:3:5] total / scores.len() as u32 = 81
debug: average is 81
```

- `dbg!(scores.iter().sum())` printed the sum and handed it to `let total`. Wrapping the last line of `average` didn't change what the function returns.
- `dbg!` **takes ownership** of its argument, like passing it to a function. For a `String` or `Vec` you still need afterwards, write `dbg!(&name)`.
- `dbg!(a, b)` prints both.

### stdout and stderr

Every program has two output streams. **stdout** (standard output) is for the program's real output: what `println!` writes. **stderr** (standard error) is for errors, warnings and diagnostics: what `eprintln!` (and `eprint!`) and `dbg!` write. In a terminal both appear on screen, but they're separate:

```text
$ cargo run > report.txt
[src/main.rs:2:22] scores.iter().sum() = 245
[src/main.rs:3:5] total / scores.len() as u32 = 81
debug: average is 81
$ cat report.txt
average: 81
```

`>` redirects only stdout to the file, so the debug lines didn't corrupt the report. The same goes when another program reads your output through a pipe. The tests on this site also compare only stdout, so debug lines on stderr never make a test fail.

### A debugging routine

1. Find where the output first goes wrong, and form a guess about why ("the cents are parsed wrong").
2. Wrap the values that would confirm or rule out the guess in `dbg!`.
3. Fix, rerun, then **remove the `dbg!` calls**. They print in release builds too. Teams often turn on clippy's `dbg_macro` lint in CI so a forgotten one can't be merged.

### Common mistakes

- **Debug output on stdout**: a stray `println!("here")` changes the program's output and breaks anything reading it. Use `eprintln!` or `dbg!`.
- **`dbg!(s)` and then using `s`**: `error[E0382]: borrow of moved value`. Use `dbg!(&s)`.
- **Printing everything at once.** Print the few values that test your current guess; a wall of output hides the clue.

steps.title: Clippy: fixing common lints
steps.text:
**Clippy** is Rust's official linter: hundreds of extra checks, on top of the compiler's, for code that is wrong, slow, or just not idiomatic. Every serious Rust team runs it, and most block pull requests that have clippy warnings. It comes with rustup (`rustup component add clippy` if it's missing):

```text
$ cargo clippy
warning: the loop variable `i` is only used to index `prices`
 --> src/main.rs:3:14
  |
3 |     for i in 0..prices.len() {
  |              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = help: for further information visit https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/rust-1.97.0/index.html#needless_range_loop
  = note: `#[warn(clippy::needless_range_loop)]` on by default
help: consider using an iterator
  |
3 -     for i in 0..prices.len() {
3 +     for <item> in &prices {
  |
```

Each warning names its **lint** (`needless_range_loop`), links to an explanation with examples, and usually suggests the fix. `cargo clippy --fix` applies the suggestions it's sure about.

### Lint groups

| Group | Default | Catches |
|---|---|---|
| `clippy::correctness` | error | code that is almost certainly a bug |
| `clippy::suspicious` | warn | code that is probably a bug |
| `clippy::style` | warn | code that works but isn't idiomatic |
| `clippy::complexity` | warn | simple things done in a complicated way |
| `clippy::perf` | warn | code that could easily be faster |
| `clippy::pedantic` | off | stricter lints, with some false alarms |
| `clippy::nursery` | off | new lints still being polished |
| `clippy::restriction` | off | team rules, like banning `unwrap` or `dbg!` |

### The lints you'll see most

| Lint | Instead of | Write |
|---|---|---|
| `needless_range_loop` | `for i in 0..v.len() { v[i] }` | `for x in &v`, or `.iter().enumerate()` if you need `i` |
| `len_zero` | `v.len() == 0` | `v.is_empty()` |
| `needless_return` | `return x;` as the last line | `x` |
| `ptr_arg` | `fn f(v: &Vec<T>)`, `fn g(s: &String)` | `fn f(v: &[T])`, `fn g(s: &str)` |
| `manual_map` | `match o { Some(x) => Some(f(x)), None => None }` | `o.map(f)` |
| `useless_format` | `format!("{}", s)` | `s.to_string()` |
| `bool_comparison` | `if done == true` | `if done` |
| `unwrap_or_default` | `.unwrap_or(String::new())` | `.unwrap_or_default()` |
| `single_match` | `match o { Some(x) => ..., _ => {} }` | `if let Some(x) = o { ... }` |
| `collapsible_if` | `if a { if b { ... } }` | `if a && b { ... }` |

Why `&[T]` over `&Vec<T>`? A slice parameter accepts a `Vec`, an array, or part of either; `&Vec<T>` only accepts a whole `Vec`, and adds an extra pointer hop. Same for `&str` over `&String`.

Here's a function with four of those warnings, and its clippy-clean version:

```rust
fn total(prices: &Vec<u32>) -> u32 {
    if prices.len() == 0 {
        return 0;
    }
    let mut sum = 0;
    for i in 0..prices.len() {
        sum += prices[i];
    }
    return sum;
}
```

```rust
fn total(prices: &[u32]) -> u32 {
    prices.iter().sum()
}

fn main() {
    let cart = vec![1999, 450, 300];
    println!("{}", total(&cart));
    println!("{}", total(&[]));
    println!("{}", total(&cart[1..]));
}
```

```text
2749
0
750
```

The empty check disappeared too: the sum of nothing is already 0. And `total(&cart[1..])` works only because the parameter is a slice.

(This site compiles with `rustc`, not clippy, so its clippy exercises use rules that reject the flagged patterns.)

### Common mistakes

- **Silencing instead of fixing**: `#[allow(clippy::...)]` has its place (next step), but most warnings point at a genuinely better way.
- **Changing behavior while "just" fixing lints**: rewrites like these should keep the output identical. Run the tests after each fix.
- **Ignoring clippy until there are 300 warnings.** Run it often; it's much easier one warning at a time.
steps.task: Rewrite `total_weight` so clippy has nothing to say: take a slice instead of `&Vec`, don't compare `len()` with 0, don't loop over indexes, and don't end with `return`. It must still return the same totals.

steps.title: Continuous integration: keeping main green
steps.text:
Tests, clippy and rustfmt only protect a codebase if they run *every time*. **Continuous integration (CI)** is a server that checks out every pushed commit and pull request, runs the checks, and reports a green tick or a red cross. With **branch protection** turned on, a pull request can't be merged until CI is green, so the main branch always builds, passes its tests and follows the team's rules.

### A GitHub Actions workflow

On GitHub, CI is a YAML file in `.github/workflows/`. A typical Rust one:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

env:
  CARGO_TERM_COLOR: always

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          components: rustfmt, clippy
      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
      - name: Formatting
        run: cargo fmt --all --check
      - name: Lints
        run: cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
      - name: Tests
        run: cargo test --all-features
      - name: Docs
        run: cargo doc --no-deps
        env:
          RUSTDOCFLAGS: -D warnings
```

- `on`: when to run: pushes to `main`, and every pull request.
- `actions/checkout` gets the code; `dtolnay/rust-toolchain` installs Rust with clippy and rustfmt; `Swatinem/rust-cache` caches compiled dependencies between runs (builds go from minutes to seconds).
- Each `run` step is a shell command. A command that exits with a non-zero code fails the step, and the job stops there.
- `-- -D warnings` turns clippy's warnings into errors (`-D` is "deny"), so a warning fails CI instead of scrolling past. `--all-targets` lints tests and examples too.
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS: -D warnings` fails on broken intra-doc links in the docs.

Exit codes are how every tool tells CI "pass" or "fail". Here's a tiny custom check, the kind teams add for their own rules, that finds forgotten debugging code:

```rust
fn main() {
    let source = "fn main() {\n    let x = dbg!(2 + 2);\n    println!(\"{x}\");\n}\n";
    let mut problems = 0;
    for (i, line) in source.lines().enumerate() {
        if line.contains("dbg!(") || line.contains("todo!(") {
            println!("line {}: leftover debug code: {}", i + 1, line.trim());
            problems += 1;
        }
    }
    println!("{problems} problem(s)");
    // A real check would end with: std::process::exit(if problems > 0 { 1 } else { 0 });
}
```

```text
line 2: leftover debug code: let x = dbg!(2 + 2);
1 problem(s)
```

### Beyond the basics

- A **matrix** runs the same job on several operating systems or Rust versions (`stable`, `beta`, and your **MSRV**, the minimum supported Rust version declared as `rust-version` in `Cargo.toml`).
- `cargo audit` and `cargo deny` check dependencies for known security advisories and unwanted licenses.
- Run the same commands locally before pushing (`cargo fmt && cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings && cargo test`). Many teams put them in a script or a git pre-push hook, so CI is a formality.

### Reading a red CI run

Open the failed step's log and read it like any compiler or test output: the first error is usually the real one. A failing `fmt --check` shows a diff of what rustfmt would change; a failing clippy step shows the lint; a failing test shows the panic message.

### Common mistakes

- **"Works on my machine"**: CI starts from a clean checkout, so a file you forgot to commit, or a test that depends on your local setup, fails there. That's CI doing its job.
- **Disabling a failing check to merge faster.** Fix it, or mark the one test `#[ignore]` with an issue link if it's genuinely flaky.
- **Letting CI get slow.** Cache dependencies, and split long jobs so feedback arrives in minutes.

modules.title: Stacks, Queues, Heaps and Ordered Maps
modules.summary: The rest of std::collections. Stacks with Vec, queues with VecDeque, priority queues with BinaryHeap, range queries with BTreeMap, why LinkedList is rare, and how to pick the right collection for a job.

steps.title: Stacks with Vec
steps.task: Write `fn is_balanced(code: &str) -> bool` that returns `true` when every `(`, `[` and `{` in `code` is closed by the matching `)`, `]` or `}` in the right order. Ignore every other character. Use a `Vec<char>` as a stack. The tests include a text of 300,000 nested brackets, so the solution must be O(n): one pass over the characters.
hints: Push every opening bracket. When you meet a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its partner.
`stack.pop()` gives an `Option<char>`: compare it with `Some('(')` (or the right opener). An empty stack gives `None`, which never matches.
After the loop, the text is balanced only if nothing is left open: `stack.is_empty()`.

steps.title: Queues with VecDeque

Run the food truck line. Read commands from standard input, one per line:

- `join NAME`: NAME joins the back of the line
- `vip NAME`: NAME goes straight to the front
- `serve`: serve the person at the front and print `served NAME`, or print `nobody waiting` if the line is empty

`join` is `push_back(name.to_string())`, `vip` is `push_front(...)`, and `serve` matches on `line_up.pop_front()`.

steps.title: Priority queues with BinaryHeap
steps.task: Write `fn top_k(scores: &[u32], k: usize) -> Vec<u32>` that returns the `k` highest scores, highest first (all of them if there are fewer than `k`). Use a `BinaryHeap<Reverse<u32>>` that never holds more than `k` items, then pop it empty and reverse. Don't sort.
hints: Push `Reverse(s)` for every score. The heap's top is then the smallest score it holds.
Right after each push, `if heap.len() > k { heap.pop(); }` throws away the smallest, so the heap keeps the k largest.
Pop everything into a Vec (`while let Some(Reverse(s)) = heap.pop()`): that's smallest first, so call `.reverse()` before returning.

require.message: Use a `BinaryHeap` for this one.
Wrap the scores in `Reverse` so the heap pops the smallest one.

steps.title: Range queries with BTreeMap and BTreeSet
steps.task:
A meeting room booking system. Write a `Calendar` with:

- `fn new() -> Self`
- `fn book(&mut self, start: u32, end: u32) -> bool` that books the half-open time slot `start..end` and returns `true`, or returns `false` (and books nothing) if it overlaps an existing booking or if `start >= end`

Half-open means `9..10` and `10..11` don't overlap. Store bookings as a `BTreeMap<u32, u32>` from start to end. The tests make 100,000 bookings, so checking every existing booking is too slow. You only need to look at **one**: the booking with the latest start before `end` (`range(..end).next_back()`). If it ends after `start`, the new slot overlaps.

`self.bookings.range(..end).next_back()` gives `Option<(&u32, &u32)>`: that booking's start and end.

steps.title: Choosing a collection
steps.task:
An API gateway needs a **rate limiter**: each user may make at most `limit` requests in any window of `window` seconds. Write:

- `fn new(limit: usize, window: u64) -> Self`
- `fn allow(&mut self, user: &str, now: u64) -> bool`

A request at time `now` counts the user's earlier **allowed** requests at times `t` with `now - t < window`. If there are fewer than `limit`, allow it (and remember `now`); otherwise reject it. Rejected requests don't count. Times never go backwards.

Use a `HashMap<String, VecDeque<u64>>`: for each user, a queue of their recent allowed times. Before deciding, pop the times that have left the window off the front. The tests make 200,000 requests from one user with a limit of 50,000, so don't rescan the whole history on every call.
hints: Get the user's queue with `self.recent.entry(user.to_string()).or_default()`.
While the front time is too old (`now - oldest >= self.window`), `pop_front` it.
Then if `times.len() < self.limit`, `push_back(now)` and return `true`; otherwise return `false`.
checkNames: allows requests up to the limit

modules.title: Searching, Sorting and Classic Techniques
modules.summary: How fast is your code? Big-O, linear and binary search, sorting (and writing your own merge sort), custom orderings, and the interview workhorses two pointers, sliding window and prefix sums.

steps.title: Big-O: counting the work
steps.task: Write `fn has_duplicate(ids: &[u64]) -> bool` in O(n) on average, using a `HashSet`. Remember that `HashSet::insert` returns `false` when the value was already there. The tests include 100,000 ids.
hints: Walk the ids once. For each id, ask the set whether you've seen it before.
`seen.insert(id)` returns `true` for a new id and `false` for one that was already there: that `false` means a duplicate.
A loop with `if !seen.insert(id) { return true; }` works, or the one-liner `!ids.iter().all(|&id| seen.insert(id))`.

require.message: Use a `HashSet` to remember the ids you've seen.

checkNames: empty and single lists have no duplicates
finds a duplicate at the very end

steps.title: Linear and binary search
steps.task: Write `fn find(sorted: &[i32], target: i32) -> Option<usize>` by hand with a half-open range (no `binary_search` or `partition_point`). The values are sorted and all different; return the index of `target`, or `None`. The tests look up 200,000 values in a slice of 200,000, so a linear scan is too slow.
hints: Start with `let mut lo = 0; let mut hi = sorted.len();` and loop `while lo < hi`.
`let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;` then compare `sorted[mid]` with `target` (a `match` on `sorted[mid].cmp(&target)` reads well).
Equal: `return Some(mid)`. Less: `lo = mid + 1`. Greater: `hi = mid`. After the loop, `None`.

forbid.message: Write the search yourself this time, without `binary_search` or `partition_point`.

steps.title: Sorting and custom orderings
steps.task: Write `fn rank_players(players: &mut [Player])` that sorts a leaderboard: highest `score` first; on equal scores, **fewer** `games` first; on equal games too, `name` A to Z.
hints: Use `players.sort_by(|a, b| ...)` and chain the three comparisons with `.then(...)`.
High to low means comparing `b` with `a`: `b.score.cmp(&a.score)`. Low to high is `a.games.cmp(&b.games)`.
`b.score.cmp(&a.score).then(a.games.cmp(&b.games)).then_with(|| a.name.cmp(&b.name))`

steps.title: Implementing sorts: insertion sort and merge sort
steps.task: Write `fn merge_sort(v: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32>` that returns a sorted copy, using recursion, `split_at` and a `merge` function you write (adapt the one above to `i32`). No `sort` methods. The tests sort 200,000 numbers, which insertion sort would take minutes for.
hints: Base case: `if v.len() <= 1 { return v.to_vec(); }`
`let (left, right) = v.split_at(v.len() / 2);` then sort both halves with `merge_sort`.
Return `merge(&merge_sort(left), &merge_sort(right))`, with `merge` written like the example but for `i32`.

steps.title: Two pointers
steps.task: Write `fn pair_with_sum(sorted: &[i32], target: i32) -> Option<(usize, usize)>` that returns the indices `(i, j)`, `i < j`, of two items of the sorted slice that add up to `target`, or `None`. Use two pointers from both ends, with no HashMap (O(1) extra memory). In every test at most one pair works. The tests include a slice of 200,000 numbers.
hints: Return `None` for fewer than two items, then start with `i = 0` and `j = sorted.len() - 1`.
While `i < j`, compare `sorted[i] + sorted[j]` with `target`: too small means `i += 1`, too big means `j -= 1`.
Equal: `return Some((i, j))`. If the pointers meet, there's no pair.

forbid.message: Use two pointers only, without extra collections or binary search.

checkNames: returns none when nothing adds up

steps.title: Sliding window
steps.task: Write `fn max_window_sum(values: &[i64], k: usize) -> Option<i64>`: the largest total of `k` consecutive values, or `None` if `k` is 0 or larger than the slice. Slide the window. The tests use 200,000 values with `k` = 100,000, so summing each window from scratch is too slow.
hints: Return `None` when `k == 0 || k > values.len()`.
The first window's sum is `values[..k].iter().sum()`. Keep it as the best so far.
For each `right` in `k..values.len()`: `sum += values[right] - values[right - k];` and update the best.
checkNames: a window of everything is the total

steps.title: Prefix sums
steps.task: Write a `RangeSum` type with `fn new(values: &[i64]) -> Self` (builds the prefix sums) and `fn sum(&self, from: usize, to: usize) -> i64` (the sum of `values[from..to]`, half-open, with `from <= to <= len`). The tests ask 200,000 questions about 200,000 values.
hints: In `new`, start the prefix Vec with a single 0, then push the running total after each value.
`prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + values[i]`, so `prefix` ends up one longer than `values`.
`sum(from, to)` is `self.prefix[to] - self.prefix[from]`.
checkNames: an empty range sums to zero

modules.title: Recursion and Dynamic Programming
modules.summary: Functions that call themselves, backtracking through choices, and dynamic programming (memoization with HashMap and bottom-up tables) for the classic problems: coin change, longest common subsequence, edit distance, grid paths and knapsack.

steps.title: Recursion: a function that calls itself
steps.task: Write `fn sum_digits(n: u64) -> u64` recursively, without loops: the sum of the decimal digits of `n` (`sum_digits(1234)` is 10). The last digit is `n % 10` and the rest of the number is `n / 10`; the sum of the digits of 0 is 0.
hints: The base case is `n == 0`, whose digit sum is 0.
Otherwise the answer is the last digit plus the digit sum of the rest: `n % 10 + sum_digits(n / 10)`.

require.message: `sum_digits` should call itself.

forbid.message: Use recursion and arithmetic (`% 10`, `/ 10`), not a loop or a string.

checkNames: zeros inside the number count as zero

steps.title: Branching recursion and backtracking
steps.task: A customer has gift cards with the given values and wants to spend exactly `target`. Write `fn count_subsets_with_sum(cards: &[u32], target: u32) -> usize`: the number of different sets of cards (each card used at most once; equal values on different cards count as different cards) whose values add up to exactly `target`. The empty set adds up to 0. Use recursion that, for each card, counts the ways **with** it and **without** it, and prune: never take a card bigger than what's left. The tests go up to 20 cards.
hints: With no cards left, there's exactly one way if `target == 0` (take nothing more) and none otherwise.
Otherwise split off the first card (`[first, rest @ ..]` or an index): count the sets without it, `count_subsets_with_sum(rest, target)`, plus the sets with it.
Only take the card when `*first <= target`, then recurse with `target - first`. Add the two counts.
checkNames: a target of zero has one way

steps.title: Memoization with a HashMap
steps.task: A crab climbs a staircase of `n` steps, taking 1, 2 or 3 steps at a time. In how many different ways can it reach the top? `count_ways(4)` is 7 (1+1+1+1, 1+1+2, 1+2+1, 2+1+1, 2+2, 1+3, 3+1). There's 1 way to climb 0 steps (do nothing). The number of ways for `n` is the sum of the ways for `n - 1`, `n - 2` and `n - 3` (whichever exist). Write the memoized helper `ways_from`. The tests ask for `n = 70`, which takes about 10¹⁸ calls without the memo.
hints: Base case: `if n == 0 { return 1; }`. Then `if let Some(&known) = memo.get(&n) { return known; }`.
Add up `ways_from(n - step, memo)` for each `step` in `1..=3` with `step <= n`.
`memo.insert(n, total);` before returning `total`.

require.message: Store and look up answers in the memo.

steps.title: Bottom-up DP: filling a table
steps.task: The classic **coin change**. Write `fn min_coins(coins: &[u32], amount: u32) -> Option<u32>`: the fewest coins (each coin value can be used any number of times) that add up to exactly `amount`, or `None` if it's impossible. Make amount 0 need 0 coins. State: `best[a]` is the fewest coins for amount `a`; for each coin `c <= a`, `best[a]` could be `best[a - c] + 1`. The tests include amounts up to 100,000.
hints: Make a table `let mut best = vec![u32::MAX; amount + 1];` where `u32::MAX` means impossible, and set `best[0] = 0`.
For each amount `a` from 1 up, and each coin `c` with `c <= a`: if `best[a - c]` is possible, `best[a] = best[a].min(best[a - c] + 1)`.
At the end, `u32::MAX` means `None`; anything else is `Some(best[amount])`.

steps.title: Two-dimensional DP: grids and strings
steps.task: Write `fn lcs_len(a: &str, b: &str) -> usize`, the length of the longest common subsequence of two texts (counting characters). The tests include two texts of 2,000 characters each, which plain recursion could never finish.
hints: Collect both texts into `Vec<char>` and make `vec![vec![0usize; b.len() + 1]; a.len() + 1]`.
For `i` in `1..=a.len()` and `j` in `1..=b.len()`: if `a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]`, take `dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1`; otherwise the larger of `dp[i - 1][j]` and `dp[i][j - 1]`.
The answer is `dp[a.len()][b.len()]`.

steps.title: The knapsack problem
steps.task: Write `fn best_value(items: &[(usize, u32)], capacity: usize) -> u32` where each item is `(weight, value)`, using a **single** `Vec` of `capacity + 1` entries (no 2D table). The tests include 150 items and a capacity of 20,000.
hints: `let mut best = vec![0u32; capacity + 1];` where `best[w]` is the most value with capacity `w`.
For each item, loop `w` over `(weight..=capacity).rev()`: high to low, so the item is used at most once. Skip items heavier than the capacity.
`best[w] = best[w].max(best[w - weight] + value);` and return `best[capacity]`.

forbid.message: Use a single Vec of capacity + 1 entries, not a 2D table.

checkNames: uses each item at most once
skips items that are too heavy
nothing fits in an empty backpack

modules.title: Graphs and Trees
modules.summary: Model networks, dependencies and maps as graphs. Adjacency lists, BFS for shortest hops, DFS with recursion or a stack, topological sort, Dijkstra with a BinaryHeap, binary trees with Option<Box<Node>>, and union-find.

steps.title: Representing graphs: adjacency lists
steps.task: Write `fn build_graph(n: usize, edges: &[(usize, usize)]) -> Vec<Vec<usize>>` for an **undirected** graph with nodes `0..n`. Clean the data while you're at it: each neighbor list must be sorted ascending with no duplicates (the same edge may appear twice, in either direction). A self-loop `(a, a)` makes `a` appear once in its own list.
hints: Start with `vec![Vec::new(); n]` and push each edge both ways.
Afterwards, loop over `&mut adj` and clean every list.
`neighbors.sort_unstable();` puts equal values next to each other, so `neighbors.dedup();` can then remove the repeats.
checkNames: keeps isolated nodes and self loops
an empty graph has no lists

steps.title: Breadth-first search with VecDeque
steps.task: Write `fn shortest_hops(adj: &[Vec<usize>], from: usize, to: usize) -> Option<usize>`: the fewest edges on a path from `from` to `to` in a directed graph given as adjacency lists, or `None` if `to` can't be reached (`Some(0)` when `from == to`). The tests include a graph of 200,000 nodes.
hints: Keep `seen = vec![false; adj.len()]` and a `VecDeque` of `(node, distance)` pairs, starting with `(from, 0)`.
Pop from the front. If it's `to`, return its distance. Otherwise push every unseen neighbor with `d + 1`, marking it seen as you push.
If the queue runs empty, `to` is unreachable: `None`.

require.message: Use a `VecDeque` as the BFS queue.

checkNames: the start is zero hops away

steps.title: Depth-first search: recursion and an explicit stack
steps.task: Count the islands on a map. Write `fn count_islands(map: &[&str]) -> usize` where each string is a row, `#` is land and `.` is water. Land cells that touch up, down, left or right belong to the same island. Use DFS with an **explicit stack** (`Vec<(usize, usize)>`): the tests include a 700 by 700 map that is all land, where recursion would overflow the stack.
hints: Turn each row into bytes (`row.as_bytes()`) and keep a `Vec<Vec<bool>>` of visited cells.
Scan every cell. An unvisited `#` starts a new island: count it, mark it, and push it onto a `Vec` stack.
While the stack isn't empty, pop a cell and push each unvisited land neighbor (marking it as you push). The `wrapping_sub(1)` and `grid.get(...)` trick from the BFS step handles the edges.
checkNames: a winding island is one island
water only and empty maps have none

steps.title: Topological sort: ordering tasks with dependencies
steps.task: Write `fn build_order(n: usize, deps: &[(usize, usize)]) -> Option<Vec<usize>>` for tasks `0..n`, where each `(a, b)` means task `a` must run before task `b`. Return the order (always taking the **smallest-numbered** ready task next), or `None` if there's a cycle. The tests include a chain of 200,000 tasks, so rescanning all tasks for a ready one each time is too slow.
hints: Build `next` (who waits for each task) and `indegree` (how many tasks each one waits for) from the pairs.
Put every task with in-degree 0 into a `BinaryHeap` as `Reverse(t)`, so `pop` gives the smallest. Pop, append, and lower the in-degree of each task in `next[t]`; push it when it reaches 0.
At the end, return `Some(order)` only if it contains all `n` tasks.
checkNames: takes the smallest ready task first
independent tasks run in number order

steps.title: Dijkstra's shortest paths with BinaryHeap
steps.task: Write `fn shortest_times(adj: &[Vec<(usize, u64)>], start: usize) -> Vec<Option<u64>>` that returns the cheapest total weight from `start` to every node (`None` for unreachable nodes). The graph is directed: `adj[u]` lists `(v, weight)` pairs. The tests include 100,000 nodes and 300,000 edges.
hints: Keep `dist: Vec<Option<u64>>` (or `u64::MAX` for unreached, converted at the end) and a heap of `Reverse((distance, node))`, starting with `Reverse((0, start))`.
Pop the smallest; skip it if `d` is bigger than the best distance already known for `u`.
For each `(v, weight)` in `adj[u]`: if `d + weight` beats `v`'s known distance (or `v` has none), store it and push `Reverse((d + weight, v))`.

require.message: Use a `BinaryHeap` (with `Reverse`) to pick the closest node.

checkNames: a cheap detour beats a direct road

steps.title: Binary trees with Option<Box<Node>>
steps.task:
The seed has a `Bst` with a working `insert`. Add three methods:

- `fn contains(&self, value: i32) -> bool`, walking down iteratively with `as_deref()`
- `fn height(&self) -> usize`: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down (0 for an empty tree, 1 for just a root)
- `fn sorted(&self) -> Vec<i32>`: all values in ascending order (an in-order walk)

Write recursive helper functions on `&Option<Box<Node>>` for `height` and `sorted`.
hints: `contains`: `let mut cur = self.root.as_deref();` then `while let Some(node) = cur`: return `true` on a match, otherwise move to `node.left.as_deref()` or `node.right.as_deref()`.
`height_of(slot)`: `None` is 0; `Some(node)` is `1 + height_of(&node.left).max(height_of(&node.right))`.
`sorted`: an in-order helper that recurses left, pushes `node.value`, then recurses right, like `in_order` in the lesson.

require.message: Walk down in `contains` with `as_deref()` and a loop.

checkNames: lists values in order without duplicates
sorted insertion makes a tall tree

steps.title: Union-find (disjoint sets)
steps.task:
Write a `UnionFind` with union by size and path compression:

- `fn new(n: usize) -> Self`: elements `0..n`, each alone
- `fn find(&mut self, x: usize) -> usize`: the root, compressing the path
- `fn union(&mut self, a: usize, b: usize) -> bool`: merge; `false` if they were already together
- `fn group_count(&self) -> usize`: how many separate groups there are
- `fn group_size(&mut self, x: usize) -> usize`: the size of `x`'s group

The tests merge 200,000 elements in a pattern that builds a 200,000-long chain without the two tricks.
hints: `new`: `parent: (0..n).collect()`, `size: vec![1; n]`, `groups: n`.

`find`: first walk up to the root; then walk the path again, setting each node's parent to the root. `union`: find both roots, return `false` if equal, otherwise hang the smaller under the bigger, add the sizes, and decrease `groups`.
`group_size(x)` is `self.size[self.find(x)]` (compute the root first, into a variable).
checkNames: union within a group returns false

modules.title: Capstone: Real Tickets
modules.summary: Six workplace tickets that combine everything in the course. Parse logs with FromStr and an error enum, build a traffic report, validate orders with thiserror, check a deploy config with serde, model an order workflow as a state machine, and refactor code for review.

steps.title: LOG-101: parse the access log
steps.task:
Implement the parser. The seed defines `LogEntry` and `ParseLogError`. Write:

- `impl fmt::Display for ParseLogError` with exactly these messages: `expected 5 fields, found N`, `unknown HTTP method: M`, `bad status code: S`, `bad latency: L`
- `impl FromStr for LogEntry`: split on whitespace; there must be exactly 5 fields (`WrongFieldCount` with the count otherwise); the method must be one of `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` (case-sensitive, `BadMethod` otherwise); the status must be a number from 100 to 599 (`BadStatus` with the text otherwise); the latency must parse as a `u32` (`BadLatency` with the text otherwise). Check in that order.

steps.title: SHOP-210: orders with validation
steps.task:
Implement `Inventory::place_order(&mut self, order: &[(&str, u32)]) -> Result<Receipt, OrderError>`. Each order line is `(sku, quantity)`. In this order:

1. An empty order is `OrderError::Empty`.
2. Going through the lines in order, the first line with quantity 0 gives `ZeroQuantity(sku)`, and the first unknown SKU gives `UnknownSku(sku)` (whichever line comes first; a line with both problems gives `ZeroQuantity`).
3. Add up the quantities per SKU. The first SKU (in order of first appearance) whose total exceeds its stock gives `OutOfStock { sku, requested: total, available: stock }`.
4. Only then reduce the stock and return a `Receipt` with one `ReceiptLine` per order line (product name, quantity, quantity times price) in order, and the total.

On any error, nothing in the inventory changes.
hints: Return `Err(OrderError::Empty)` first. Then loop over the lines checking `quantity == 0` and `self.products.contains_key(sku)`, and add each quantity to a per-SKU total (a small `Vec<(&str, u32)>` keeps first-appearance order).
Loop over the totals: if one is bigger than `self.products[sku].stock`, return `OutOfStock { sku: sku.to_string(), requested, available }`. Nothing has been changed yet.
Only now loop over the order again with `self.products.get_mut(sku)`: subtract the quantity, compute `price_cents * quantity as u64`, and push a `ReceiptLine`.

rejects orders bigger than the stock
adds up repeated lines for the same product
out of stock products cannot be ordered

projects.title: Higher or lower
projects.summary: The classic number guessing game, built up one feature at a time. Read guesses from input, count attempts, survive bad input, and generate the secret number yourself without any library.

milestones.title: Higher or lower
milestones.text:
Nearly every interactive program is a **loop** with the same three parts: read what the user did, work out what it means, and show the result. A text editor, a shell and a game server all have this loop at their heart. This project builds the smallest real example: a guessing game.

In this first version the secret number is simply the first line of input (you'll generate it yourself in milestone 4). Every line after that is a guess. For each guess, print one of:

- `Too low!` when the guess is smaller than the secret,
- `Too high!` when it's bigger,
- `You got it!` when it matches, and then stop reading: the game is over.

For this input:

```
42
50
25
42
```

the program prints:

```
Too high!
Too low!
You got it!
```

### How the starter code reads input

The starter code already reads the secret with `read_line` and `parse`, exactly as in the input module. The `for line in io::stdin().lock().lines()` loop then hands you the remaining lines one at a time, until the input ends. Each `line` is a `Result` (reading can fail), which is why there's an `.expect(...)` before you can use it as a `String`.

When you play this in a terminal, "input" is what you type. Here the tests feed the lines in, which is also how you'd test a real command-line tool: give it a known input, check the output.

Why `break` on the right guess instead of reading everything? Because the game is over. Anything after the winning line isn't a guess anymore, and a program shouldn't react to input that no longer means anything.
hints: Inside the loop, parse the line just like the secret: `let guess: i32 = line.trim().parse().expect("...");`
An `if guess < secret { ... } else if guess > secret { ... } else { ... }` chain covers the three cases.
In the `else` branch (the right guess), print `You got it!` and then `break;` to leave the loop.

milestones.title: Count the guesses
milestones.text:
A game without a score isn't much fun. Count every guess, and when the player wins, say how many it took:

```
You got it in 3 guesses!
```

With exactly one guess, it's `You got it in 1 guess!` (singular). Small details like this are what make a program feel finished.

There's a second case to handle: the input can run out before the player finds the number. Then print, after the loop:

```
Out of guesses! The number was 42.
```

### Remembering what happened

After the loop ends you need to know *why* it ended: did the player win (and you hit `break`), or did the guesses run out? The loop itself doesn't tell you, so keep a variable for it. A `let mut won = false;` before the loop, set to `true` on the winning guess, is the simplest way. Variables like this, which record what has happened so far, are the program's **state**. Here the state is two values: how many guesses so far, and whether the game was won.

For the plural, remember that `if` is an expression in Rust, so it can produce a value:

```rust
fn main() {
    let attempts = 1;
    let word = if attempts == 1 { "guess" } else { "guesses" };
    println!("{attempts} {word}");
}
```

```text
1 guess
```
hints: Add `let mut attempts = 0;` and `let mut won = false;` before the loop, and `attempts += 1;` for every guess.
`let word = if attempts == 1 { "guess" } else { "guesses" };` picks the right word.
After the loop, `if !won { println!("Out of guesses! The number was {secret}."); }`

milestones.title: Survive bad input
milestones.text:
Real users mistype. Right now, typing `fifty` crashes the whole game, because `.expect()` panics when `parse` fails. A crash is fine for a quick experiment, but a program people use should explain the problem and carry on.

Handle three kinds of line, and **don't count any of them as a guess**:

- A blank line (or only spaces): skip it silently.
- Something that isn't a whole number, like `fifty` or `12.5`: print `"fifty" is not a number` (the trimmed text, in double quotes).
- A number outside 1 to 100: print `Guesses go from 1 to 100`.

For this input:

```
42
50
fifty

420
42
```

the program prints:

```
Too high!
"fifty" is not a number
Guesses go from 1 to 100
You got it in 2 guesses!
```

### match instead of expect

`parse` returns a `Result`: `Ok(number)` when it worked, `Err(...)` when it didn't. Instead of `.expect()`, which turns an `Err` into a crash, `match` on it and decide what to do in each case:

```rust
fn main() {
    for text in ["17", "seventeen"] {
        let n: i32 = match text.parse() {
            Ok(n) => n,
            Err(_) => {
                println!("skipping {text}");
                continue;
            }
        };
        println!("got {n}");
    }
}
```

```text
got 17
skipping seventeen
```

The `Ok` arm gives the number to `n`. The `Err` arm prints a message and `continue`s to the next line, so it never needs to produce a number. (`continue` has the type `!`, "never returns", which fits anywhere.)

The order of checks matters: skip blank lines first, then parse, then check the range, and only then count the attempt. That way nothing invalid ever reaches the game logic. Validating input at the edge of a program, before it touches the real work, is a habit worth keeping in every program you write.

To print a double quote inside a string, escape it: `println!("\"{text}\" is not a number");`.

**Workplace note:** run `cargo clippy` (Rust's linter) on this and it suggests writing the range check as `!(1..=100).contains(&guess)`. Both mean the same thing; the `contains` form reads as "is in this range", and you'll see it a lot in real code.
hints: Trim the line once (`let text = line.trim();`) and `continue` if `text.is_empty()`.
Replace `.expect()` with `match text.parse() { Ok(n) => n, Err(_) => { println!(...); continue; } }`.
Check `guess < 1 || guess > 100` right after parsing, and `continue` before `attempts += 1`.

milestones.title: A secret of its own
milestones.text:
A guessing game where the player types the secret isn't much of a game. Real games pick it at random. But "random" output can't be tested (every run would differ), so games and simulations use a **pseudo-random number generator**: a formula that turns a starting number, the **seed**, into numbers that look random. The same seed always gives the same numbers, which is exactly what makes them testable. (Minecraft world seeds work this way.)

You'll write the oldest and simplest kind, a **linear congruential generator** (LCG). One step is: multiply by a big constant, add another constant, and let the result wrap around at 2^32:

```rust
fn main() {
    let seed: u32 = 1;
    let state = seed.wrapping_mul(1_103_515_245).wrapping_add(12_345);
    let secret = state / 65_536 % 100 + 1;
    println!("state {state}, secret {secret}");
}
```

```text
state 1103527590, secret 39
```

Piece by piece:

- `u32` is an unsigned 32-bit integer (0 to 4,294,967,295). Multiplying it by 1,103,515,245 goes way past that limit.
- In a debug build, plain `*` would **panic** with `attempt to multiply with overflow`: Rust treats overflow as a bug unless you say otherwise. `wrapping_mul` and `wrapping_add` say "wrapping around is what I want". The LCG depends on it.
- `state / 65_536` throws away the low 16 bits, which are the least random part of an LCG. `% 100` gives 0 to 99, and `+ 1` makes it 1 to 100.

**Now change the game:**

- The first line of input is a **seed** (a `u32`), not the secret. Compute the secret from it with one LCG step, as above. Convert it with `as i32` so you can compare it with the guesses.
- The player gets at most **7 guesses**. After the 7th wrong guess, stop reading and print `Out of guesses! The number was N.` (the same message as when the input runs out). Invalid lines still don't count.

Put the limit in a constant, `const MAX_ATTEMPTS: i32 = 7;`, rather than writing `7` in the middle of the loop. A named constant says what the number means, and when a designer asks for 10 guesses you change one line.

With seed `1` the secret is 39, so this game takes 6 guesses:

```
1
50
25
37
43
40
39
```
hints: Parse the first line as `let seed: u32`, then `let state = seed.wrapping_mul(1_103_515_245).wrapping_add(12_345);`
`let secret = (state / 65_536 % 100) as i32 + 1;` turns the state into 1 to 100.
After printing `Too low!` or `Too high!`, check `if attempts == MAX_ATTEMPTS { break; }`. The `if !won` after the loop then prints the message.

milestones.title: Polish: functions and close calls
milestones.text:
Your `main` now does everything: it makes the secret, validates input, compares, and formats messages. It works, but it's getting long, and long functions are where bugs hide. Professional code splits a program into small functions that each do one job and have a name that says what that job is. Then `main` reads like a summary of the game.

Split out these three functions (exact names are up to you, but these are good ones):

- `fn make_secret(seed: u32) -> i32`: the LCG step from the last milestone.
- `fn hint(guess: i32, secret: i32) -> String`: the message for a wrong guess.
- `fn guesses(n: i32) -> String`: `"1 guess"` or `"3 guesses"`.

And while you're in there, make the hints friendlier. When a wrong guess is **within 5** of the secret, say so:

```
Too low, but close!
Too high, but close!
```

Farther away, keep `Too low!` and `Too high!`. With seed `1` (secret 39), the game from the last milestone now prints:

```
Too high!
Too low!
Too low, but close!
Too high, but close!
Too high, but close!
You got it in 6 guesses!
```

### Building the message in a function

`hint` returns a `String`, built with `format!`. The distance between two numbers is the difference without its sign, which `.abs()` gives you:

```rust
fn hint(guess: i32, secret: i32) -> String {
    let direction = if guess < secret { "low" } else { "high" };
    if (guess - secret).abs() <= 5 {
        format!("Too {direction}, but close!")
    } else {
        format!("Too {direction}!")
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", hint(36, 39));
    println!("{}", hint(80, 39));
}
```

```text
Too low, but close!
Too high!
```

Notice what the function *doesn't* do: it doesn't print. It returns the text and lets the caller decide what to do with it. Functions that compute values without printing are easier to reuse and to test (in the testing module you'll write `assert_eq!(hint(36, 39), "Too low, but close!")` for exactly this kind of function).

Once it all works, read your `main` from top to bottom. It should tell the story of the game without you having to decode any arithmetic.

In `hint`, compute `direction` as `"low"` or `"high"`, then pick between two `format!` calls with `if (guess - secret).abs() <= 5`.
In `main`, handle `guess == secret` first; for every other guess print `hint(guess, secret)`.

projects.title: A to-do list manager
projects.summary: A command interpreter for your to-do list. Read commands like `add`, `done` and `remove` from input, keep tasks in a Vec of structs, give them stable ids, and parse every line into an enum before acting on it.

milestones.title: Add and list
milestones.text:
Shells, database consoles, chat bots and game consoles all work the same way: read a line, figure out which **command** it is, run it, print the result, repeat. That loop is called a **command interpreter** (or a REPL, for "read, evaluate, print, loop"). In this project you'll build one for a to-do list.

Each line of input is one command. In this first milestone there are two:

- `add Buy milk` adds a task and prints `Added #1: Buy milk`. The number is the task's position in the list, starting at 1.
- `list` prints every task as `1. [ ] Buy milk` (the `[ ]` becomes `[x]` once a task is done, in the next milestone). If there are no tasks, it prints `No tasks.`

Any other command prints `Error: unknown command "fly"` (with the command's name).

```
add Buy milk
add Walk the dog
list
```

prints:

```
Added #1: Buy milk
Added #2: Walk the dog
1. [ ] Buy milk
2. [ ] Walk the dog
```

### What the starter code gives you

The `Task` struct holds one task. The list is a `Vec<Task>`: tasks keep the order they were added in, and a `Vec` grows as you push. The loop reads one line at a time, trims it and skips blank lines.

Two new tools appear in the starter code:

- `let line = line.trim();` **shadows** the `String` with a trimmed `&str` view of it. The original `String` still lives until the end of the loop body (shadowing hides a variable, it doesn't drop it), so the borrow is fine.
- `line.split_once(' ')` splits a string at the first space and returns `Some((before, after))`, or `None` if there's no space at all. `"add Buy milk"` becomes `("add", "Buy milk")`. A line like `list` has no space, so the `None` arm uses the whole line as the command and `""` as the rest.

Then `match command { "add" => ..., "list" => ..., _ => ... }` picks the command. Matching on string slices works just like matching on numbers.

To print the tasks with their numbers, `tasks.iter().enumerate()` gives you each task together with its index, starting at 0:

```rust
fn main() {
    let names = vec!["crab", "ferris"];
    for (i, name) in names.iter().enumerate() {
        println!("{} {}", i + 1, name);
    }
}
```

```text
1 crab
2 ferris
```

For `add`: `tasks.push(Task { text: rest.to_string(), done: false });` then print `tasks.len()` as the number.
For `list`: `let mark = if task.done { 'x' } else { ' ' };` inside `for (i, task) in tasks.iter().enumerate()`, and print `i + 1`.

milestones.title: Check things off
milestones.text:
A to-do list is only satisfying if you can tick things off. Add the `done` command:

- `done 2` marks task number 2 as done and prints `Completed #2: Walk the dog`. After that, `list` shows it as `2. [x] Walk the dog`.
- If it's already done, print `Task #2 is already done`.

The number comes from the user, so it can be wrong in several ways. Handle each with a clear message instead of a crash:

- Not a number (`done zero`, `done -1`): `Error: "zero" is not a task number`.
- No such task (`done 7` with 2 tasks, or `done 0`): `Error: no task #7`.
- And while you're validating input: `add` with no description prints `Error: add needs a description` and adds nothing.

### People count from 1, vectors from 0

The user types `done 1` for the first task, which lives at `tasks[0]`. Converting between the two is a classic source of **off-by-one** bugs. Check the range *before* indexing: `tasks[number - 1]` with `number == 0` would subtract below zero (a panic for `usize`), and a number past the end panics with `index out of bounds`.

```rust
if number == 0 || number > tasks.len() {
    println!("Error: no task #{number}");
    continue;
}
let task = &mut tasks[number - 1];
```

`&mut tasks[number - 1]` borrows that one task mutably, so you can set `task.done = true` and still print `task.text`.

Parse the number as a `usize` (the type of `Vec` indexes and lengths) with a `match` on `rest.parse()`, as in the input module. A negative number like `-1` simply fails to parse as `usize`, so it gets the "not a task number" message for free.
hints: Parse with `let number: usize = match rest.parse() { Ok(n) => n, Err(_) => { println!(...); continue; } };`
Reject `number == 0 || number > tasks.len()` before you touch the vector.
`let task = &mut tasks[number - 1];` then check `task.done` before setting it to `true`.
