milestones.title: Remove tasks, keep their ids
milestones.text:
Add `remove`, and you'll hit a real design problem. Say the list is:

```
1. [ ] Buy milk
2. [ ] Walk the dog
3. [ ] Call mom
```

After `remove 2`, "Call mom" moves to position 2. A user (or a script) that still thinks "Call mom" is task 3 now types `done 3` and gets an error, or worse, in a longer list, ticks off the wrong task. Numbers that change under your feet are a bug factory.

The fix every real system uses (databases, issue trackers, this site's lesson ids) is a **stable id**: each task gets a number when it's created, and keeps it forever. Ids are never reused, even after a removal.

**Change the program so that:**

- Each `Task` has an `id: u32`. The first task added gets 1, the next 2, and so on, from a counter that only goes up.
- `list`, `done` and the messages use the id instead of the position: after removing task 2, the list shows `1. [ ] Buy milk` and `3. [ ] Call mom`, and `done 3` completes "Call mom".
- `remove 2` removes the task with id 2 and prints `Removed #2: Walk the dog`. The same errors as `done` apply: `Error: "x" is not a task number` and `Error: no task #9`.

### Give the list its own type

The list now has two pieces of state that belong together: the tasks and the next id. Put them in a struct with methods, so `main` doesn't have to know how ids are handed out:

```rust
struct TodoList {
    tasks: Vec<Task>,
    next_id: u32,
}

impl TodoList {
    fn new() -> Self { ... }                                       // next_id starts at 1
    fn add(&mut self, text: String) -> &Task { ... }               // returns the new task
    fn find_mut(&mut self, id: u32) -> Option<&mut Task> { ... }
    fn remove(&mut self, id: u32) -> Option<Task> { ... }
}
```

- `find_mut` walks the tasks with `for task in &mut self.tasks` and returns `Some(task)` when the id matches, `None` after the loop. (In the iterators module you'll write this as one line, `self.tasks.iter_mut().find(|task| task.id == id)`, which is what clippy suggests. The loop does exactly the same work.)
- `remove` needs the *position* to call `Vec::remove`, so loop over `0..self.tasks.len()` and return `Some(self.tasks.remove(i))`. `Vec::remove` hands the removed task back to you (it moves out of the vector), so the caller can still print its text.
- `add` returns a reference to the task it just pushed (`&self.tasks[self.tasks.len() - 1]`), which is handy for printing its id.

This is **encapsulation**: the rule "ids only go up" lives in one place, `add`, and nothing else can break it.
hints: Add `id: u32` to `Task` and a `TodoList { tasks, next_id }` struct whose `add` gives out `next_id` and then increments it.
`find_mut`: `for task in &mut self.tasks { if task.id == id { return Some(task); } } None`.
A small `fn parse_id(text: &str) -> Option<u32>` keeps `done` and `remove` short: `let Some(id) = parse_id(rest) else { ...; continue; };`

milestones.title: Parse commands into an enum
milestones.text:
Look at your `main`: the loop splits the line, checks arguments, parses numbers, *and* changes the list, all mixed together. Every new command makes it longer, and nothing stops you from forgetting a check in one of the arms.

Professional interpreters split this into two phases:

1. **Parse**: turn the text into a value that says exactly what to do, or explain why the line is wrong.
2. **Execute**: carry out a command that is already known to be valid.

The "value that says what to do" is a perfect job for an enum, one variant per command, carrying exactly the data that command needs:

```rust
enum Command {
    Add(String),
    Done(u32),
    Remove(u32),
    List,
    Clear,
}
```

An `Add` always has its text and a `Done` always has a valid id, so the execute phase never has to check again. And when you add a sixth command later, the compiler points at every `match` that doesn't handle it yet. That's the main reason Rust programmers reach for enums: the compiler keeps track of the cases for you.

### A function that can fail: Result

Parsing can fail, and the caller needs to know why. You've been matching on `Result` since the input module (`parse` returns one). Your own functions can return one too: `Ok(value)` on success, `Err(error)` on failure. Here the error is just the message:

```rust
fn parse_command(line: &str) -> Result<Command, String> {
    ...
    match command {
        "add" if rest.is_empty() => Err(String::from("add needs a description")),
        "add" => Ok(Command::Add(rest.to_string())),
        ...
    }
}
```

The errors module covers `Result` in depth (including the `?` operator, a shortcut for "if this failed, return the error").

**Make these changes:**

- Write `parse_command` and use it in `main`: on `Err(message)` print `Error: {message}`; on `Ok(command)`, `match` on the command and run it.
- Improve the messages for missing numbers: `done` alone prints `Error: done needs a task number`, and `remove` alone prints `Error: remove needs a task number`. (A non-number is still `Error: "x" is not a task number`.)
- Add the `clear` command: it removes every finished task and prints `Cleared 2 finished tasks` (or `Cleared 1 finished task`, or `Cleared 0 finished tasks`).

For `clear`, `Vec::retain` keeps only the elements for which a test returns `true`: `self.tasks.retain(|task| !task.done);`. Compare the length before and after to know how many were removed.
hints: Start with `enum Command { Add(String), Done(u32), Remove(u32), List, Clear }` and move the splitting code into `fn parse_command(line: &str) -> Result<Command, String>`.
A helper `fn parse_id(command: &str, rest: &str) -> Result<u32, String>` can return `Err(format!("{command} needs a task number"))` when `rest` is empty.
`clear_done`: remember `self.tasks.len()`, call `self.tasks.retain(|task| !task.done);`, and return the difference.

milestones.title: Polish: filters and a progress line
milestones.text:
Time to make the list pleasant to use, and to finish the parse/execute split.

**New behavior:**

- `list` still shows every task, and now ends with a progress line: `1 of 3 done`.
- `list todo` shows only unfinished tasks, and `list done` only finished ones. Both end with the same progress line, which always counts the whole list.
- Any other filter is an error: `Error: unknown filter "later" (use todo or done)`.
- When the list is completely empty, every `list` still prints just `No tasks.`, with no progress line.

```
add Buy milk
add Walk the dog
add Call mom
done 2
list todo
```

ends with:

```
1. [ ] Buy milk
3. [ ] Call mom
1 of 3 done
```

### An enum inside an enum

The filter is another small enum, carried by the `List` variant:

```rust
enum Filter {
    All,
    Todo,
    Done,
}

enum Command {
    ...
    List(Filter),
}
```

Give `Filter` a method `fn matches(&self, task: &Task) -> bool` with a `match` inside. Then the list command is just "print every task the filter matches", and the knowledge of what "todo" means lives in one place.

Why not a `String` for the filter? Because then every piece of code that looks at it has to handle typos like `"tood"`. With an enum, a filter that exists is a filter that's valid: the parser rejects bad ones once, at the edge, and the rest of the program can't even express them. "Make invalid states unrepresentable" is a design rule you'll hear a lot in Rust teams.

### Move execution into its own function

Finally, pull the big `match command { ... }` out of `main` into `fn run(list: &mut TodoList, command: Command)`. Then `main` reads like the description of the program: read a line, parse it, report an error or run it. Each function now does one job, and you could test `parse_command` on its own without any input at all.
hints: Add `enum Filter { All, Todo, Done }`, change the variant to `List(Filter)`, and in `parse_command` match `rest` against `""`, `"todo"` and `"done"`.
`Filter::matches` is a `match self { Filter::All => true, Filter::Todo => !task.done, Filter::Done => task.done }`.
In the list command, `return` right after printing `No tasks.` so the progress line only appears for a non-empty list.

projects.title: A bank ledger
projects.summary: Process a day of banking from a ledger file. Transactions become an enum, every rule is checked with Result and the ? operator, transfers never leave money half-moved, and each account gets a statement.

milestones.title: Accounts in a map
milestones.text:
Banks, shops and payment apps all keep a **ledger**: a list of transactions, processed in order, that moves money between accounts. In this project your program reads a ledger, one transaction per line, keeps every balance up to date, and explains clearly when a line can't be processed.

This first milestone handles three commands, and you can assume every line is valid:

| Line | Effect | Prints |
|---|---|---|
| `open alice 100` | creates account `alice` with 100 | `opened alice with 100` |
| `deposit alice 25` | adds 25 | `alice: +25, balance 125` |
| `withdraw alice 30` | takes 30 out | `alice: -30, balance 95` |

After the last line, print every account in name order:

```
Balances:
  alice: 95
  bob: 50
```

### Why a BTreeMap

You look accounts up by name, so a map from `String` to balance fits. A `HashMap` would work for the lookups, but it iterates in an unpredictable order, and a bank report that shuffles itself every run is useless (and untestable). A `BTreeMap` keeps its keys sorted, so the final report comes out in name order for free.

Balances are `u64`: whole coins that can never be negative. Real systems also use integers for money (counting cents instead of dollars), because floating point can't represent 0.10 exactly.

### Splitting the line

The starter code turns each line into a `Vec<&str>` of words: `split_whitespace()` produces the words and `.collect()` gathers them into a vector. A **slice pattern** then matches the command and its arguments in one go, and names them:

```rust
fn main() {
    let line = "deposit alice 25";
    let parts: Vec<&str> = line.split_whitespace().collect();
    match parts.as_slice() {
        ["deposit", name, amount] => println!("deposit {amount} into {name}"),
        _ => println!("something else"),
    }
}
```

```text
deposit 25 into alice
```

For `deposit` and `withdraw`, `balances.get_mut(*name)` gives an `Option<&mut u64>`. Since the input is valid for now, `.expect("unknown account")` is fine: milestone 3 replaces it with proper errors. (`name` is a `&&str` here, a reference to an element of the vector; `*name` gets the `&str`.)
hints: `match parts.as_slice() { ["open", name, amount] => { ... } ... }` gives you the pieces by name.
Parse the amount in each arm with `let amount: u64 = amount.parse().expect("...");`, then `*balance += amount;` through `balances.get_mut(*name)`.
At the end, `for (name, balance) in &balances { println!("  {name}: {balance}"); }` prints them sorted.

milestones.title: Transactions as an enum
milestones.text:
Real ledger files contain mistakes: a typo in a command, a missing amount, `ten` instead of `10`. Right now any of them crashes the program and loses the whole day. Instead, a bad line should be reported with its line number and skipped, and the rest of the ledger processed.

```
open alice 100
deposit alice ten
fly away
open bob
withdraw alice 30
```

prints:

```
opened alice with 100
line 2: invalid amount "ten"
line 3: unknown command "fly"
line 4: usage: open NAME AMOUNT
alice: -30, balance 70
Balances:
  alice: 70
```

### Two steps: parse, then apply

Turning text into an action is one job; doing the action is another. Give the first job its own function that returns a value saying exactly what to do, or an error explaining why it can't:

```rust
enum Transaction {
    Open { name: String, amount: u64 },
    Deposit { name: String, amount: u64 },
    Withdraw { name: String, amount: u64 },
}

fn parse_line(line: &str) -> Result<Transaction, String> { ... }
fn apply(balances: &mut BTreeMap<String, u64>, tx: Transaction) -> String { ... }
```

Why an enum? A transaction is exactly *one of* a few kinds, and each kind carries its own data. Once a line is a `Transaction`, the amount is already a number and the command is already known; `apply` can't receive a malformed line, because there's no way to build one. (`apply` returns the message to print, and `main` does the printing.)

### The ? operator does the plumbing

Parsing the amount can fail in every arm. Write it once:

```rust
fn parse_amount(text: &str) -> Result<u64, String> {
    text.parse().map_err(|_| format!("invalid amount \"{text}\""))
}
```

`map_err` swaps parse's error type for your own message. Then, inside `parse_line`, `parse_amount(amount)?` means "give me the number, or return this error from `parse_line` right now". No nested `match` needed.

The error messages to produce:

- wrong number of words for a known command: `usage: open NAME AMOUNT` (with that command's name),
- an unknown command: `unknown command "fly"`,
- an amount that isn't a non-negative whole number: `invalid amount "ten"`.

In `main`, print errors as `line N: message`, where N counts every line of input from 1 (blank lines included, so the number matches what you'd see in an editor). `.lines().enumerate()` gives you the index alongside each line.
hints: Each slice pattern arm builds a variant: `["deposit", name, amount] => Ok(Transaction::Deposit { name: name.to_string(), amount: parse_amount(amount)? })`.
An `@` binding catches the usage errors: `[command @ ("open" | "deposit" | "withdraw"), ..] => Err(format!("usage: {command} NAME AMOUNT"))`. Put it after the full patterns.
In `main`, loop with `for (i, line) in io::stdin().lock().lines().enumerate()` and print errors as `line {}: {message}` with `i + 1`.

milestones.title: Transfers that never half-happen
milestones.text:
Add the most important banking operation:

```
transfer alice bob 30
```

moves 30 from Alice to Bob and prints `transferred 30 from alice to bob`. A transfer is a withdrawal and a deposit glued together, and the glue is the hard part.

### All or nothing

Imagine writing it as "withdraw from Alice, then deposit to Bob". If Bob's account doesn't exist, the deposit fails *after* Alice's money is gone. The money has vanished. Databases call the property you need **atomicity**: either the whole transfer happens, or none of it does.

The simple way to get it in your code: **check everything first, change things last.**

1. The amount is positive.
2. The two accounts are different (`cannot transfer from alice to itself`).
3. The sender exists, then the receiver exists (`no account named "carol"`).
4. The sender has enough (`insufficient funds: alice has 10, needs 30`).
5. Only now, update both balances.

Every `?` and `return Err(...)` happens in steps 1 to 4, before anything is modified, so an error can never leave the bank half-updated. Check in exactly this order, since the first failing check decides the message.

A read-only helper makes the checks easy:

```rust
fn balance(&self, name: &str) -> Result<u64, String> {
    match self.accounts.get(name) {
        Some(balance) => Ok(*balance),
        None => Err(format!("no account named \"{name}\"")),
    }
}
```

Then read both balances with `?`, check, and write both back with `insert`.

**Also:** add the `Transfer { from, to, amount }` variant, parse `transfer FROM TO AMOUNT`, and report a wrong word count as `usage: transfer FROM TO AMOUNT`. When you add the variant, notice how the compiler immediately complains that `apply`'s `match` doesn't cover it. That's the enum keeping you honest.
hints: Add `Transfer { from: String, to: String, amount: u64 }`, a `["transfer", from, to, amount]` arm in `parse_line`, and a `["transfer", ..]` usage arm after it.
In `transfer`, do every check (`check_positive`, `from == to`, `self.balance(from)?`, `self.balance(to)?`, enough money) before changing anything.
Write the new balances with `self.accounts.insert(from.to_string(), from_balance - amount);` and the same for `to`.

milestones.title: Polish: history and statements
milestones.text:
Every bank gives customers a **statement**: the transactions on their account, with the balance after each. Add a `statement NAME` command:

```
open alice 100
open bob 50
deposit alice 25
transfer alice bob 30
withdraw bob 20
statement alice
```

ends with:

```
statement for alice
  opened                  +100     100
  deposit                  +25     125
  transfer to bob          -30      95
```

For Bob, the transfer appears as `transfer from alice` with `+30`, and his withdrawal as `withdrawal` with `-20`. Rejected transactions never appear: they didn't happen. `statement` for an unknown account is an error (`no account named "carol"`), and a wrong word count is `usage: statement NAME`.

Each entry line is two spaces, the description padded to 22 characters, the change with its sign in 6 characters, and the balance in 8: `format!("  {what:<22}{change:>+6}{balance:>8}")`. The `+` flag prints the sign of positive numbers too.

### Keep the history, replay it

Real ledgers don't store "Alice's statement". They store the transactions, and compute everything else from them. Add `history: Vec<Transaction>` to `Bank`, and record each transaction **only after** it succeeds:

```rust
fn record(&mut self, tx: Transaction) -> Result<String, String> {
    let message = self.apply(&tx)?;
    self.history.push(tx);
    Ok(message)
}
```

This is why `apply` borrows the transaction: `record` keeps ownership so it can move `tx` into the history afterwards.

A statement then walks the history, asks "how did this transaction change *this* account?", and keeps a running balance. Write that question as its own function, returning `None` for transactions that don't touch the account:

```rust
fn effect(tx: &Transaction, name: &str) -> Option<(String, i64)>
```

A `match` with guards (`Transaction::Transfer { from, to, amount } if from == name => ...`) answers it neatly. The change is an `i64` because it can be negative.

### A statement isn't a transaction

You could add a `Statement` variant to `Transaction`, but then the history could contain statements, and every `match` on transactions would need a "this isn't really a transaction" arm. Instead, wrap the two kinds of line in a separate enum:

```rust
enum Command {
    Record(Transaction),
    Statement(String),
}
```

`parse_line` returns a `Command`, and `process` matches on it. A `Transaction` now always means money moved, and the type system guarantees it.
hints: Add `history: Vec<Transaction>` to `Bank` and a `record` method that calls `self.apply(&tx)?` and then pushes `tx`.
`effect` is a `match tx` with guards, for example `Transaction::Deposit { name: n, amount } if n == name => Some((String::from("deposit"), *amount as i64))`, and `_ => None` at the end.

`statement` checks the account with `self.balance(name)?`, then loops over `&self.history`, adds each change to a running `i64` balance and appends `format!("\n  {what:<22}{change:>+6}{balance:>8}")`.

projects.title: A text statistics report
projects.summary: Build a tool that reads any text and reports lines, words and characters, word frequencies, the most common and longest words, and averages, in a tidy, deterministic report.

milestones.title: Count like wc
milestones.text:
Unix systems ship a tiny tool called `wc` ("word count") that has been counting lines and words since 1971. Editors show the same numbers in their status bar, and every writing app has a word counter. In this project you'll build a richer version: a text statistics report.

Start with the basics. Read the whole input (the starter code does this with `read_to_string`) and print:

```
lines: 2
words: 11
characters: 47
bytes: 47
```

- **lines**: how many lines the text has. `text.lines()` splits at line endings (and doesn't count an empty piece after the final newline).
- **words**: pieces separated by whitespace, exactly what `split_whitespace()` gives.
- **characters**: Unicode characters, newlines included: `text.chars().count()`.
- **bytes**: the size in UTF-8 bytes: `text.len()`.

`lines()` and `split_whitespace()` don't build a list; they hand out pieces one at a time. `.count()` counts the pieces without storing any of them.

### Why characters and bytes differ

For plain English text the last two numbers are equal. For anything else they aren't: `é` is 2 bytes, `🦀` is 4. Rust's `String` is always UTF-8, and `len()` reports bytes because that's what the string actually stores. Whenever a number is shown to a person ("this tweet has 280 characters"), you almost always want characters, not bytes.

```rust
fn main() {
    let s = "crab 🦀";
    println!("{} chars, {} bytes", s.chars().count(), s.len());
}
```

```text
6 chars, 9 bytes
```
hints: Each number is one expression: `text.lines().count()`, `text.split_whitespace().count()`, `text.chars().count()` and `text.len()`.
Print them as `println!("lines: {}", text.lines().count());` and so on, in the order lines, words, characters, bytes.

milestones.title: Word frequencies
milestones.text:
Counting *how often* each word appears is the first step of search engines, spam filters and plagiarism checkers. But first you have to decide what "the same word" means. In `The crab, the CRAB!`, a person sees `the` twice and `crab` twice. `split_whitespace` sees four different pieces: `The`, `crab,`, `the`, `CRAB!`.

So each piece needs **normalizing** before counting:

1. Strip punctuation from both ends (but keep it inside, so `don't` and `well-known` survive).
2. Lowercase it.
3. If nothing is left (a piece like `--` or `...`), it isn't a word: skip it.

```rust
fn normalize(raw: &str) -> String {
    raw.trim_matches(|c: char| !c.is_alphanumeric()).to_lowercase()
}

fn main() {
    for raw in ["Crab,", "\"Hello!\"", "don't", "--", "ÉLAN"] {
        println!("{raw} -> {:?}", normalize(raw));
    }
}
```

```text
Crab, -> "crab"
"Hello!" -> "hello"
don't -> "don't"
-- -> ""
ÉLAN -> "élan"
```

`trim_matches` removes characters from both ends for as long as a test says yes. The test here is a **closure**, `|c: char| !c.is_alphanumeric()`: a small unnamed function that takes a `char` and returns `true` for anything that isn't a letter or digit. You'll study closures properly later; for now read `|c| ...` as "given `c`, compute ...". `to_lowercase` works on all of Unicode (`É` becomes `é`), which is why it returns a new `String` rather than changing letters in place.

### Counting

Count the normalized words in a `BTreeMap<String, usize>` with the entry API you met in the hashmaps module:

```rust
*counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1;
```

After the four lines from milestone 1, print how many different words there are, then every word with its count, in alphabetical order:

```
unique words: 8
  a: 1
  ate: 1
  crab: 2
  fish: 1
  ...
```

A `BTreeMap` iterates in key order, so the alphabetical list costs nothing extra. With a `HashMap` the order would change from run to run, which makes output impossible to compare or test. (The `words:` line keeps counting raw pieces like `wc` does, so `--` still counts there.)
hints: `fn normalize(raw: &str) -> String { raw.trim_matches(|c: char| !c.is_alphanumeric()).to_lowercase() }`
Loop over `text.split_whitespace()`, normalize each piece, `continue` if it's empty, and count it with `*counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1;`.
Print `unique words: {}` with `counts.len()`, then `for (word, count) in &counts` prints them in alphabetical order.

milestones.title: The top five
milestones.text:
A full word list is fine for a sentence but useless for a book. What people actually want is the **most common** words. Replace the full list with the top five:

```
unique words: 8
top words:
  1. the              3
  2. crab             2
  3. a                1
  4. ate              1
  5. fish             1
```

Each line is two spaces, the rank, a period and a space, then the word left-aligned in 15 characters and the count right-aligned in 3: `println!("  {}. {word:<15}{count:>3}", i + 1)`. If there are fewer than five words, show them all.

### Sorting by count, then by word

A map is sorted by its keys, but now you need to sort by the *values*. The usual approach: copy the entries into a `Vec` and sort that.

```rust
use std::collections::BTreeMap;

fn main() {
    let mut counts: BTreeMap<String, usize> = BTreeMap::new();
    for word in ["rust", "crab", "rust", "fast", "crab", "safe"] {
        *counts.entry(word.to_string()).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }
    let mut ranked: Vec<(&String, &usize)> = counts.iter().collect();
    ranked.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(a.1).then(a.0.cmp(b.0)));
    println!("{ranked:?}");
}
```

```text
[("crab", 2), ("rust", 2), ("fast", 1), ("safe", 1)]
```

- `counts.iter().collect()` makes a vector of `(&String, &usize)` pairs. They borrow from the map, so no strings are copied.
- `sort_by` takes a closure that compares two elements and returns an `Ordering` (`Less`, `Equal` or `Greater`).
- `b.1.cmp(a.1)` compares the counts **backwards** (b before a), which sorts from most to least common.
- `.then(a.0.cmp(b.0))` breaks ties alphabetically. Without a tie-breaker, words with equal counts could come out in any order the sort likes, and "any order" is the enemy of reproducible output.

After sorting, `ranked.truncate(5)` keeps the first five (and does nothing if there are fewer).

### Width and alignment

`{word:<15}` pads the word with spaces on the right to 15 characters; `{count:>3}` pads the number on the left to 3. That's how command-line tools print tidy columns without any table library. (A word longer than 15 characters simply pushes its count to the right; widths are minimums, nothing is ever cut.)
hints: `let mut ranked: Vec<(&String, &usize)> = counts.iter().collect();` gives you something you can sort.
`ranked.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(a.1).then(a.0.cmp(b.0)));` sorts by count (most first), then alphabetically. Then `ranked.truncate(5);`.
Print with `for (i, (word, count)) in ranked.iter().enumerate()` and `println!("  {}. {word:<15}{count:>3}", i + 1);`.

milestones.title: Longest words and averages
milestones.text:
Readability formulas (the ones that tell you a text reads at a "grade 8 level") are built from exactly two kinds of numbers: how long the words are, and how long the sentences are. Add the word side. After `unique words:`, print the average word length, and after the top words, the three longest words:

```
unique words: 8
average word length: 3.09
top words:
  ...
longest words:
  1. crab (4)
  2. fish (4)
  3. rock (4)
```

- **Average word length**: the total number of characters in all normalized words (counting every occurrence, so `the` used 3 times adds 9) divided by the number of normalized words, with 2 decimals (`{:.2}`).
- **Longest words**: distinct words (each listed once), longest first, ties in alphabetical order, at most three. Length means characters, not bytes, so `élan` has length 4.

### Reuse what you have

Both numbers can be computed from the `counts` map; there's no need to read the text again. Each entry already tells you a word and how many times it occurs.

For the average, convert to `f64` before dividing: `letters as f64 / total as f64`. Dividing two integers would throw away the fraction (`47 / 14` is `3`).

For the longest words, sort the map's keys with the same two-level comparison as before: by length (backwards), then alphabetically:

```rust
let mut words: Vec<&String> = counts.keys().collect();
words.sort_by(|a, b| b.chars().count().cmp(&a.chars().count()).then(a.cmp(b)));
```

(`cmp` takes its argument by reference, hence the `&` in `cmp(&a.chars().count())`: the counts are fresh numbers, not references into the map like before.)

One surprise to know about: comparing strings with `cmp` orders them by Unicode code point, so `zeal` sorts *before* `élan` (`é` comes after every ASCII letter). For a report that's fine and, more importantly, deterministic. Sorting the way a dictionary in a given language does is called **collation**, and it needs a dedicated library.
hints: Loop over `&counts` once, adding `word.chars().count() * count` to `letters` and `count` to `total`; print `letters as f64 / total as f64` with `{:.2}`.
`let mut words: Vec<&String> = counts.keys().collect();` then sort by `b.chars().count().cmp(&a.chars().count()).then(a.cmp(b))` and `truncate(3)`.
Print the average right after `unique words:`, and the longest words after the top words.

milestones.title: Sorted stock and category totals
milestones.text:
A stock list in whatever order it was typed is hard to read. Sort it **by category, then by name**, and after the items, print a summary line per category with its number of units and the total value of that stock (price times quantity):

```
apple      food      $0.40  x200
drill      tools    $89.99  x3
hammer     tools    $12.50  x10
teddy      toys     $15.00  x8
food: 200 units, $80.00
tools: 13 units, $394.97
toys: 8 units, $120.00
```

Categories come in the order food, tools, toys: the order the variants are declared in.

### Deriving an order

To sort by category, Rust has to know how to compare two categories. You could write that by hand, but `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]` on the enum does it for you: variants compare in **declaration order**, so `Food < Tools < Toys`. Then:

```rust
self.items.sort_by(|a, b| a.category.cmp(&b.category).then(a.name.cmp(&b.name)));
```

sorts by category and breaks ties by name, the same two-level comparison you'd use in any sort.

The derived order pays off twice: a `BTreeMap<Category, (u32, Money)>` needs keys that implement `Ord`, and it then keeps the categories sorted for the summary. One derive line, two features.

### Arithmetic on Money

You need "price times quantity" and "add this to the running total". Give `Money` small methods:

```rust
impl Money {
    fn times(self, qty: u32) -> Money { ... }
    fn plus(self, other: Money) -> Money { ... }
}
```

(In the std-traits module you'll learn to make `+` itself work on your types; methods are perfectly idiomatic too.) Because `Money` derives `Copy`, these can take `self` by value without moving anything away.

### A Shop type

Put the items in a `struct Shop { items: Vec<Item> }` with two methods, `sort(&mut self)` and `print_stock(&self)`. `main` then just loads, sorts and prints. Notice which method needs `&mut self` and which only `&self`: the signature tells every reader whether a call can change the shop.

For the totals, the entry API gives you mutable access to both halves of the tuple at once:

```rust
let (units, value) = by_category.entry(item.category).or_insert((0, Money(0)));
*units += item.qty;
*value = value.plus(item.price.times(item.qty));
```
hints: Add `PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord` to the `#[derive(...)]` on `Category`, then sort with `a.category.cmp(&b.category).then(a.name.cmp(&b.name))`.
`Money::times` is `Money(self.0 * qty as u64)` and `Money::plus` is `Money(self.0 + other.0)`.
In `print_stock`, print each item while adding it to a `BTreeMap<Category, (u32, Money)>`, then loop over the map for the summary lines `{category}: {units} units, {value}`.

milestones.title: Bad lines and a real error type
milestones.text:
Stock lists are typed by people, exported from spreadsheets and edited by scripts, so they contain mistakes. Right now one bad line panics and the shop can't open. Instead, report each bad line with its line number, skip it, and load the rest:

```
line 5: unknown category "garden"
line 6: invalid price "0.1"
line 8: duplicate item "apple"
line 9: expected 4 fields, found 3
```

The error lines come first (as each line is loaded), then the sorted stock and summary as before.

| Problem | Message |
|---|---|
| not exactly 4 comma-separated fields | `expected 4 fields, found 3` |
| a price that isn't dollars with exactly two decimals (`12.50`), or whole dollars (`12`) | `invalid price "0.1"` |
| a quantity that isn't a whole number 0 or above | `invalid quantity "many"` |
| a category other than food, tools, toys | `unknown category "garden"` |
| a name that's already in the shop | `duplicate item "apple"` |

### One enum for everything that can go wrong

Model the errors as an enum, one variant per problem, carrying the data the message needs:

```rust
#[derive(Debug)]
enum ShopError {
    FieldCount(usize),
    BadPrice(String),
    BadQuantity(String),
    UnknownCategory(String),
    Duplicate(String),
}
```

Then implement `Display` (a `match` with one `write!` per variant) and the standard `std::error::Error` trait (an empty `impl` is enough: its methods all have defaults). With those two impls, `ShopError` is a proper Rust error: it prints nicely, works with `?`, and can be boxed into `Box<dyn Error>` by any code that uses yours.

Why an enum instead of `String` messages? Because code can *react* to an enum. A future web version could return 404 for `UnknownItem` and 400 for `BadPrice` by matching on the variant; with strings it would have to parse its own error messages.

### Plumbing with ?

Make the parsers return `Result<_, ShopError>`: `parse_money`, a new `parse_quantity`, `parse_category` and `parse_item`. Inside `parse_item`, every field becomes a one-liner with `?`:

```rust
Ok(Item {
    name: name.trim().to_string(),
    category: parse_category(category.trim())?,
    price: parse_money(price.trim())?,
    qty: parse_quantity(qty.trim())?,
})
```

`map_err` converts the standard library's parse errors into yours: `text.parse().map_err(|_| ShopError::BadQuantity(text.to_string()))`.

Duplicates can only be detected by the shop, so give `Shop` an `add(&mut self, item: Item) -> Result<(), ShopError>` method. Then loading one line is a two-step chain:

```rust
fn load(shop: &mut Shop, line: &str) -> Result<(), ShopError> {
    shop.add(parse_item(line)?)
}
```

and `main` prints `line N: {e}` for any error. Check the price carefully: `split_once('.')` must give exactly two digits after the point (`0.1` is rejected, since nobody can tell whether it meant 10 cents or 1), and no point at all means whole dollars.
hints: Start with the `ShopError` enum, an `impl fmt::Display for ShopError` with one `write!` per variant, and `impl std::error::Error for ShopError {}`.
In `parse_money`, `match text.split_once('.')` with three arms: `Some((whole, cents)) if cents.len() == 2`, `Some(_)` (an error), and `None` (whole dollars, cents "00").
`Shop::add` loops over the existing items and returns `Err(ShopError::Duplicate(item.name))` on a name match, otherwise pushes and returns `Ok(())`.

milestones.title: Checkout
milestones.text:
Now the shop can sell. After the stock list comes a **blank line**, then the customer's order, one `NAME QUANTITY` per line:

```
hammer, tools, 12.50, 10
apple, food, 0.40, 200
drill, tools, 89.99, 3

apple 60
drill 4
hammer 2
```

After the stock report (unchanged: it shows the stock *before* the order), print `receipt:` and one line per order line, then the total:

```
receipt:
  apple       60 x   $0.40 =   $24.00
line 6: cannot sell 4 drill: only 3 in stock
  hammer       2 x  $12.50 =   $25.00
total: $49.00
```

Selling takes the units out of stock, so later lines see the reduced quantity. If there are no order lines at all, print neither `receipt:` nor the total. The new errors (with line numbers, as before):

| Problem | Message |
|---|---|
| not exactly two words | `expected NAME QUANTITY` |
| bad quantity | `invalid quantity "x"` (as for stock) |
| no such item | `no item named "pear"` |
| not enough in stock | `cannot sell 4 drill: only 3 in stock` |

### Reading in two sections

Read the input into two lists first: every non-blank line before the first blank line is stock, every non-blank line after it is the order. Keep each line's number with it, as a `(usize, &str)` tuple, so errors can still point at the right line. Then process the stock list, print the report, and process the order.

### A receipt line is a type too

Each successful order line becomes a `ReceiptLine { name, qty, price }` with a `subtotal()` method and its own `Display` impl: `"  {:<10}{:>4} x {:>7} = {:>8}"` with the name, quantity, unit price and subtotal. Your `Money` padding from milestone 1 is what makes those columns line up.

### Borrowing out of the shop

`Shop` gets two methods:

```rust
fn find_mut(&mut self, name: &str) -> Result<&mut Item, ShopError>
fn sell(&mut self, name: &str, qty: u32) -> Result<&Item, ShopError>
```

`sell` finds the item, checks the quantity, subtracts, and hands back a shared reference to the item so the caller can read its name and price. Returning a reference into the shop is cheap (nothing is copied), and the borrow checker makes sure nobody changes the shop while the receipt code is still looking at that item.

A `checkout(shop, line)` function ties it together with `?`: parse the order line, sell, build the `ReceiptLine`.
hints: Split the input with a flag: `if line.trim().is_empty() { in_order = true; } else if in_order { order.push((i + 1, line)); } else { stock.push((i + 1, line)); }`.
`sell`: `let item = self.find_mut(name)?;`, return `ShopError::NotEnough { .. }` if `qty > item.qty`, otherwise subtract and `Ok(item)`.
`checkout`: `let (name, qty) = parse_order(line)?; let item = shop.sell(name, qty)?; Ok(ReceiptLine { name: item.name.clone(), qty, price: item.price })`.

milestones.title: Discounts with a trait
milestones.text:
Shops run promotions, and promotions change every week. This week:

- **Bulk:** 10% off any order line of 10 or more units, and 20% off for 50 or more.
- **Sale:** 15% off everything in the tools category.

Each order line gets the **single biggest** discount that applies (they don't stack). The discount is a percentage of the line's subtotal, rounded down to the cent. Lines with a discount show it after the subtotal, and the end of the receipt shows three totals:

```
receipt:
  apple       60 x   $0.40 =   $24.00  -$4.80 (20% off 50+)
  hammer       2 x  $12.50 =   $25.00  -$3.75 (15% off tools)
subtotal: $49.00
discounts: -$8.55
total: $40.45
```

### A trait for "something that prices an order line"

Bulk discounts and category sales are different structs with different data, but the checkout code wants to ask them the same question: "do you apply here, and how much?" That shared behavior is a **trait**:

```rust
trait PriceRule {
    /// A short description for the receipt, like "10% off 10+".
    fn label(&self) -> String;

    /// The percentage off for this purchase, or None if the rule doesn't apply.
    fn percent_off(&self, item: &Item, qty: u32) -> Option<u64>;

    /// The discount for buying `qty` of `item`.
    fn discount(&self, item: &Item, qty: u32) -> Option<Discount> {
        let percent = self.percent_off(item, qty)?;
        Some(Discount { amount: item.price.times(qty).percent(percent), label: self.label() })
    }
}
```

Two **required** methods that every rule must write, and one **default** method built on top of them. A new kind of rule only has to answer two small questions, and the arithmetic (the part that's easy to get subtly wrong) lives in one place. The standard library's `Iterator` is designed exactly like this: you write `next`, and you get `map`, `filter`, `sum` and dozens more for free.

Implement it for `BulkDiscount { min_qty, percent }` (label `10% off 10+`) and `CategorySale { category, percent }` (label `15% off tools`). Parameters a rule doesn't need get a leading underscore, like `_item`, which tells the compiler (and readers) it's unused on purpose.

### A generic function over any rule

```rust
fn best_discount<R: PriceRule>(rules: &[R], item: &Item, qty: u32) -> Option<Discount>
```

works for a slice of *any* type that implements `PriceRule`. The compiler generates one copy for `BulkDiscount` and one for `CategorySale` (monomorphization), so there's no runtime cost. Call it once per kind of rule and keep the bigger result. (A single `Vec<Box<dyn PriceRule>>` holding both kinds is the other classic design; that's the trait objects module.)

Give `Money` a `percent(self, percent: u64)` method (`Money(self.0 * percent / 100)`: integer division rounds down) and a `minus` method for the final total. `Money` needs `PartialOrd` to compare discounts, so derive `PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord` on it too. When two discounts are equal, keep the bulk one.
hints: Write the `PriceRule` trait with `label` and `percent_off` as required methods and `discount` as a default method, then two small `impl PriceRule for ...` blocks.
`best_discount<R: PriceRule>` loops over the rules, calls `rule.discount(item, qty)`, and keeps it if it's bigger than the best so far.
Combine the two kinds with a helper like `fn bigger(a: Option<Discount>, b: Option<Discount>) -> Option<Discount>` that matches on `(a, b)`.

milestones.title: Polish: promotions in one place, and restock warnings
milestones.text:
Two finishing touches, the kind a code review would ask for.

### Group the promotions

`checkout` now takes the shop, the line, the bulk rules *and* the sales rules. Every new kind of promotion would add another parameter to every function on the way down. When several values always travel together, they want to be a struct:

```rust
struct Promotions {
    bulk: Vec<BulkDiscount>,
    sales: Vec<CategorySale>,
}

impl Promotions {
    fn this_week() -> Self { ... }
    fn best_for(&self, item: &Item, qty: u32) -> Option<Discount> { ... }
}
```

`this_week()` is the one place that says what's on offer, and `best_for` is the one place that knows promotions don't stack. `checkout` becomes `checkout(shop: &mut Shop, promotions: &Promotions, line: &str)`, and adding a third kind of rule later touches only `Promotions`.

### Restock warnings

After everything else (after the receipt, or after the stock report if there was no order), list every item with **fewer than 5** units left, in stock-report order:

```
restock soon: drill (0 left)
restock soon: kite (2 left)
```

Put the threshold in a constant, `const LOW_STOCK: u32 = 5;`, and the question in a method, `fn low_stock(&self) -> Vec<&Item>`, that returns references to the items rather than copies. The items stay owned by the shop; the caller just gets to look at them.

Run your program on the examples once more and read `main` from top to bottom. It should read like the description of a till: load the stock, report it, check out the order, print the totals, warn about low stock.
hints: Move the two rule lists into `struct Promotions` with `fn this_week() -> Self` and `fn best_for(&self, item: &Item, qty: u32) -> Option<Discount>`.
`low_stock` loops over `&self.items` and pushes every `item` with `item.qty < LOW_STOCK` into a `Vec<&Item>`.
At the very end of `main`: `for item in shop.low_stock() { println!("restock soon: {} ({} left)", item.name, item.qty); }`.

projects.summary: Build the front end of a programming language in miniature. A tokenizer that borrows from the input, a recursive-descent parser with precedence and parentheses, variables, and error messages that point at the exact spot.

milestones.title: A tokenizer that borrows
hints: First skip whitespace: `while let Some(c) = self.peek() { if !c.is_whitespace() { break; } self.pos += c.len_utf8(); }`. Then `let start = self.pos;` and `let Some(c) = self.peek() else { return Ok(None); };`.
For a number, keep moving `self.pos += 1` while the next character is an ASCII digit or `.`. For an operator, `match c` to pick the `Kind`, then move one character.
Build the token from the slice you walked over: `Ok(Some(Token { kind, text: &self.src[start..self.pos] }))`. An unknown character is `Err(CalcError::UnexpectedChar { ch: c, pos: start })`.

milestones.title: Parentheses and unary minus
milestones.text:
Add the two features every calculator needs. Parentheses override precedence, and a minus sign in front of a value negates it:

```
(1 + 2) * 3
-(4 - 10) / 4
2 * -3
--3
```

prints `9`, `1.5`, `-6` and `3`. Only `factor` changes:

```
factor = NUMBER | "-" factor | "(" expr ")"
```

- `"-" factor`: consume the minus, parse a factor, negate it. `--3` is minus (minus 3).
- `"(" expr ")"`: consume the `(`, parse a **whole expression**, then require a `)`.

### Recursion is the whole trick

`factor` calling `expr` is what makes nesting work: `((1 + 2) * 3)` is a factor containing an expression containing a term containing a factor containing an expression... Each level is just a method call, so the parser handles any depth without a stack of your own (the call stack *is* the stack).

Why doesn't it loop forever? Because every path through `factor` consumes at least one token before recursing, and there are only so many tokens. That's the rule to remember when writing recursive-descent parsers: never call yourself without making progress.

### Requiring a token

Write a helper that consumes a token of a given kind or fails with a useful error:

```rust
fn expect(&mut self, kind: Kind, what: &'static str) -> Result<Token<'a>, CalcError>
```

`self.expect(Kind::RParen, "')'")?` then gives `expected ')', found the end` for `(1 + 2` and `expected ')', found '3'` for `(1 + 2 3`.
hints: In `factor`, add a `Kind::Minus` arm (`self.pos += 1; Ok(-self.factor()?)`) and a `Kind::LParen` arm.
The `LParen` arm: move past `(`, `let value = self.expr()?;`, then `self.expect(Kind::RParen, "')'")?;` and `Ok(value)`.
`expect`: `match self.peek() { Some(token) if token.kind == kind => { self.pos += 1; Ok(token) } _ => Err(self.expected(what)) }`.

milestones.title: Polish: errors that point at the problem
milestones.text:
`error at column 13` makes the user count characters. Every good compiler instead shows the line and points at the spot, like rustc does for you all the time. Replace the error format with two lines: the input line, then a caret `^` under the problem and the message:

```
2 + * 3
    ^ expected a value, found '*'
```

The caret goes under the character at the error's position (under the first character of a token, or one past the end of the line for "found the end"). There are as many spaces before it as there are characters before that position: `line[..pos].chars().count()`. Count characters, not bytes, or the caret drifts right after every `é`. `" ".repeat(n)` makes the spaces.

Put this in its own function, `fn report(line: &str, error: &CalcError)`. Formatting errors is its own job, and keeping it apart from parsing means the parser could later be reused by a GUI that highlights the spot instead.

### Division by zero

Right now `10 / (5 - 5)` prints `inf`. That's correct IEEE floating point, and nearly always a mistake when a person typed it. Make it an error that points at the `/`:

```
10 / (5 - 5)
   ^ division by zero
```

Add a `DivisionByZero { pos }` variant. In `term`, remember the slash token's position, parse the divisor, and check it *before* dividing: `if divisor == 0.0 { return Err(...) }`.

When you add the variant, the compiler sends you to every `match` on `CalcError` that needs a new arm (`pos()` and `Display`). That's the enum doing code review for you. Run all the earlier examples again: each error now shows exactly where it is, and you've built the same pipeline (lexer, parser, evaluator, diagnostics) that every compiler has, just smaller.
hints: `fn report(line: &str, error: &CalcError)`: `let column = line[..error.pos()].chars().count();`, print the line, then `println!("{}^ {error}", " ".repeat(column));`.
In `term`'s slash arm, bind the position with `Some(Token { kind: Kind::Slash, pos, .. })`, then check the divisor for `0.0` before `value /= divisor`.
Add the `DivisionByZero { pos: usize }` variant to `CalcError` and the matching arms in `pos()` and `Display` (message `division by zero`).

projects.title: A JSON inventory tool
projects.summary: A command-line tool around a JSON file, the way real back-office tools work. Load it with serde, survive format changes, validate what the types can't, apply a batch of changes described by a tagged enum, save the result and publish a JSON summary.

milestones.title: Load and list
milestones.text:
A huge amount of work-day Rust is exactly this: read a JSON file (an export, a config, an API response), check it, change it, write it back, and report. In this project you'll build such a tool for a warehouse inventory stored in `inventory.json`:

```json
{
  "warehouse": "North",
  "items": [
    {"sku": "NUT-10", "name": "Hex nut M10", "qty": 100, "price_cents": 8},
    {"sku": "BOLT-10", "name": "Hex bolt M10", "qty": 120, "price_cents": 25},
    {"sku": "WASH-10", "name": "Washer M10", "qty": 12, "price_cents": 5}
  ]
}
```

The tests put `inventory.json` in the program's working directory, so `std::fs::read_to_string("inventory.json")` reads it (the file name is the `INVENTORY` constant in the starter code). Print the warehouse and item count, one line per item **sorted by SKU**, and the total stock value:

```
North: 3 items
BOLT-10    Hex bolt M10           120 x $0.25
NUT-10     Hex nut M10            100 x $0.08
WASH-10    Washer M10              12 x $0.05
total value: $38.60
```

Item lines are `"{:<10} {:<20} {:>5} x {}"` with the SKU, name, quantity and `money(price_cents)`.

### The structs are the schema

With serde you don't walk the JSON by hand. You describe the shape you expect as Rust types, derive `Deserialize`, and `serde_json::from_str` fills them in or tells you exactly what didn't match:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
struct Inventory {
    warehouse: String,
    items: Vec<Item>,
}
```

Each field name matches a JSON key, a `Vec<Item>` matches an array of objects, and the types do the first round of validation for free: `"qty": -5` fails to load because `qty` is a `u32`, and a missing `price_cents` fails with `missing field`. You'll still need to say which type to parse into: `let inventory: Inventory = serde_json::from_str(&text)?;` (or let the function's return type say it).

### Errors at the top, once

The starter code uses the shape every command-line tool should have. All the work happens in `run() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>`, where `?` passes any error up. `main` handles it once: it prints `error: ...` with `eprintln!` and ends the program with `std::process::exit(1)`.

- `eprintln!` writes to **standard error**, a second output stream meant for problems. When someone redirects the tool's output into a file or another program, the error messages still reach their terminal instead of corrupting the data.
- The **exit code** is how scripts and CI pipelines know a command failed: 0 means success, anything else means failure. Tests in this project check it.

A raw `No such file or directory (os error 2)` doesn't say *which* file. Add context as the error passes by: `.map_err(|e| format!("cannot read {path}: {e}"))?` turns the error into a `String` with a better message, and `?` converts that `String` into a `Box<dyn Error>` for you. Do the same for the parse error (`"{path} is not a valid inventory: {e}"`). The tests check the exit code; read the message in your own runs.
hints: Define `Inventory { warehouse: String, items: Vec<Item> }` and `Item { sku: String, name: String, qty: u32, price_cents: u64 }`, both with `#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]`.
In `run`: `let text = fs::read_to_string(INVENTORY).map_err(|e| format!("cannot read {INVENTORY}: {e}"))?;` then `let inventory: Inventory = serde_json::from_str(&text)?;`.

Sort references instead of the items themselves: `let mut items: Vec<&Item> = inventory.items.iter().collect(); items.sort_by(|a, b| a.sku.cmp(&b.sku));`. Add up `price_cents * qty as u64` for the total.

milestones.title: Renames, optional fields and defaults
milestones.text:
The inventory is now exported by the purchasing team's web service, which is written in JavaScript, and the format changed:

```json
{"sku": "NUT-10", "name": "Hex nut M10", "qty": 40, "priceCents": 8, "reorderLevel": 50, "supplier": "Acme"}
```

- Keys are **camelCase** (`priceCents`), the JavaScript convention.
- `reorderLevel` is new and **optional**: when stock is at or below it, it's time to order more. Missing means 10.
- `supplier` is new and optional too: it may be missing, or `null`.

Rust field names stay snake_case; you tell serde how the JSON spells them. After the total, print a line for every item (in SKU order) whose quantity is at or below its reorder level:

```
reorder GEAR-2: 4 left (reorder level 10), no supplier
reorder NUT-10: 40 left (reorder level 50), supplier Acme
```

### Three attributes do all of it

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
struct Item {
    sku: String,
    name: String,
    qty: u32,
    price_cents: u64,                 // reads "priceCents"
    #[serde(default = "default_reorder_level")]
    reorder_level: u32,               // missing -> default_reorder_level()
    supplier: Option<String>,         // missing or null -> None
}

fn default_reorder_level() -> u32 {
    10
}
```

- `rename_all = "camelCase"` renames every field at once. Use `#[serde(rename = "...")]` on a single field when only one is odd.
- An `Option` field may be missing or `null`; both become `None`. That's how JSON's "maybe there's a value" maps onto Rust's.
- `default = "path"` calls a function when the key is missing. Plain `#[serde(default)]` would use `Default::default()`, which is 0, the wrong business rule here: an item with no reorder level would never be reordered.

Decide deliberately what a missing field *means*. "Missing means 10" is a business rule, and the struct definition is now the one place where it's written down.

By default serde **ignores** keys it doesn't know, so a newer export with extra fields still loads. If you'd rather fail loudly on typos like `"qtty"`, add `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` to the struct. Teams choose per format: ignore for data from other systems, deny for config files people type by hand.

Note that old files (with `price_cents`) no longer load: the tool now speaks only the new format, and says so with a `missing field` error.
hints: Put `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` under the derive on `Item`, add `reorder_level: u32` with `#[serde(default = "default_reorder_level")]`, and `supplier: Option<String>`.
`fn default_reorder_level() -> u32 { 10 }` is the function serde calls for a missing key.
After the total, loop over the sorted items again and print the ones with `item.qty <= item.reorder_level`, matching on `&item.supplier` for the last part.

milestones.title: Validate before you trust
milestones.text:
serde guarantees the file has the right **shape**: every field present, every number a number. It can't know what the values **mean**. An empty name, a price of zero or two items with the same SKU all load perfectly, and then quietly break everything downstream (orders for the wrong item, revenue of $0).

Check the meaning after loading. Every SKU must look like `BOLT-10`: one or more uppercase ASCII letters, a dash, one or more digits. Names can't be empty (or only spaces), prices must be above 0, and SKUs must be unique. Report **every** problem, in item order (and for one item, in that order of rules), not just the first:

```
problem: item 1 (bolt10): invalid sku
problem: item 2 (PIN-3): name is empty
problem: item 2 (PIN-3): price must be positive
problem: item 3 (PIN-3): duplicate sku
```

Items are numbered from 1 in file order. If there are any problems, don't print the table: return an error from `run` (`inventory.json has 4 problem(s), nothing was changed`), so the tool exits with code 1. A valid file prints the same report as before.

### Collect, don't stop

Stopping at the first problem is fine for a compiler error you fix in a second. For a data file someone exported from another system, it's maddening: fix one problem, run again, find the next, and so on twenty times. Collect them all:

```rust
fn validate(inventory: &Inventory) -> Vec<String>
```

returns every problem; an empty `Vec` means valid. Keeping validation a separate function that only *returns* problems also means you can test it, or reuse it in a web form, without any printing.

For duplicates, remember the SKUs you've seen in a `BTreeSet<&str>`. `insert` returns `false` when the value was already there, so detection and recording are one call:

```rust
if !seen.insert(item.sku.as_str()) {
    problems.push(format!("{at}: duplicate sku"));
}
```

For the SKU format, `split_once('-')` gives the two halves, and `chars().all(|c| c.is_ascii_uppercase())` checks every character of one. (The `regex` crate would do this in one line, `^[A-Z]+-[0-9]+$`. For a rule this small, plain code is just as clear and has no dependency.)
hints: `valid_sku`: `match sku.split_once('-')` and check both halves are non-empty, `letters.chars().all(|c| c.is_ascii_uppercase())` and `digits.chars().all(|c| c.is_ascii_digit())`.
In `validate`, loop with `for (i, item) in inventory.items.iter().enumerate()`, build `let at = format!("item {} ({})", i + 1, item.sku);` and push one message per broken rule.
In `run`, if the problems aren't empty, print each as `problem: {problem}` and `return Err(format!(...).into());`.

milestones.title: A batch of changes
milestones.text:
Now let the tool change the inventory. Changes arrive as a second file, `changes.json`: a list of operations, each tagged with `"op"`:

```json
[
  {"op": "sell", "sku": "NUT-10", "qty": 30},
  {"op": "restock", "sku": "GEAR-2", "qty": 20},
  {"op": "add", "item": {"sku": "CHAIN-8", "name": "Roller chain", "qty": 5, "priceCents": 2475}},
  {"op": "remove", "sku": "BOLT-10"}
]
```

After validating, apply them in order, printing one line each, then print the report (which now shows the state *after* the changes):

| Change | Prints |
|---|---|
| `restock` | `restocked GEAR-2: 4 -> 24` |
| `sell` | `sold 30 of NUT-10: 40 -> 10` |
| `add` | `added CHAIN-8 (Roller chain)` |
| `remove` | `removed BOLT-10` |

A change that can't be applied is skipped with its number (from 1): `change 3 skipped: no item with sku "GEAR-9"`, `change 2 skipped: cannot sell 500 of BOLT-10: only 120 in stock`, `change 5 skipped: sku "NUT-10" already exists` (for an `add`). If `changes.json` doesn't exist, there's simply nothing to apply. If it exists but isn't valid (an unknown `op`, a missing field), that's an error: exit 1 without changing anything.

### An internally tagged enum

Each change is one of four shapes, chosen by `"op"`: an enum. serde supports several JSON layouts for enums; this one, with the variant name *inside* the object, is called **internally tagged**:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
#[serde(tag = "op", rename_all = "lowercase")]
enum Change {
    Restock { sku: String, qty: u32 },
    Sell { sku: String, qty: u32 },
    Add { item: Item },
    Remove { sku: String },
}
```

`tag = "op"` says which key holds the variant name, and `rename_all = "lowercase"` maps `Restock` to `"restock"`. An unknown op like `"steal"` fails to load with a clear message, and a `Sell` without `qty` can't exist. Then a plain `match` applies each change. `Add { item: Item }` reuses your `Item` type, defaults and all.

### Typed errors with thiserror

Applying a change has its own failure modes. Give them a small error type; `thiserror` writes the `Display` and `Error` impls from the `#[error]` messages:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
enum ChangeError {
    #[error("no item with sku \"{0}\"")]
    UnknownSku(String),
    #[error("cannot sell {wanted} of {sku}: only {available} in stock")]
    NotEnough { sku: String, wanted: u32, available: u32 },
    #[error("sku \"{0}\" already exists")]
    Duplicate(String),
}
```

`fn apply(inventory: &mut Inventory, change: Change) -> Result<String, ChangeError>` returns the line to print. A helper `find_mut` that returns `Result<&mut Item, ChangeError>` makes restock and sell two lines each: `inventory.items.iter_mut().find(|item| item.sku == sku).ok_or_else(...)`.

To check whether the changes file exists, use `std::path::Path::new(CHANGES).exists()`. A missing optional file isn't an error; a broken one is.
hints: Derive `Deserialize` on `enum Change` with `#[serde(tag = "op", rename_all = "lowercase")]`, and load it with a `load_changes` function that returns an empty `Vec` when `!Path::new(CHANGES).exists()`.
`apply` is a `match change { Change::Restock { sku, qty } => { let item = find_mut(inventory, &sku)?; ... } ... }`; for `Remove`, compare the length before and after `retain`.

In `run`, after validation: `for (i, change) in changes.into_iter().enumerate()` and print either the message or `change {} skipped: {e}` with `i + 1`. Then print the table as before (make `inventory` mutable).

milestones.title: Polish: save it, and speak JSON
milestones.text:
Two things turn this into a tool other people can build on: it should **save** its changes, and it should publish a summary that **other programs** can read.

### Saving

When changes were applied, write the inventory back to `inventory.json` with `serde_json::to_string_pretty` (plus a final newline) and `fs::write`, then print `saved inventory.json`. With no changes, don't touch the file: rewriting a file that didn't change confuses backups and version control.

Saving needs `Serialize` on `Inventory` and `Item`, and two attributes keep the file tidy: an item with no supplier shouldn't gain `"supplier": null`, and an item with no tags shouldn't gain `"tags": []`:

```rust
#[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
supplier: Option<String>,
#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty")]
tags: Vec<String>,
```

(Items now have an optional `tags` list, like `["fastener", "steel"]`; missing means empty.) The output keeps field order, so `rename_all` and the defaults round-trip: a file you save loads back exactly the same.

Then **read the file back** with your own `load` function and use what you read for the report. It costs one extra parse and proves the file you just wrote is valid. Finding that out now beats finding it tomorrow morning when the next run fails.

### A JSON summary for other programs

After the human-readable report, print a summary as pretty JSON. A dashboard or a purchasing script can parse this instead of scraping your table (the table's layout is for people and may change; a JSON format is a contract):

```json
{
  "warehouse": "North",
  "itemCount": 4,
  "totalUnits": 276,
  "totalValueCents": 8880,
  "reorder": [
    "GEAR-2",
    "NUT-10"
  ],
  "unitsByTag": {
    "fastener": 272,
    "steel": 160
  }
}
```

Build it as a struct deriving `Serialize` with `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]`:

- `reorder` lists the SKUs at or below their reorder level, sorted, and is left out entirely when empty (`skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty"`).
- `unitsByTag` adds up the quantities of the items carrying each tag. Use a `BTreeMap<String, u32>`: serde writes a map as a JSON object, and a `BTreeMap` makes the key order alphabetical and stable. (A `HashMap` would produce a different key order on every run: harmless to a parser, but it makes diffs and tests noisy.)

Money stays in integer cents in the JSON too (`totalValueCents`), for the same reason as in your structs: JSON numbers are usually read as floating point.
hints: Add `Serialize` to the derives on `Inventory` and `Item`, the `skip_serializing_if` attributes, and `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty")] tags: Vec<String>`.
After applying a non-empty list of changes: `fs::write(INVENTORY, serde_json::to_string_pretty(&inventory)? + "\n")?;`, then `inventory = load(INVENTORY)?;` and print `saved inventory.json`.

`struct Summary` derives `Serialize` with `rename_all = "camelCase"`; fill it in one loop over the items (`*summary.units_by_tag.entry(tag.clone()).or_insert(0) += item.qty;`), sort `reorder`, and print `serde_json::to_string_pretty(&summary)?`.

projects.title: A log analyzer for the command line
projects.summary: Build loglens, a small tool in the spirit of the ones every operations team writes. Parse access-log lines with FromStr, read the file named on the command line, aggregate statistics per endpoint, filter with flags, and report through exit codes that scripts and CI can act on.

milestones.title: Parse a line with FromStr
milestones.text:
Every web server writes an **access log**: one line per request, saying when it came in, what was asked for, how it ended and how long it took. When the site is slow or broken at 3 a.m., someone reads these logs, and the first thing they reach for is a tool that turns thousands of lines into a few useful numbers. In this project you'll write that tool, `loglens`.

The log format is:

```
2026-03-14T10:00:01Z GET /api/users 200 35ms
```

Five fields separated by whitespace: an ISO 8601 **timestamp** (in UTC, hence the `Z`), the HTTP **method**, the **path**, the **status code**, and the **duration** with an `ms` suffix.

Start with the core: turning one line into a `LogEntry`. This milestone has no `main` (hidden tests call your code), so you can focus on parsing.

### FromStr: making your type work with parse

You've used `"42".parse::<u32>()` since the beginning. `parse` works for any type that implements `std::str::FromStr`, including yours:

```rust
impl FromStr for LogEntry {
    type Err = ParseError;

    fn from_str(line: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Err> {
        ...
    }
}
```

After that, `line.parse::<LogEntry>()` works like any other parse, and so does `?`. Implement it for `Method` too (`"GET"` becomes `Method::Get`; methods are uppercase, so `get` is an error); you'll reuse that impl for a command-line flag later. Implementing a standard trait instead of inventing `fn parse_log_line` is what makes your types feel native: code that knows `parse` already knows how to use them.

### The rules

Check them in this order; the first that fails decides the error:

| Rule | Error |
|---|---|
| exactly 5 whitespace-separated fields | `ParseError::FieldCount(n)` with the number found |
| method is GET, POST, PUT or DELETE | `ParseError::Method(text)` |
| path starts with `/` | `ParseError::Path(text)` |
| status is a whole number from 100 to 599 | `ParseError::Status(text)` |
| duration is a whole number followed by `ms` | `ParseError::Duration(text)` |

The timestamp is kept as a `String`. (Parsing it into a real date type is what the `chrono` crate is for; you'll see in milestone 4 why the string is enough here.) The starter code already declares `ParseError` with **thiserror**, so each variant has its message, like `invalid status "2oo"`.

### Destructuring the fields

A slice pattern with `let ... else` takes the five fields apart and handles "wrong count" in one statement:

```rust
let fields: Vec<&str> = line.split_whitespace().collect();
let [timestamp, method, path, status, duration] = fields[..] else {
    return Err(ParseError::FieldCount(fields.len()));
};
```

For the duration, `strip_suffix("ms")` returns the text before `ms`, or `None` if it doesn't end with it. Chain it with `and_then` and `ok_or_else` to get a number or a `ParseError::Duration`. For the status, parse into `u16` and use a match guard to check the range.
hints: `Method::from_str` is a `match s { "GET" => Ok(Method::Get), ..., other => Err(ParseError::Method(other.to_string())) }`.
After the slice pattern, `let method: Method = method.parse()?;` checks the method first. Then `if !path.starts_with('/') { return Err(ParseError::Path(path.to_string())); }`.

Status: `match status.parse::<u16>() { Ok(code) if (100..=599).contains(&code) => code, _ => return Err(...) }`. Duration: `duration.strip_suffix("ms").and_then(|ms| ms.parse().ok()).ok_or_else(|| ParseError::Duration(duration.to_string()))?`.
checkNames: rejects the wrong number of fields
rejects paths without a leading slash
durations need a whole number and ms
error messages say what was wrong

milestones.title: Read the file named on the command line
milestones.text:
Now `loglens` becomes a real command. It takes the log file as its argument:

```text
$ loglens access.log
requests: 7
skipped: 1
period: 2026-03-14T10:00:01Z to 2026-03-14T10:04:59Z
slowest: POST /api/orders -> 503 in 1200ms
```

- Read the file, skip blank lines, and parse every other line with your `FromStr`.
- A line that doesn't parse is **not** fatal (logs from real servers always contain some junk): print `warning: line 6: unknown method "FETCH"` to **standard error** and count it as skipped.
- Print the number of parsed requests and skipped lines, then (only if there is at least one request) the period covered, from the earliest to the latest timestamp, and the slowest request. If several are equally slow, the first one in the file wins.
- The method needs a `Display` impl to print as `POST`. Use `f.pad`, so widths work later.

### Arguments, usage errors and exit codes

`std::env::args()` yields the program name first, then the arguments; `.skip(1)` drops the name. Turn the arguments into a `Config` struct in one place, `Config::from_args(&args) -> Result<Config, String>`, so the rest of the program never touches raw strings. A slice pattern makes it short:

```rust
match args {
    [file] => Ok(Config { file: file.clone() }),
    [] => Err(String::from("missing log file")),
    [_, extra, ..] => Err(format!("unexpected argument {extra}")),
}
```

Command-line tools agree on a few conventions, and following them makes your tool play well with scripts:

| Situation | Exit code | stderr |
|---|---|---|
| success | 0 | warnings, if any |
| the command line itself is wrong | 2 | `error: missing log file` and the usage line |
| something failed while running (unreadable file) | 1 | `error: reading missing.log: No such file or directory (os error 2)` |

Make `main` return `std::process::ExitCode` (`ExitCode::SUCCESS`, `ExitCode::FAILURE`, `ExitCode::from(2)`), and put the real work in `fn run(config: &Config) -> anyhow::Result<()>`. In `run`, `.with_context(|| format!("reading {}", config.file))?` wraps the I/O error with what you were trying to do. In `main`, print it with `{e:#}`: the alternate format prints the whole chain on one line, `reading missing.log: No such file or directory (os error 2)`.

Only the report goes to standard output. Warnings and errors go to standard error, so `loglens access.log > report.txt` produces a clean report file while problems still show up in the terminal. (The tests here check standard output and the exit code.)

### Earliest, latest, slowest

ISO 8601 timestamps in the same time zone sort correctly **as plain strings**: `2026-03-14T10:00:01Z` < `2026-03-14T10:04:59Z` character by character. That's not luck; the format was designed so. So `entries.iter().map(|e| e.timestamp.as_str()).min()` finds the earliest one, even if the lines are out of order.

For the slowest request, `reduce` keeps a running "best so far" and only replaces it when a request is *strictly* slower, so the first one wins ties: `entries.iter().reduce(|best, e| if e.duration_ms > best.duration_ms { e } else { best })`.
hints: `main`: `let args: Vec<String> = env::args().skip(1).collect();`, then match `Config::from_args(&args)`: on `Err`, `eprintln!` the error and `USAGE`, and `return ExitCode::from(2);`.
In `run`, loop over `text.lines().enumerate()`, skip blank lines, and on a parse error `eprintln!("warning: line {}: {e}", i + 1)` and count it.
Print `period` and `slowest` only when there are entries: `if let (Some(first), Some(last)) = (min, max) { ... }` is one way.

milestones.title: Statistics per endpoint
milestones.text:
Totals tell you *that* something is wrong; a breakdown tells you *where*. After the overview, print a table with one row per **endpoint** (a method and a path), busiest first:

```text
endpoint                  count   4xx   5xx   avg ms   max ms
GET /api/users                3     0     0     40.0       55
POST /api/orders              2     0     1    660.0     1200
DELETE /api/orders/7          1     0     0     15.0       15
GET /api/users/42             1     1     0      8.0        8
```

- **count**: requests to that endpoint; **4xx** and **5xx**: how many ended with a client error (400 to 499) or a server error (500 to 599).
- **avg ms** with one decimal, and **max ms**.
- Busiest first. Endpoints with the same count are ordered by path, then by method (in the order GET, POST, PUT, DELETE).
- The header is `"{:<24}{:>7}{:>6}{:>6}{:>9}{:>9}"` with the column names, and each row uses the same widths with `"{method} {path}"` as the endpoint (and `.1` precision for the average). If there are no requests at all, print no table.

### Aggregating with a map

Group the entries in a `BTreeMap` whose key is the endpoint and whose value accumulates the statistics:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Default)]
struct EndpointStats {
    count: u32,
    client_errors: u32,
    server_errors: u32,
    total_ms: u64,
    max_ms: u32,
}

let mut by_endpoint: BTreeMap<(&str, Method), EndpointStats> = BTreeMap::new();
for entry in entries {
    let stats = by_endpoint.entry((entry.path.as_str(), entry.method)).or_default();
    stats.count += 1;
    ...
}
```

A few details doing real work here:

- The key is a **tuple**, and tuples compare element by element, so the map is ordered by path, then method. `Method` derives `Ord` (in declaration order), which is what makes it usable in a `BTreeMap` key at all.
- The key **borrows** the path from the entry (`&str`) instead of cloning it. On a million-line log that's a million allocations saved, and the borrow checker guarantees the entries outlive the map.
- `or_default()` creates a zeroed `EndpointStats` the first time a key is seen, thanks to `#[derive(Default)]`.
- `match entry.status { 400..=499 => ..., 500..=599 => ..., _ => {} }` counts the error classes with range patterns.

Then move the map into a `Vec` and sort by count, descending. `sort_by_key(|(_, stats)| Reverse(stats.count))` does it: `std::cmp::Reverse` wraps a value and flips its ordering. Rust's `sort_by_key` is **stable** (equal elements keep their order), so endpoints with equal counts stay in the map's path order: the tie-breaking comes for free.

Use `f64` for the average: `stats.total_ms as f64 / stats.count as f64`.
hints: Derive `Default` on `EndpointStats` and use `by_endpoint.entry((entry.path.as_str(), entry.method)).or_default()`.
`let mut rows: Vec<_> = by_endpoint.into_iter().collect(); rows.sort_by_key(|(_, stats)| Reverse(stats.count));` keeps ties in map order.
Each row: `println!("{endpoint:<24}{:>7}{:>6}{:>6}{avg:>9.1}{:>9}", ...)` with `let endpoint = format!("{method} {path}");`.

milestones.title: Filters from the command line
milestones.text:
The question during an incident is never "how is everything?" but "how are the POSTs since 10:02?" or "show me only the 5xx". Add filter flags:

```text
loglens access.log --method POST --since 2026-03-14T10:02:00Z
loglens access.log --status 5xx
```

| Flag | Keeps requests... |
|---|---|
| `--method METHOD` | with that method (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`) |
| `--status CODE` or `--status Nxx` | with that exact status (`404`), or that class (`5xx`, from `1xx` to `5xx`) |
| `--since TIMESTAMP` | at or after that timestamp |

Flags can come in any order, before or after the file. After `skipped:`, print `matching: N`, the number of requests that pass every filter; the period, slowest request and table now describe **only the matching requests**.

Bad command lines are usage errors (exit code 2, message and usage line on stderr): an unknown flag (`unknown option --bogus`), a flag without its value (`--method needs a value`), an invalid value (`unknown method "FETCH"`, `invalid status filter "7xx" (use a code like 404 or a class like 5xx)`), or a second file.

### A Config that holds what was asked

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Default)]
struct Config {
    file: String,
    method: Option<Method>,
    status: Option<StatusFilter>,
    since: Option<String>,
}
```

Each filter is an `Option`: `None` means "not given, don't filter". To read flags that take a value, walk the arguments with an iterator and call `next()` again inside the loop to grab the value:

```rust
let mut args = args.iter();
while let Some(arg) = args.next() {
    match arg.as_str() {
        "--method" => {
            let value = args.next().ok_or("--method needs a value")?;
            config.method = Some(value.parse().map_err(|e: ParseError| e.to_string())?);
        }
        ...
        flag if flag.starts_with("--") => return Err(format!("unknown option {flag}")),
        _ => ... // the file (only one allowed)
    }
}
```

Your `FromStr` for `Method` pays off here: the flag reuses it. Write one more, `impl FromStr for StatusFilter`, for `enum StatusFilter { Exact(u16), Class(u16) }`, with a `matches(&self, status: u16) -> bool` method (`status / 100 == class` for a class).

### One method decides

Put the filtering logic on `Config`:

```rust
fn matches(&self, entry: &LogEntry) -> bool {
    self.method.is_none_or(|method| entry.method == method)
        && self.status.is_none_or(|status| status.matches(entry.status))
        && self.since.as_ref().is_none_or(|since| entry.timestamp >= *since)
}
```

`Option::is_none_or` reads exactly like the rule: "no filter, or it matches". Then `entries.into_iter().filter(|e| config.matches(e)).collect()` is the whole filtering step. The `--since` comparison is the ISO 8601 string trick from milestone 2 again.

At work you'd likely let the **clap** crate generate this parsing (and `--help`) from a struct with `#[derive(Parser)]`. Writing it once by hand shows you what clap does for you, and the `Config` struct is the same idea either way.
hints: Give `Config` the three `Option` fields (derive `Default`), and parse the arguments with `let mut args = args.iter(); while let Some(arg) = args.next() { match arg.as_str() { ... } }`.
`StatusFilter::from_str`: `match s.strip_suffix("xx")` gives a class (`Some(class)`) or an exact code (`None`); then check the class is 1 to 5 or the code 100 to 599.
In `run`, print `matching:` after `skipped:`, using `let matching: Vec<LogEntry> = entries.into_iter().filter(|e| config.matches(e)).collect();`, and report on `matching`.
