milestones.title: Polish: exit codes that scripts can act on
milestones.text:
A tool that only prints is a tool someone has to read. A tool with meaningful **exit codes** can run unattended: in a CI pipeline after a load test, in a cron job, in a deployment script that rolls back when things look bad:

```text
loglens access.log --since 2026-03-14T10:00:00Z --fail-on-5xx || rollback-deploy
```

Two additions:

- A last report line counting the matching requests per status class, in class order, leaving out classes with no requests: `status classes: 2xx=5 4xx=1 5xx=1`.
- A `--fail-on-5xx` flag: when it's given and any **matching** request has a 5xx status, still print the full report, then print `error: 2 server error(s) found` to stderr and exit with code **3**. Without the flag, or with no 5xx among the matching requests, exit 0 as before.

Why a new code instead of 1? Because the caller may want to tell "the log looks bad" (3) apart from "the tool couldn't even read the log" (1) and "you called it wrong" (2). Document your codes; here, a comment above `run` is the right place:

```rust
/// Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 runtime error, 2 bad command line, 3 server errors found with --fail-on-5xx.
fn run(config: &Config) -> anyhow::Result<ExitCode> {
```

`run` now returns the `ExitCode` to use on success, and `main` returns it. The decision about *what* to report stays in `run`; `main` only maps errors to codes.

For the class counts, a `BTreeMap<u16, u32>` keyed by `status / 100` keeps the classes in order. Building the line is a good fit for an iterator chain ending in `join`:

```rust
let classes: Vec<String> = classes.iter().map(|(class, n)| format!("{class}xx={n}")).collect();
println!("status classes: {}", classes.join(" "));
```

Run your tool against the examples one last time with different flags. You've built the same shape as most command-line tools at work: typed parsing at the edges (`FromStr`, `Config`), a `run` that returns `Result`, errors with context, output for people on stdout, problems on stderr, and exit codes for machines.
hints: Add `fail_on_5xx: bool` to `Config` and a `"--fail-on-5xx" => config.fail_on_5xx = true,` arm.
At the end of the report, count `entry.status / 100` in a `BTreeMap<u16, u32>` and print the `status classes:` line with `join(" ")`.

Change `run` to return `anyhow::Result<ExitCode>`: after printing, if the flag is set and `matching.iter().filter(|e| e.status >= 500).count()` is above 0, `eprintln!` the message and `return Ok(ExitCode::from(3));`.

projects.title: A generic matrix library
projects.summary: Write a small linear-algebra library the way crates are written. A generic Matrix type with validated construction, Index and Display, + and * through operator overloading, and fast powers by repeated squaring. Graded by hidden unit tests, like a real library.

milestones.title: Storage and shape
milestones.text:
Matrices are grids of numbers, and they're everywhere: 3D graphics (every rotation is a matrix), machine learning (a neural network layer is a matrix multiplication), physics simulations, image filters, even spreadsheets. In this project you'll write a small **library**, not a program: there's no `main`, and hidden unit tests check your API, exactly how library crates are tested at work.

A matrix has `rows` and `cols`, and an entry at each `(row, col)`, counted from 0:

```text
[1 2 3]      rows: 2, cols: 3
[4 5 6]      entry (1, 2) is 6
```

### One Vec, row by row

The obvious representation is `Vec<Vec<T>>`. Libraries don't use it: each inner `Vec` is a separate heap allocation, the rows end up scattered in memory, and nothing stops two rows from having different lengths. Instead, store all the entries in **one** `Vec`, row after row (**row-major order**), and compute where an entry lives:

```text
data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
(row, col) is at data[row * cols + col]      (1, 2) -> 1 * 3 + 2 = 5 -> 6
```

One allocation, entries next to each other in memory (fast to walk), and the shape is two numbers that can't disagree with each other.

The struct is **generic**, `Matrix<T>`, so the same code works for `i32`, `f64`, `u64`, even `String`. That's why each `impl` block says which abilities of `T` it needs:

```rust
impl<T> Matrix<T> { ... }          // works for any T: rows, cols, get
impl<T: Clone> Matrix<T> { ... }   // needs to copy entries: filled, from_rows
```

`filled` clones `value` into every slot, so it needs `T: Clone`; `get` only hands out a reference, so it works for any `T`. Asking for the least you need keeps the type usable for as many `T`s as possible.

### What to write

- `rows()` and `cols()`.
- `get(row, col) -> Option<&T>`: the entry, or `None` outside the matrix. Careful: on a 2x3 matrix, `(0, 4)` gives position 4, which **exists** in the `Vec`. Check `row < rows && col < cols`, not just the position, or `get(0, 4)` would quietly return the entry at `(1, 1)`.
- `filled(rows, cols, value)`: every entry is `value` (`vec![value; n]` does it).
- `from_rows(Vec<Vec<T>>) -> Result<Matrix<T>, MatrixError>`: builds the matrix from a list of rows. No rows, or an empty first row, is `MatrixError::Empty`. A row whose length differs from the first is `MatrixError::Ragged { row, expected, found }` (the first bad row, counted from 0).
- `Display` for `MatrixError`: `a matrix needs at least one row and one column` and `row 1 has 2 entries, expected 3`.

`from_rows` takes the rows **by value**, so it can move the entries into the new `Vec` (`data.extend(row)`) instead of cloning them. When a function will consume its input anyway, taking ownership saves the copies. To know which row is ragged, loop with `for (i, row) in rows.into_iter().enumerate()`: `into_iter()` hands you each row by value, and `enumerate()` pairs it with its index.
hints: `get`: `if row < self.rows && col < self.cols { Some(&self.data[row * self.cols + col]) } else { None }`.

`from_rows`: find `cols` with `match rows.first() { Some(first) if !first.is_empty() => first.len(), _ => return Err(MatrixError::Empty) }`, remember `rows.len()`, then move each row into `data` after checking its length.
Loop with `for (i, row) in rows.into_iter().enumerate()` so you know which row is ragged: `return Err(MatrixError::Ragged { row: i, expected: cols, found: row.len() })`.
checkNames: from rows keeps the shape and the entries
get outside the matrix is none
filled works for any cloneable type

milestones.title: Index, IndexMut and Display
milestones.text:
`m.get(1, 2)` works, but a matrix library should let you write `m[(1, 2)]`, and assign with `m[(1, 2)] = 7`. Square brackets are an operator, and like every operator in Rust they're a trait you can implement:

```rust
impl<T> Index<(usize, usize)> for Matrix<T> {
    type Output = T;

    fn index(&self, (row, col): (usize, usize)) -> &T {
        &self.data[self.offset(row, col)]
    }
}
```

- The type parameter of `Index` is the type that goes between the brackets: here a tuple, so `m[(1, 2)]`. The parameter pattern `(row, col)` takes the tuple apart right in the signature.
- `type Output = T` is an **associated type**: what you get back. `index` returns a reference to it, and Rust adds the `*` for you, so `m[(1, 2)]` reads as a `T`.
- `IndexMut` is the same with `&mut self` and `&mut T`, and it's what makes `m[(1, 2)] = 7` and `m[(0, 1)] += 2` work.

### Out of bounds must panic

Indexing a `Vec` past its end panics; indexing your matrix must too. And remember the `(0, 4)` trap from milestone 1: on a 2x3 matrix that's position 4, a perfectly valid `Vec` index, so `Vec` would **not** panic. You'd silently get the entry at `(1, 1)`, the worst kind of bug. Write one private helper that both impls use:

```rust
fn offset(&self, row: usize, col: usize) -> usize {
    assert!(
        row < self.rows && col < self.cols,
        "index ({row}, {col}) is outside a {}x{} matrix",
        self.rows,
        self.cols
    );
    row * self.cols + col
}
```

Why panic and not return a `Result`? `Index` must return a reference, so there's no room for an error. That's the standard library's convention too: `[]` panics on bad input (a bug in the caller), and `get` returns an `Option` for callers who expect misses.

### Display, aligned

Print one row per line, entries separated by one space and right-aligned to the **widest entry in the whole matrix**, each row in brackets, no newline after the last row:

```text
[  1  20]
[300   4]
```

That takes two passes: format every entry into a `String` first, find the widest (`chars().count()`), then print with that width. `{:>width$}` uses a variable as the width.

One more nicety: if the caller asks for a precision, like `format!("{m:.2}")`, apply it to every entry:

```text
[ 1.50 -2.00]
[ 0.25 10.00]
```

`f.precision()` tells you whether one was asked for (`Some(2)`) or not (`None`), and `format!("{x:.p$}")` formats with a precision held in the variable `p`. Respecting the formatter's options is what makes your type behave like the built-in ones. The `impl` needs `T: fmt::Display`, since you can only print a matrix whose entries can be printed.

Finally, add `transpose(&self) -> Self` (rows become columns: entry `(r, c)` moves to `(c, r)`, and a 2x3 matrix becomes 3x2). Use your new indexing to write it.
hints: `IndexMut::index_mut(&mut self, (row, col): (usize, usize)) -> &mut T`: compute `let i = self.offset(row, col);` first, then return `&mut self.data[i]`.

In `Display`, build `cells: Vec<String>` with `match f.precision() { Some(p) => format!("{x:.p$}"), None => x.to_string() }`, take the widest, then print each row as `[`, cells joined by spaces with `{:>width$}`, `]`, and `writeln!(f)?` between rows.
`transpose`: loop over `col` in the outside and `row` inside, pushing `self[(row, col)].clone()`, and swap `rows` and `cols` in the result.
checkNames: display passes the precision to every entry

milestones.title: Adding with +
milestones.text:
Now the part that makes a math library pleasant: real operators. `&a + &b` should add two matrices entry by entry, and `&m * 3` should multiply every entry by a number.

### Operators are traits

`a + b` is shorthand for `Add::add(a, b)`. Implement `std::ops::Add` and `+` works on your type:

```rust
impl<T: Copy + Add<Output = T>> Add for &Matrix<T> {
    type Output = Matrix<T>;

    fn add(self, other: Self) -> Matrix<T> { ... }
}
```

Read the bound `T: Copy + Add<Output = T>` as: "entries can be copied, and adding two entries gives an entry". That's exactly what entry-by-entry addition needs, and it holds for `i32`, `f64`, `u64` and so on. Without the bound, the compiler wouldn't let you write `x + y` for two `T`s, because it can't assume an arbitrary type can be added.

Notice the impl is for `&Matrix<T>`, a **reference**. A matrix can be big, and `a + b` on owned values would move both operands into the function, so you could never use `a` again. Implementing `Add` for references lets callers write `&a + &b` and keep their matrices. Add a second impl for owned matrices that just delegates (`&self + &other`), for when you're done with them; the standard library does the same for its own numeric types.

### Shapes must match

Adding a 2x3 matrix to a 3x2 one is meaningless. Two APIs, two conventions:

- `checked_add(&self, other: &Matrix<T>) -> Result<Matrix<T>, MatrixError>` returns `MatrixError::ShapeMismatch { op: "add", left: (2, 3), right: (3, 2) }`, displayed as `cannot add a 2x3 matrix and a 3x2 matrix`. Use it when shapes come from user input.
- `+` panics with that same message. An operator can't return a `Result` without making every formula unreadable, and a shape mismatch in `a + b` is a bug in the program, like an out-of-bounds index. This mirrors `checked_add` and `+` on integers.

So `+` is just `match self.checked_add(other) { Ok(sum) => sum, Err(e) => panic!("{e}") }`, and the error message is written once.

To add entry by entry, walk both `data` vectors in step. `zip` pairs them up: `for (a, b) in self.data.iter().zip(&other.data) { data.push(*a + *b); }` (`*a` copies the entry out of the reference, which `T: Copy` allows).

### Scaling: Mul with a different right-hand side

`Mul` has a type parameter for the right-hand side, and it doesn't have to be `Self`. `impl<T: Copy + Mul<Output = T>> Mul<T> for &Matrix<T>` means "a matrix reference times a `T`", so `&m * 3` multiplies every entry by 3.
hints: `checked_add`: compare `(self.rows, self.cols) != (other.rows, other.cols)` and return the `ShapeMismatch` error; otherwise build a new `data` with `zip`.
`impl<T: Copy + Add<Output = T>> Add for &Matrix<T>` with `type Output = Matrix<T>;` and `fn add(self, other: Self) -> Matrix<T>`; the owned impl's body is `&self + &other`.
`impl<T: Copy + Mul<Output = T>> Mul<T> for &Matrix<T>`: `fn mul(self, k: T) -> Matrix<T>` pushes `*x * k` for every entry.
checkNames: indexing display and get still work

milestones.title: Matrix multiplication
milestones.text:
Matrix multiplication is the operation the whole field runs on (every GPU is, at heart, a matrix multiplication machine). It isn't entry by entry. Entry `(r, c)` of `A * B` is row `r` of `A` combined with column `c` of `B`: multiply them pairwise and add up:

```text
[1 2 3]   [1 4]   [1*1 + 2*2 + 3*3   1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6]   [14 32]
[4 5 6] * [2 5] = [4*1 + 5*2 + 6*3   4*4 + 5*5 + 6*6] = [32 77]
          [3 6]
```

So `A`'s columns must match `B`'s rows: a 2x3 times a 3x2 gives a 2x2. Write:

- `checked_mul(&self, other) -> Result<Matrix<T>, MatrixError>`: the product, or `ShapeMismatch { op: "multiply", ... }` when `self.cols != other.rows`.
- `Mul for &Matrix<T>` (and for owned matrices), panicking on a mismatch, just like `+`.
- `identity(n)`: the n x n matrix with 1 on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere. Multiplying by it changes nothing, like multiplying a number by 1.

Unlike numbers, `A * B` and `B * A` are usually **different** (when they're both even defined). That's not a bug in your code: it's what makes matrices able to describe "rotate, then move" as different from "move, then rotate".

### Where do zero and one come from?

The sum for each entry starts at zero, and the identity needs ones, but `T` is generic: you can't write `0` and hope it becomes a `T`. Two standard traits help:

- `Default`: for every number type, `T::default()` is zero. Add `Default` to the bounds and start each sum at `T::default()`.
- `From<u8>`: `i32`, `i64`, `u32`, `u64`, `f32` and `f64` all implement `From<u8>` (a `u8` fits in each of them without loss), so `T::from(0)` and `T::from(1)` give zero and one of any of them. `identity` lives in its own `impl<T: Copy + From<u8>> Matrix<T>` block.

The product's bounds are getting long: `T: Copy + Default + Add<Output = T> + Mul<Output = T>`. That's normal for numeric generic code. (In the advanced traits module you'll see how a `Number` trait with a blanket impl can name that whole list once. Production crates like `nalgebra` and `ndarray` do exactly that.)

`Mul` now has two impls for `&Matrix<T>`: `Mul<T>` (times a scalar) from the last milestone and `Mul<&Matrix<T>>` (times a matrix). Rust picks one from the type on the right of `*`. Overloading on the right-hand side is allowed because they're different traits as far as the compiler is concerned (`Mul<T>` versus `Mul<&Matrix<T>>`).
hints: `checked_mul`: after the shape check, `let mut result = Matrix::filled(self.rows, other.cols, T::default());` and three nested loops: `sum = sum + self[(row, k)] * other[(k, col)]`.
`impl<T: Copy + Default + Add<Output = T> + Mul<Output = T>> Mul for &Matrix<T>` mirrors your `Add` impl, calling `checked_mul`.
`identity`: start from `Matrix::filled(n, n, T::from(0))` and set `m[(i, i)] = T::from(1)` for each `i`.

milestones.title: Polish: powers, trace and a Fibonacci trick
hints: Add `NotSquare { rows: usize, cols: usize }` to `MatrixError` and its message to `Display`.
Put `pow` and `trace` in an `impl` block with all the bounds they need: `T: Copy + Default + From<u8> + Add<Output = T> + Mul<Output = T>`.
`trace` starts from `T::default()` and adds `self[(i, i)]` for each `i`; `pow` is the repeated-squaring loop from the text, after the square check.

projects.title: A parallel task scheduler
projects.summary: The core of every build system and CI pipeline. Parse tasks and their dependencies, order them with a topological sort, name the cycle when there is one, run independent tasks in parallel waves on scoped threads with deterministic output, and find the critical path.

milestones.title: Parse the task file
milestones.text:
`cargo build`, `make`, CI pipelines, data workflows and even a cooking recipe have the same structure: **tasks** that take some work, and **dependencies** between them (you can't test before you compile, you can't butter toast that isn't toasted). Under the hood, every one of these tools is a **scheduler**: it works out an order that respects the dependencies and runs as much as possible at the same time. In this project you'll build one.

Tasks come from standard input, one per line:

```text
# A small build
fetch (2):
configure (1): fetch
compile (5): configure fetch
test (3): compile
docs (2): configure
package (1): compile test docs
```

Each line is `name (cost): dependencies`. The **cost** is how much work the task takes (think seconds), and the dependencies are the tasks that must finish first, separated by spaces. Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored.

For now, read the file and print every task in name order, with its dependencies in name order (or `-` for none):

```text
compile (5): configure, fetch
configure (1): fetch
docs (2): configure
fetch (2): -
package (1): compile, docs, test
test (3): compile
```

### The data structure is the graph

```rust
struct Task {
    cost: u32,
    deps: BTreeSet<String>,
}
```

in a `BTreeMap<String, Task>` keyed by name. That map *is* a **directed graph** stored as an adjacency list: each task points at the tasks it depends on. Using `BTreeMap` and `BTreeSet` instead of the hash versions keeps every walk over them in sorted order, which will make the scheduler's output identical on every run. A set also quietly merges a dependency listed twice.

### Report every problem

If anything is wrong, print every problem as `error: ...` and exit with code 1 (`ExitCode::FAILURE`), without printing the list:

| Problem | Message |
|---|---|
| no `:` or no `(cost)` | `line 4: expected "name (cost): dependencies"` |
| a name with characters other than letters, digits, `-` and `_` | `line 7: invalid task name "bad name"` |
| a cost that isn't a whole number above 0 | `line 3: invalid cost "x"` |
| a name used twice | `line 2: task "fetch" is defined twice` |
| a dependency that isn't defined anywhere | `task "deploy" depends on unknown task "package"` |

Line errors come in line order. Unknown dependencies are checked **after** reading every line, because a task may depend on one defined later in the file (forward references are normal in real build files); they're reported in task-name order, then dependency order. (The errors go to standard output so the tests can check them; a real tool would print them with `eprintln!`.)

Parsing a line is a chain of small steps that can each fail: `split_once(':')`, then `strip_suffix(')')` and `split_once('(')` on the part before the colon, then parsing the cost. Writing it as `fn parse_line(line: &str) -> Result<(String, Task), String>` with `?` and `ok_or_else` keeps it flat.
hints: `parse_line`: `let (head, deps) = line.split_once(':').ok_or_else(...)?;` then `head.trim().strip_suffix(')').and_then(|h| h.split_once('('))` gives the name and the cost text.
In `parse_tasks`, loop over `input.lines().enumerate()`, skip blank and `#` lines, and push `format!("line {}: {e}", i + 1)` for every error; check `tasks.contains_key(&name)` before inserting.
After the loop, check every dependency of every task with `tasks.contains_key(dep)`. Return `Ok(tasks)` only if `errors` is empty.

milestones.title: An order that respects the dependencies
milestones.text:
A scheduler's first job is an order to run things in, where every task comes **after** all of its dependencies. That's called a **topological order**, and there are usually many: in the example, `docs` could run before or after `compile`. Your tool must always pick the same one, so define the tie-break: whenever several tasks are ready, take the **alphabetically first**.

Replace the list with the order and the total cost of all tasks:

```text
order: fetch, configure, compile, docs, test, package
total cost: 14
```

### Kahn's algorithm

1. For every task, count how many dependencies it's still waiting for.
2. Every task waiting for 0 is **ready**.
3. Repeatedly take a ready task, append it to the order, and tell each task that depends on it that one of its dependencies is done (decrease its count). A task whose count reaches 0 becomes ready.

Step 3 needs the edges the other way round: not "what does `compile` depend on" but "who depends on `fetch`". Build that **reversed adjacency list** first, `BTreeMap<&str, Vec<&str>>`. And make the ready list a `BTreeSet<&str>`: `pop_first()` removes the smallest element, which is exactly the alphabetical tie-break, at O(log n) per step.

```rust
while let Some(name) = ready.pop_first() {
    order.push(name);
    // decrease the count of every task that depends on `name`...
}
```

The maps borrow the names from the task map (`&str`, not `String`), so the whole algorithm allocates no new strings, and the returned order is a `Vec<&str>` borrowing from the tasks.

### What if it never finishes?

If tasks depend on each other in a circle (`a` needs `c`, `c` needs `b`, `b` needs `a`), none of them ever reaches 0: the loop ends with tasks left over. So Kahn's algorithm detects cycles for free: if the order is shorter than the number of tasks, there's a **cycle**. Return `Option<Vec<&str>>` and, on `None`, print `error: the tasks contain a cycle` and exit with code 1. (The next milestone names the cycle.)

If the file defines no tasks at all, print `no tasks` and exit successfully.
hints: Build `waiting: BTreeMap<&str, usize>` (each task's number of dependencies) and `dependents: BTreeMap<&str, Vec<&str>>` (for each dependency, who needs it).

Start `ready` as a `BTreeSet<&str>` of the tasks waiting for 0, then `while let Some(name) = ready.pop_first()`: push it, and for each dependent decrease its count and insert it into `ready` when it hits 0.
Return `Some(order)` if `order.len() == tasks.len()`, else `None`. In `main`, use `let Some(order) = topo_order(&tasks) else { ... };`.

milestones.title: Name the cycle
milestones.text:
"The tasks contain a cycle" is true but useless: in a real build file with hundreds of tasks, which ones? Print the cycle itself, following the dependencies:

```text
error: cycle: a -> c -> b -> a
```

Read `->` as "depends on": `a` depends on `c`, which depends on `b`, which depends on `a` again. A task that depends on itself is the shortest cycle: `error: cycle: lint -> lint`.

### Depth-first search with three colors

Kahn's algorithm can tell you a cycle exists, but not where. **Depth-first search** can. Walk the graph from a task, following dependencies as deep as possible, and keep the current path on a stack. Each task is in one of three states:

- **not visited** yet (not in the map),
- **visiting**: on the current path, its dependencies are being explored right now,
- **done**: it and everything below it was explored, and no cycle was found there.

Reaching a *visiting* task means you've walked in a circle: the cycle is the part of the path from that task to the end, plus the task again. Reaching a *done* task means nothing new is down there, so you can return immediately; that's what keeps the search linear in the size of the graph instead of exponential.

```rust
enum Mark {
    Visiting,
    Done,
}

fn visit<'a>(
    name: &'a str,
    tasks: &'a BTreeMap<String, Task>,
    marks: &mut BTreeMap<&'a str, Mark>,
    path: &mut Vec<&'a str>,
) -> Option<Vec<&'a str>>
```

The lifetime `'a` says that every name in `marks`, `path` and the returned cycle borrows from the task map (or is the `name` argument, which has the same lifetime). The compiler needs to hear it: with two reference parameters in and references out, elision can't guess where the output borrows from.

`visit` marks the task as visiting, pushes it on the path, recursively visits each dependency (returning a cycle as soon as one is found), then pops it and marks it done. `find_cycle` calls `visit` for every task in name order, so the cycle you report is always the same one.

Keep Kahn's algorithm for the order, and call `find_cycle` only when it returns `None`: then there must be a cycle, so `find_cycle(&tasks).expect(...)` is a fine use of `expect` (it documents a guarantee rather than ignoring an error).
hints: In `visit`, first `match marks.get(name)`: `Some(Mark::Done)` returns `None`; `Some(Mark::Visiting)` finds `name` in `path` with `position`, and returns `path[start..]` plus `name`.
Otherwise: `marks.insert(name, Mark::Visiting); path.push(name);`, visit each of `tasks[name].deps` (return early on `Some`), then `path.pop();` and mark it `Done`.
In `main`'s `else` branch, print `error: cycle: {}` with `cycle.join(" -> ")`.

hints: `waves`: for each `name` in the order, `let l = tasks[name].deps.iter().map(|dep| level[dep.as_str()] + 1).max().unwrap_or(0);`, record it in `level`, and push the name into `waves[l]` (adding a new wave when `l == waves.len()`). Sort each wave at the end.
In `run_waves`, print the wave line, then use `thread::scope` with one `s.spawn(move || work(name, tasks[name].cost))` per task, and join the handles in order.
Print the results only after the scope has returned: `for (name, hash) in wave.iter().zip(hashes) { println!("  {name}: {hash:016x}"); }`.

require.message: Run each wave's tasks on scoped threads with `std::thread::scope`.
Spawn one thread per task in the wave (`s.spawn(...)` inside the scope).

}

drills.prompt:
Build a small **worker pool**. Write `fn process_jobs(jobs: Vec<u64>, workers: usize) -> Vec<u64>` that returns the square of every job, in job order, computed by `workers` threads:

1. Make a job channel. The workers share its `Receiver` through `Arc<Mutex<Receiver<(usize, u64)>>>` (a `Receiver` can't be cloned).
2. Make a results channel; each worker gets a clone of its `Sender`.
3. Each worker loops: lock the receiver, take one job with `recv()`, **let the lock go**, and send `(index, job * job)` back. When `recv()` returns `Err` (no more jobs), it stops.
4. Send every job with its index, drop both original senders, collect the results, sort them by index, and return the values.

`result_rx.iter().collect()` into a `Vec<(usize, u64)>`, sort it, then `.map(|(_, value)| value)`.

require.message: Use two channels, one for jobs and one for results.
Share the job Receiver between workers with `Arc<Mutex<...>>`.

pro.title: rustup, Cargo and continuous integration
pro.summary: Install Rust the way professionals do, build a small command-line crate with Cargo, and keep it clean with rustfmt, clippy and tests that run on every push.
pro.readme:
# 01 · rustup, Cargo and continuous integration

On the RustArena site, one click compiled and ran your code. At work you'll run the same toolchain yourself: **rustup** installs Rust, **Cargo** builds, tests and manages dependencies, **rustfmt** and **clippy** keep code consistent, and **CI** runs all of it on every push so nobody merges broken code. In this project you finish a small command-line tool, `wordfreq`, and get it through the checks a Rust team's CI would run.

**You'll practice:** rustup and toolchains, Cargo commands, `Cargo.toml` and dependencies, debug and release profiles, rustfmt, clippy, unit and integration tests, and reading CI results.

## Background

### rustup: one installer for every Rust

A **toolchain** is a compiler (`rustc`), Cargo and the standard library for one **channel**: `stable` (a new release every six weeks), `beta` or `nightly`, or a pinned version like `1.85.0`. rustup installs and switches them. **Components** are optional tools for a toolchain.

```bash
rustup show                          # installed toolchains and which one is active
rustup update                        # upgrade stable (do it every few weeks)
rustup component add rustfmt clippy  # the formatter and the linter
rustup toolchain install 1.85        # an older compiler, to test your minimum version
cargo +1.85 test                     # run one command with that toolchain
```

Teams often commit a `rust-toolchain.toml` so every laptop and CI machine uses the same channel:

```toml
[toolchain]
channel = "stable"
components = ["rustfmt", "clippy"]
```

Versions are not **editions** (2018, 2021, 2024): an edition is a set of language rules each crate picks in `Cargo.toml`, and crates on different editions work together.

### Cargo, the tool you'll type all day

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `cargo check` | type-check without producing a binary: the fastest feedback |
| `cargo build` / `cargo run -- ARGS` | compile (and run) a debug build; `--` separates your program's arguments from Cargo's |
| `cargo test` | build and run unit, integration and doc tests |
| `cargo doc --open` | generate HTML docs for your crate and every dependency |
| `cargo add name` / `cargo tree` | add a dependency / show the dependency graph |
| `cargo fmt` / `cargo clippy` | format the code / lint it |

This package has **two crates**: a library (`src/lib.rs`, where the logic lives so it can be unit tested) and a binary (`src/main.rs`, which handles arguments and I/O and calls `wordfreq::count_words`). That split is how most Rust command-line tools are organized.

### Cargo.toml and dependencies

```toml
[package]
name = "wordfreq"
version = "0.1.0"          # semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
edition = "2024"
rust-version = "1.85"      # the oldest compiler you support (your MSRV)
description = "Prints the most frequent words in a text"
license = "MIT"            # an SPDX identifier; crates.io requires it

[dependencies]
unicode-segmentation = "1"
```

`"1"` is a **caret requirement**: any version from 1.0.0 up to (not including) 2.0.0, because semver promises no breaking changes within a major version. The exact versions Cargo picked go in **`Cargo.lock`**. Commit it: it makes every build, yours and CI's, use the same code. `cargo update` moves to newer compatible versions on purpose, as its own reviewable commit.

### Profiles: debug and release builds

`cargo build` uses the **dev** profile: quick to compile, unoptimized, with debug info, and integer overflow **panics** so you find bugs. `cargo build --release` uses the **release** profile: optimized (often 10 to 100 times faster), and overflow wraps silently. Builds land in `target/debug/` and `target/release/` (here, one `target/` at the repository root shared by every project, set in `.cargo/config.toml`). Profiles are tunable:

```toml
[profile.release]
lto = true      # link-time optimization: optimize across crates, smaller and faster binaries
strip = true    # remove symbols from the binary: much smaller files
```

Never benchmark or ship a debug build.

### rustfmt and clippy

**rustfmt** formats code one standard way, so code review is about logic, not spacing. `cargo fmt` rewrites files; `cargo fmt --check` only reports. **clippy** is a linter with hundreds of lints for bugs, slow code and unidiomatic code; each warning links to an explanation. CI runs it with `-D warnings` so every warning is an error. When a lint is wrong for one spot, silence it there with `#[allow(clippy::lint_name)]` and a comment saying why.

### Continuous integration

Open `.github/workflows/grade.yml`. On every push, GitHub Actions starts a fresh Ubuntu machine, installs stable Rust with rustfmt and clippy, restores cached dependencies and runs `bash tools/grade.sh <project>`: the same `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy` and `cargo test` you run locally, plus project checks. A fresh machine catches "works on my laptop" problems (a file you forgot to commit), and a green check is what lets teammates trust and merge a change.

## Your tasks

Work in `projects/01-toolchain` (`cd projects/01-toolchain`).

1. **Check your tools.** Run `rustup show`, `cargo --version` and `bash ../../tools/doctor.sh`. Then `cargo run -- --help` builds and runs the program, and `cargo test` fails with `not yet implemented`: that's what you'll fix.
2. **Fill in the metadata.** In `Cargo.toml`, add `description`, `license` and `rust-version = "1.85"` (edition 2024 needs at least 1.85).
3. **Add a dependency.** Splitting text into words correctly (apostrophes, decimals, accents) is harder than it looks, and Unicode already defines it. Run `cargo add unicode-segmentation`, then look at what changed in `Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock`, and run `cargo tree`. Read its docs with `cargo doc --open`.
4. **Write the library.** Complete TODO 1 and TODO 2 in `src/lib.rs`:
   - `count_words`: `use unicode_segmentation::UnicodeSegmentation;` adds `unicode_words()` to `&str`. Lowercase each word with `to_lowercase()` and count with `*counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1`.
   - `top_words`: collect the pairs into a `Vec`, sort with `sort_by` comparing counts in reverse and then words (`Ordering::then_with`), and `truncate(n)`.
5. **Unit tests.** Do TODO 3: at least 3 `#[test]` functions in `src/`, for example how `top_words` breaks ties.
6. **Format and lint.** `cargo fmt`, then `cargo clippy --all-targets`. `main.rs` was written in a hurry: fix every warning clippy reports (read the explanation link each time).
7. **Release build.** Add the `[profile.release]` section above. Run `cargo build` and `cargo build --release`, then compare `ls -lh ../../target/debug/wordfreq ../../target/release/wordfreq`. Try it: `cargo run --release -- --top 5 < README.md`.
8. **Grade it** like CI does: `bash ../../tools/grade.sh 01-toolchain`. Then commit, push, and watch the **Actions** tab turn green.

## What the grader checks

- `Cargo.toml` has a description, a license and a rust-version, depends on `unicode-segmentation`, and its release profile sets `lto` and `strip`,
- `tests/cli.rs` is unchanged: these integration tests run the real binary through `CARGO_BIN_EXE_wordfreq`, checking output, exit codes (0 success, 1 runtime error, 2 usage error) and that errors go to standard error,
- `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` are clean,
- every test passes, and `src/` has at least 3 unit tests,
- the release build runs and prints the right answer.

## Hints

- `cargo test name_part` runs only the tests whose names contain `name_part`. Add `-- --nocapture` to see `println!` output.
- Reproduce a failing integration test by hand: `printf 'a b a' | cargo run -- --top 1`.
- `cargo clippy --fix --allow-dirty` applies the machine-fixable suggestions. Read the diff before committing.

## Going further

- Prove your `rust-version` is honest: `rustup toolchain install 1.85 && cargo +1.85 test`.
- Run `cargo run --release < big.txt | head -n 1` on a large file: `println!` panics when `head` closes the pipe. Write through `std::io::stdout().lock()` with `writeln!` and stop quietly on `ErrorKind::BrokenPipe`.

pro.title: Git and pull requests
pro.summary: Work the way teams do. Feature branches, pull requests, a real merge conflict in Rust code, undoing mistakes and tagging a release.
pro.readme:
# 02 · Git and pull requests

Every professional team uses Git, and almost all of them work through **pull requests** (PRs): you change code on a branch, open a PR, the CI checks run, a teammate reviews it, and then it's merged. This project walks you through that whole loop on a small Rust crate, including the parts that scare beginners: a merge conflict in Rust code, undoing a commit that broke the build, and tagging a release.

There's little code to write. The grader reads your repository's **history**, then checks that the merged code still compiles, is formatted, and passes its tests.

**You'll practice:** commits and commit messages, branches, pull requests, merge conflicts, `git revert`, semantic versioning and annotated tags.

## Background

### The mental model

- A **commit** is a snapshot of the whole project, plus a message and a pointer to its parent commit(s).
- A **branch** is just a movable name pointing at a commit. `main` is the shared branch; you work on your own.
- A **merge commit** has two parents and joins two lines of history.
- A **remote** (`origin`) is the copy on GitHub. `git push` sends your commits there; `git pull` brings other people's here.

```bash
git status                        # what changed?
git diff                          # exactly how?
git add path/to/file              # stage it for the next commit
git commit -m "Add the parser"    # take the snapshot
git log --oneline --graph --all   # the history as a graph
```

### Commit messages

Teams read history all the time (`git log`, `git blame`, release notes), so messages follow conventions: a **subject line** of at most 72 characters (50 is better), in the **imperative** ("Add parser", not "Added parser"), starting with a capital letter, with **no trailing period**. If it needs explaining, add a blank line and a body that says **why**; the diff already shows what.

### Pull requests

A PR asks "please merge my branch into `main`". It shows the diff, runs CI (here, the **Grade** workflow) and collects review comments. Keep PRs small and focused, describe what changed and how you tested it, and only merge when the checks are green. Teams usually protect `main` so a PR is the only way in.

### Merge conflicts

When two branches change the **same lines**, Git can't decide which version wins and stops with markers in the file:

```rust
pub fn captain() -> &'static str {
<<<<<<< HEAD
    "ferris"
=======
    "nova"
>>>>>>> feature/captain-b
}
```

You edit the file into the version you want (often a mix of both), delete every marker line, then `git add` and `git commit` to finish the merge. In Rust, **always run `cargo test` before committing the resolution**: a leftover marker doesn't compile, and two changes that merge without a conflict can still break each other (one branch renames a function that the other starts calling). That's why CI runs again after every merge.

### Undoing things safely

| Situation | Command |
|---|---|
| Unstage a file | `git restore --staged file` |
| Throw away uncommitted edits | `git restore file` |
| Undo a commit that's already pushed | `git revert <commit>`: a **new** commit that reverses it |
| Rewrite commits you haven't pushed yet | `git commit --amend`, `git rebase -i` |

Never rewrite history other people already have (no `git push --force` on `main`). `revert` is the safe tool once something is public.

### Releases and tags

Rust crates use **semantic versioning** (`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`) in `Cargo.toml`. A release is a commit that sets the version, marked with a **tag**. Use an **annotated** tag (`git tag -a`): it records who tagged, when and why, like a commit does. A plain `git tag` is just a name.

## Your tasks

Run the commands from the repository root. You can use the GitHub website for the PR steps.

1. **Set your identity** (once per machine):
   ```bash
   git config --global user.name "Your Name"
   git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
   ```
2. **A feature branch and a pull request.**
   ```bash
   git switch -c feature/intro
   # create projects/02-git/intro.md with at least 3 lines about you
   git add projects/02-git/intro.md
   git commit -m "Add an introduction"
   git push -u origin feature/intro
   ```
   On GitHub, open **Pull requests > New pull request**, pick `feature/intro`, create it, look at the checks, then **Merge pull request** with *Create a merge commit*. Back in the terminal: `git switch main && git pull`.
3. **Make (and fix) a merge conflict.** Two teammates pick a captain in `src/lib.rs` at the same time:
   ```bash
   git switch -c feature/captain-a
   # in projects/02-git/src/lib.rs, change "TBD" to one name from PLAYERS
   git commit -am "Make ferris the captain"
   git push -u origin feature/captain-a
   git switch main
   git switch -c feature/captain-b
   # change "TBD" to a DIFFERENT name from PLAYERS
   git commit -am "Make nova the captain"
   git push -u origin feature/captain-b
   ```
   Open and merge a PR for `feature/captain-a`. Then open a PR for `feature/captain-b`: GitHub reports a conflict. Resolve it locally:
   ```bash
   git fetch origin
   git switch feature/captain-b
   git merge origin/main             # CONFLICT in projects/02-git/src/lib.rs
   # edit the file: keep one captain, and add a vice_captain() function
   # returning the other name, if you like; delete the marker lines
   cargo test --manifest-path projects/02-git/Cargo.toml
   git add projects/02-git/src/lib.rs
   git commit                        # finishes the merge
   git push
   ```
   Merge the PR once it's green, then `git switch main && git pull`.
4. **Undo a mistake with revert.** On `main`, set `MAX_PLAYERS` to `6`, commit it as "Allow six players" and push. The Grade check for 02-git fails because a test enforces the rules. Undo it the safe way:
   ```bash
   git revert HEAD
   git push
   ```
5. **Release 0.1.0.** In `projects/02-git/Cargo.toml` change `version = "0.0.0"` to `"0.1.0"`, run `cargo build` in that folder so `Cargo.lock` picks it up, and commit both files as "Release 0.1.0". Then:
   ```bash
   git tag -a v0.1.0 -m "roster 0.1.0"
   git push origin main v0.1.0
   ```
6. **Check yourself:** `bash tools/grade.sh 02-git`.

## What the grader checks

- `intro.md` exists with at least 3 non-empty lines,
- at least three `feature/` branches were merged (PR merge commits or `git merge`),
- a merge commit joins two branches that both changed `src/lib.rs`, and no conflict markers are left,
- `tests/roster.rs` is unchanged, and the crate passes `cargo fmt --check`, clippy and its tests,
- a `Revert "..."` commit touches this project,
- `v0.1.0` is an annotated tag in your history, on a commit whose `Cargo.toml` says `version = "0.1.0"`,
- your commit subjects in this project are at most 72 characters, start with a capital letter and don't end with a period.

## Hints

- Lost? `git log --oneline --graph --all` shows where every branch points. `git merge --abort` gets you out of a merge you want to restart.
- A lightweight tag fails the check. Delete it (`git tag -d v0.1.0`, plus `git push origin :refs/tags/v0.1.0` if pushed) and use `-a`.
- Your editor or VS Code shows *Accept Current / Incoming / Both* buttons on conflicts. Handy, but read the result before committing.

## Going further

- Protect `main` (**Settings > Branches**): require pull requests and a passing Grade check. That's how most companies configure it.
- Try `git rebase main` on a branch instead of merging, and compare the graph.
- Find the commit that broke a test with `git bisect run cargo test`.
- Turn your tag into a **GitHub Release** with notes (Releases > Draft a new release).

pro.title: Testing like a team
pro.summary: Write the test suite for a money-handling library yourself. Graded by mutation testing, so every hidden bug must make one of your tests fail.
pro.readme:
# 03 · Testing like a team

On the Arena site the tests were written for you. At work, **you** write them: every change ships with tests, and code review asks "where's the test?" In this project you write the whole test suite for a small money-handling library, using every kind of test Rust has, and the grader checks whether your tests would actually catch bugs.

**How it's graded: mutation testing.** Coverage only tells you a line *ran*, not that a test would notice if it were wrong. So the grader makes 8 **mutants**: copies of the library, each with one small, realistic bug planted (an off-by-one, a lost minus sign, the wrong rounding...). Your tests must pass on the real library and **fail on every mutant**. A mutant that survives means some rule in the documentation has no test.

**You'll practice:** unit tests, integration tests, doc tests, property-based tests with proptest, edge cases, and thinking like a tester.

## Background

### The library

`src/money.rs` defines `Money`, an amount stored as whole cents (never floating point, which can't represent 0.10 exactly), with parsing, formatting, percentages and fair splitting. `src/account.rs` defines `Ledger`, a balance with a history. **Don't change these two files**: the grader checks they're untouched. Read their documentation comments carefully: every sentence is a rule to test.

### Unit tests

Unit tests live inside the crate, so they can reach **private** items. Usually they sit at the bottom of the file in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests { ... }`. Here the library files end with `#[cfg(test)] mod tests;`, which loads the module from `src/money/tests.rs` and `src/account/tests.rs`: the same thing, kept in a separate file (big projects do this too). `#[cfg(test)]` means the code is only compiled for `cargo test`.

```rust
use super::*; // everything in the parent module, private items included

#[test]
fn withdraw_refuses_overdrafts() {
    let mut ledger = Ledger::new();                       // arrange
    ledger.deposit(Money::from_cents(300)).unwrap();
    let result = ledger.withdraw(Money::from_cents(301)); // act
    assert!(result.is_err());                             // assert
    assert_eq!(ledger.balance(), Money::from_cents(300));
}
```

Your tools: `assert!(cond)`, `assert_eq!(left, right)` and `assert_ne!` (both values are printed on failure), an optional message (`assert!(x > 0, "x was {x}")`), `matches!(value, Pattern { .. })`, and `#[should_panic(expected = "zero parts")]` for code that must panic.

### Integration tests

Every file in `tests/` is compiled as a **separate crate** that uses yours through its public API, exactly like a user would: `use ledger::{Ledger, Money};`. They catch a different class of mistakes: a missing `pub`, an awkward API, parts that work alone but not together.

### Doc tests

Code blocks in `///` and `//!` documentation are compiled and run by `cargo test`, so examples in the docs can never go stale. Lines starting with `# ` run but are hidden from the rendered docs:

```rust
//! ```
//! use ledger::Money;
//! let price: Money = "12.50".parse()?;
//! assert_eq!(price.cents(), 1250);
//! # Ok::<(), ledger::ParseMoneyError>(())
//! ```
```

### Property-based tests

An example test checks one input you thought of. A **property** is a rule that holds for *every* input, and proptest checks it against hundreds of random ones. When one fails, proptest **shrinks** it to the simplest input that still fails, and saves it in `proptest-regressions/` (commit that folder: the case is then retried on every run).

```rust
use proptest::prelude::*;

proptest! {
    #[test]
    fn split_never_loses_a_cent(cents in -1_000_000i64..1_000_000, parts in 1usize..20) {
        let total: i64 = Money::from_cents(cents).split(parts).iter().map(|m| m.cents()).sum();
        prop_assert_eq!(total, cents);
    }
}
```

Good properties: round trips (`parse(format(x)) == x`), invariants (a balance is never negative), and comparisons with a simpler model. Choose ranges with care: `any::<i64>()` almost never produces a small number like -5, which is exactly where formatting bugs hide.

### What makes a good test

- **One behavior per test**, named after it: `withdraw_refuses_overdrafts`, not `test2`.
- **Check the side effects too.** A refused operation must change *nothing*: check the balance **and** the history afterwards.
- **Edge cases are where bugs live**: zero, negative, one, exactly the limit, one past it, rounding halves, empty.
- Read the docs one sentence at a time and ask: "which test fails if this sentence is violated?"

### Running tests

```bash
cargo test                       # everything: unit, integration, doc tests
cargo test split                 # only tests whose name contains "split"
cargo test --lib                 # only unit tests
cargo test --test properties     # only tests/properties.rs
cargo test --doc                 # only doc tests
cargo test -- --nocapture        # show println! output
```

## Your tasks

Work in `projects/03-testing`.

1. Read the documentation in `src/money.rs` and `src/account.rs`. List the rules.
2. **Unit tests** in `src/money/tests.rs` and `src/account/tests.rs`. Test the private helper `all_digits` directly, and read private fields like `ledger.history` to check that refused operations leave them alone.
3. **Integration tests** in `tests/` (add files as you like, e.g. `tests/ledger.rs`).
4. **A doc test**: add an `# Examples` section to the crate documentation at the top of `src/lib.rs`.
5. **Property tests** with proptest (already in `[dev-dependencies]`), e.g. in `tests/properties.rs`: round trips, `split` adding up, the balance never going negative.
6. Grade it: `bash ../../tools/grade.sh 03-testing`. Each surviving mutant tells you which rule is untested. Add tests until all 8 die, then commit and push.

## What the grader checks

- `src/money.rs`, `src/account.rs` and `mutants/` are unchanged,
- `cargo fmt --check` and clippy are clean, and every test passes on the real library,
- at least 15 tests, including at least 3 unit tests, 3 integration tests and 1 doc test in `src/lib.rs`,
- at least one `proptest!` block,
- each mutant in `mutants/` makes at least one of your tests fail. Property tests run with a fixed seed (`PROPTEST_RNG_SEED`) while grading, so results are the same every time.

## Hints

- "Rounded to the nearest cent, halves away from zero" is only observable when the exact result has a fraction. Pick numbers that make it exactly half a cent.
- "Newest first" needs at least two *different* entries to be observable.
- If a mutant survives and you can't see why, open its patch in `mutants/`: it shows the exact change, like a real mutation testing tool would. Then write the test that would have caught it.

## Going further

- Run a real mutation testing tool on your crate: `cargo install cargo-mutants && cargo mutants`. It invents mutants for you.
- Measure coverage with `cargo llvm-cov` and see that 100% line coverage still lets bugs through.
- Write a `transfer(&mut self, to: &mut Ledger, amount: Money)` test-first: tests, then the code.

pro.title: A command-line tool with clap
pro.summary: Build a real CLI with subcommands, flags, files, helpful errors and proper exit codes, tested end to end like a user would run it.
pro.readme:
# 04 · A command-line tool with clap

Command-line tools are everywhere at work: internal tools, deploy scripts, developer tooling. Rust is a favorite for them (ripgrep, fd, bat and Cargo itself are Rust CLIs) because the result is one fast binary with no runtime to install. In this project you finish `taskr`, a to-do manager that stores its tasks in a JSON file, built the way production CLIs are: **clap** for arguments, **anyhow** for errors, **serde** for data, and end-to-end tests with **assert_cmd**.

**You'll practice:** clap's derive API, subcommands and options, environment variables, error context with anyhow, JSON with serde, exit codes, stdout vs. stderr, and testing a binary like a user would.

## Background

### What users expect from a CLI

```
taskr [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>
taskr add "Buy milk" --priority high      # a subcommand, a positional argument, an option
taskr list --all                          # a flag
taskr --file work.json list               # an option that applies to every subcommand
```

- `--help` and `--version` work, and every argument is documented in the help.
- **Standard output is for results**: users pipe it into other programs (`taskr list --json | jq`) or files. **Errors go to standard error**, so they still reach the user's screen and never corrupt the data in a pipe.
- **The exit code** tells scripts what happened: `0` success, `1` the command failed (a missing task, an unreadable file), `2` it was used wrongly (unknown option, missing argument). Check it with `echo $?`.
- Settings can come from **environment variables** (`TASKR_FILE`), so users don't retype them. A flag on the command line beats the variable, which beats the default.

### clap's derive API

You describe the command line as Rust types and clap generates the parser, the help text and the error messages. Doc comments become help text.

```rust
#[derive(Parser)]
#[command(version, about)]                // --version reads Cargo.toml
struct Cli {
    /// The tasks file
    #[arg(long, short, global = true, default_value = "tasks.json", env = "TASKR_FILE")]
    file: PathBuf,
    #[command(subcommand)]
    command: Command,
}

#[derive(Subcommand)]
enum Command {
    /// Mark a task as done
    Done {
        /// The task's id, as shown by `taskr list`
        id: u32,                         // positional; "abc" is rejected with exit code 2
    },
    /// Delete every task that is done
    Clear,
}
```

`Cli::parse()` handles `--help`, `--version` and usage errors itself, and exits with code 2 on errors. Some attributes need a Cargo **feature** of clap: `env = ...` only compiles with `features = ["derive", "env"]` in `Cargo.toml`. Features let crates keep rarely used code out of your build.

### Errors with anyhow

In an application, most errors end the same way: tell the user, exit with 1. `anyhow::Result<T>` holds any error type, `?` converts errors for you, and **context** says what you were doing when it failed:

```rust
use anyhow::{Context, Result};

let text = fs::read_to_string(path)
    .with_context(|| format!("could not read {}", path.display()))?;
let task = tasks.iter_mut().find(|t| t.id == id)
    .with_context(|| format!("no task with id {id}"))?;      // works on Option too
```

`main` prints errors with `{:#}`, which shows the whole chain on one line: `error: could not parse tasks.json: expected value at line 1 column 1`. Compare that with a bare `No such file or directory (os error 2)`: which file? Use anyhow in applications; libraries define their own error types with thiserror (project 05).

### Data with serde

`#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` lets `serde_json::from_str` and `serde_json::to_string_pretty` convert your structs to and from JSON; `#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]` makes `Priority::High` the string `"high"`. Two habits of careful tools: a **missing** file means "no tasks yet", but a **corrupt** file is an error and is never overwritten, because it's the user's data. And save **atomically**: write a temporary file, then `fs::rename` it over the real one. A rename is all-or-nothing, so a crash or a full disk mid-write can't leave half a file behind.

### Testing a CLI end to end

`tests/cli.rs` runs the real binary in a fresh temporary folder for every test:

```rust
let dir = tempfile::TempDir::new().unwrap();      // deleted when dropped
assert_cmd::Command::new(env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_taskr"))
    .current_dir(dir.path())
    .args(["done", "42"])
    .assert()
    .code(1)
    .stdout("")
    .stderr(predicates::str::contains("no task with id 42"));
```

`assert()` runs the command; `success()`, `code(n)`, `stdout(...)` and `stderr(...)` check the result, with exact strings or **predicates** (`contains`, `starts_with`, `is_empty().not()`). On failure you see the command, its exit code and both outputs. A temporary folder per test keeps tests independent, so Cargo can run them in parallel.

## Your tasks

Work in `projects/04-cli`. `tests/cli.rs` is the specification: read it first.

1. **Explore.** `cargo run -- --help`, `cargo run -- add --help`. Note the `--` between Cargo's arguments and taskr's.
2. **Load and save** (TODO 1 and 2 in `src/task.rs`), with the error messages the comments give: `could not read <file>`, `could not parse <file>`, `could not write <file>`.
3. **New subcommands** (TODO 3 in `src/main.rs`): `Done { id: u32 }`, `Remove { id: u32 }` and `Clear`, each with a doc comment.
4. **Handle them** (TODO 4):
   - `done ID` marks the task done and prints `Completed task 1: Buy milk`,
   - `remove ID` deletes it and prints `Removed task 1: Buy milk`,
   - an unknown id is an error: `no task with id 42`,
   - `clear` deletes every task that is done and prints `Removed 2 done tasks` (with the real count).
5. **The environment variable** (TODO 5): enable clap's `env` feature in `Cargo.toml` and add `env = "TASKR_FILE"` to `--file`.
6. **Your own tests**: create `tests/clear.rs` with at least 2 tests for `clear`, in the style of `tests/cli.rs`.
7. Run `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --all-targets` and `bash ../../tools/grade.sh 04-cli`. Commit and push.
8. Use it for real: `cargo install --path .`, then `export TASKR_FILE=~/tasks.json` and `taskr add "Finish project 05"`.

## What the grader checks

- `tests/cli.rs` is unchanged and every test passes: output, exit codes, files, `--file` and `TASKR_FILE`, error messages on standard error,
- `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` are clean,
- it runs your `taskr` itself: add three tasks, complete tasks 1 and 3, then `clear` must print `Removed 2 done tasks` and leave only task 2,
- `tests/` has at least 2 tests of your own besides `cli.rs`.

## Hints

- One test at a time: `cargo test --test cli remove`. Add `-- --nocapture` to see what you print.
- `iter_mut().find(...)` gives the task to change; `iter().position(...)` gives an index for `Vec::remove`; `Vec::retain` keeps the elements you choose.
- `error[E0599]: no method named env` means the `env` feature isn't enabled yet.
- Save the file *before* printing the confirmation, so you never claim a change that wasn't saved.

## Going further

- Generate shell completions with the `clap_complete` crate (a hidden `completions` subcommand).
- Default to the user's data folder instead of the current directory, with the `directories` crate.
- Add `taskr edit ID [--title ...] [--priority ...]`, with tests first.
- Color the list only when standard output is a terminal (`std::io::IsTerminal`) and `NO_COLOR` isn't set.

pro.title: Designing a library crate
pro.summary: Split code into a library and a binary in a Cargo workspace, design a public API with typed errors and full documentation, and prepare it for crates.io.
pro.readme:
# 05 · Designing a library crate

Most Rust code at work lives in libraries that other code depends on. A library's public API is a promise: once someone builds on it, every name, signature and error variant is hard to change. So teams work to get it right: types that make mistakes impossible, errors callers can act on, documentation whose examples are tested, and version numbers that tell the truth.

You'll finish **semver-lite**, a library that parses, compares and matches [semantic versions](https://semver.org) (the `^1.2` rules Cargo itself uses), and a small `semver` command-line tool built on it, in one Cargo workspace.

**You'll practice:** workspaces, API design (newtypes, builders, `impl Trait`, `AsRef`), typed errors with `thiserror`, rustdoc and doc tests, cargo features, semver, and packaging for crates.io.

## The workspace

```
05-library/
  Cargo.toml        [workspace]: the members, plus settings and dependencies they share
  semver-lite/      the library (the product)
  semver-cli/       the `semver` binary: reads arguments, calls the library, prints
```

A workspace builds several packages with one `Cargo.lock` and one `target/` folder. Real projects (ripgrep, tokio, serde) split this way so the library can be tested and reused without the binary, and the binary stays thin. Shared settings go in `[workspace.package]` and `[workspace.dependencies]`, and members inherit them with `edition.workspace = true`.

```bash
cd projects/05-library
cargo build --workspace            # everything
cargo test -p semver-lite          # one member (-p = --package)
cargo run -p semver-cli -- sort 1.10.0 1.2.0 v1.2.0-rc.1
```

The CLI depends on the library with `path = "semver-lite", version = "0.1.0"`: the path is used here, and the version is what the dependency becomes if the CLI is ever published (crates.io doesn't allow path-only dependencies).

## Background

### API design: make the right thing easy

- **Re-export from `lib.rs`.** Users write `semver_lite::Version`, never `semver_lite::version::Version`. The module layout stays private, so you can reorganize it without breaking anyone.
- **Newtypes.** `Prerelease` wraps a `String` in a struct with a private field. The only way to make one is `Prerelease::new`, which validates, so every `Prerelease` in existence is valid, and its ordering rule lives with the data. A plain `String` would let anyone build `"rc..1"`.
- **Standard traits.** Users expect `"1.2.3".parse()` (`FromStr`), `println!("{v}")` (`Display`), `versions.sort()` (`Ord`), plus `Debug`, `Clone`, `PartialEq`, `Hash`. They can't add them from outside your crate.
- **Builders.** `Parser::new().allow_v_prefix(true).allow_partial(true)` reads well at the call site, unlike `parse(s, true, false)`, and adding an option later breaks nobody.
- **`impl Trait` and `AsRef`.** `parse_all(inputs: impl IntoIterator<Item = impl AsRef<str>>)` accepts `["1.0.0"]`, a `Vec<String>`, or `&args` without the caller converting anything. Returning `impl Iterator` (see `VersionReq::matching`) lets callers chain or collect without the crate committing to a collection type.

### Typed errors with thiserror

Applications report errors to people, so `anyhow` (project 04) is fine there. Libraries report errors to *code*, so they return an enum the caller can `match` on:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
#[non_exhaustive]
pub enum Error {
    #[error("invalid version number \"{part}\"")]
    InvalidNumber { part: String },
    #[error("invalid version requirement \"{req}\"")]
    InvalidReq { req: String, source: Box<Error> },   // a field named `source` is the cause
}
```

`thiserror` writes the `Display` and `std::error::Error` impls, including `source()`, so a program can print the whole chain (try `semver match "^1.x" 1.0.0`). `#[non_exhaustive]` makes users add a `_` arm when they match, so a new variant later isn't a breaking change.

### Documentation is part of the API

`///` documents the next item and `//!` the enclosing one (the crate, at the top of `lib.rs`). Code blocks in docs are **compiled and run** by `cargo test`, so examples can't silently rot. Inside them, lines starting with `# ` are hidden from the rendered page; `# Ok::<(), semver_lite::Error>(())` at the end lets an example use `?`. Conventional sections are `# Examples`, `# Errors` (when a function returns `Result`) and `# Panics`, and `` [`Version`] `` links to an item. `#![deny(missing_docs)]` at the top of `lib.rs` makes any undocumented public item a compile error. Read the result with `cargo doc --open`.

### Optional features

Not every user wants serde. An optional dependency plus a feature lets them choose:

```toml
[features]
serde = ["dep:serde"]

[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1", optional = true }
```

Code that needs it goes behind `#[cfg(feature = "serde")]` (a whole module is easiest). Features must be **additive**: turning one on may add API, never remove or change it, because Cargo unifies features across the whole dependency graph. Test both ways (`cargo test` and `cargo test --all-features`), as the grader does.

### Semver for your own crate

`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`: bump PATCH for fixes, MINOR for new API, MAJOR for breaking changes. Breaking includes removing or renaming a public item, changing a signature, adding a variant to an exhaustive enum, and adding a field to a struct with public fields (it breaks struct literals and patterns). Before 1.0, Cargo treats the first non-zero number as the major one: `^0.2.3` means `>=0.2.3, <0.3.0`. You are about to implement exactly that rule.

### Ready for crates.io

crates.io needs a `description`, a `license` (an SPDX expression like `MIT OR Apache-2.0`) and a link (`repository`). Good crates also set `readme`, `keywords`, `categories` and `rust-version` (the oldest Rust they support). `cargo package --list` shows exactly which files would be uploaded, and `cargo package` builds the `.crate` and compiles it in isolation, which catches files you forgot to include. **Don't run `cargo publish` for this project**: published versions are permanent.

## Your tasks

1. **Errors** (`semver-lite/src/error.rs`): derive `thiserror::Error`, write the messages listed in the comments, add `#[non_exhaustive]`.
2. **Prerelease** (`prerelease.rs`): `new` (validation) and `Ord` (precedence).
3. **Version and Parser** (`version.rs`, `parser.rs`): parsing, ordering, `Display`, bumps. Now `cargo test -p semver-lite --test api` and `cargo test -p semver-cli` pass.
4. **Documentation:** add `#![deny(missing_docs)]` and crate docs to `lib.rs`, then document every public item, including `req.rs` (written by a colleague, undocumented). At least 6 examples in total; `cargo test --doc -p semver-lite` runs them.
5. **The `serde` feature:** add it to `semver-lite/Cargo.toml` and implement `Serialize`/`Deserialize` for `Version` *as a string* in a `#[cfg(feature = "serde")]` module. Run `cargo test -p semver-lite --features serde`.
6. **Metadata:** fill in `[workspace.package]` and `semver-lite/Cargo.toml`, write `semver-lite/README.md` (what crates.io shows), then run `cargo package -p semver-lite --list` and `cargo package -p semver-lite --allow-dirty`.
7. Grade (`bash ../../tools/grade.sh 05-library`), then commit and push.

## What the grader checks

- `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy --all-features` are clean; the provided tests are unchanged.
- `Error` uses thiserror and is `#[non_exhaustive]`; `lib.rs` has `#![deny(missing_docs)]`.
- Tests pass without features and with `serde`; serde isn't compiled when the feature is off.
- At least 6 doc tests; `cargo doc` passes with `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings"` (no broken links).
- `cargo package` succeeds with no warnings and includes `README.md`.

## Hints

- Since `Prerelease` knows its own ordering, `Version` can simply `#[derive(PartialOrd, Ord)]`: derived ordering compares fields in declaration order.
- `u64::from_str` accepts `"+2"`. Check that every byte is an ASCII digit first.
- Pre-release numbers have no leading zeros, so a longer number is a bigger number: compare lengths, then text. No overflow possible.
- For serde, `serializer.collect_str(self)` writes your `Display` output; for deserializing, read a `String` and `parse()` it, turning the error into `serde::de::Error::custom`.
- `#![warn(clippy::missing_errors_doc)]` reminds you to write `# Errors` sections.

## Going further

- Install [cargo-semver-checks](https://github.com/obi1kenobi/cargo-semver-checks), make a breaking change (add a public field to `Version`), and watch it catch it.
- Use the README as the crate docs with `#![doc = include_str!("../README.md")]`, so its examples become doc tests too.
- Support build metadata (`1.0.0+build.5`), which is ignored when comparing versions.
- Run `cargo publish --dry-run -p semver-lite` to see the last checks crates.io would do, without uploading.

pro.title: Concurrency with threads, channels and rayon
pro.summary: Build a parallel log indexer, first with threads and channels, then with rayon, and prove it gives the same answers as the single-threaded version, faster.
pro.readme:
# 06 · Concurrency with threads, channels and rayon

Every machine you'll deploy to has several cores, and a program that uses one of them leaves most of the hardware idle. Rust is famous for "fearless concurrency": a **data race** (two threads touching the same memory, at least one writing, without synchronization) is a compile error, not a 3 a.m. bug. What the compiler can't do is choose a design for you, stop **deadlocks**, or make parallel code fast. That's your job here.

You'll build a log indexer that counts lines, levels, services and words across many log files, three ways: threads sharing a lock, threads sending messages, and rayon. Then you'll prove they all give the serial answer, and measure which is faster.

**You'll practice:** `std::thread::spawn` and `thread::scope`, `Arc`, `Mutex` and atomics, `mpsc` channels, rayon, `Send` and `Sync`, deadlocks, and measuring speedups in release mode.

## The project

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `src/index.rs` | `Index`: the counts, with `add_document` and `merge` (provided) |
| `src/lib.rs` | `index_serial`, the single-threaded reference (provided) |
| `src/shared.rs`, `src/channels.rs`, `src/with_rayon.rs` | **your three versions** |
| `src/main.rs` | the benchmark: times all four on 58 MB of generated logs |

```bash
cd projects/06-concurrency
cargo test                           # do they agree with index_serial?
cargo run --release                  # how fast is each one?
cargo run --release -- --threads 2   # try 1, 2, 4, 8...
```

## Background

### Threads, `'static` and scopes

`thread::spawn(closure)` starts an OS thread and returns a `JoinHandle`; `join()` waits for it and returns `Err` if it panicked. The closure must be `'static` (own everything it uses, usually via `move`), because the new thread may outlive the function that started it. To share read-only data, wrap it in an `Arc` (an atomically reference-counted pointer) and give each thread a clone: a pointer copy, not a data copy.

`thread::scope(|s| { s.spawn(...); })` waits for every thread spawned in it before returning, so those threads may **borrow** local data. No `Arc` needed.

### Send and Sync

Two marker traits, implemented automatically by the compiler:

- `Send`: a value may **move** to another thread. `Rc` isn't `Send`: its reference count isn't atomic, so two threads cloning it could corrupt it.
- `Sync`: a value may be **shared** (`&T`) between threads. `RefCell` isn't `Sync`: its borrow flag isn't atomic. A `Mutex<T>` is `Sync` because the lock serializes access.

`thread::spawn` requires its closure to be `Send`, so passing an `Rc` to a thread fails to compile (`src/lib.rs` has an example that the doc tests prove does not compile). That's how safe Rust rules out data races. It does not rule out *logic* races, like two threads reading a balance and both deciding there's enough money.

### Shared state: `Arc<Mutex<T>>`

```rust
let total = Arc::new(Mutex::new(Index::default()));
// in each thread, with its own clone of the Arc:
total.lock().unwrap().merge(part);   // the guard unlocks at the end of the statement
```

The lock is held as long as the guard lives. Every moment a thread holds it, the others wait, so keep critical sections short: do the work on local data and lock only to combine. `lock()` returns `Err` if another thread panicked while holding it ("poisoning"). For a single counter, an atomic (`AtomicUsize::fetch_add`) needs no lock at all.

### Message passing: channels

"Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating." `mpsc::channel()` gives a `Sender` (clone it for each producer) and a `Receiver` (one consumer). Each worker owns its data, and the only thing that crosses threads is the finished result. `for msg in rx` ends when **every** `Sender` has been dropped. `mpsc::sync_channel(n)` is bounded: `send` blocks when it's full, which is how you stop fast producers from using all your memory (backpressure).

### rayon and work stealing

```rust
use rayon::prelude::*;
let total: u64 = docs.par_iter().map(|d| d.len() as u64).sum();
```

`par_iter()` runs the iterator on rayon's global pool (one thread per core). Work is split in halves recursively; each thread keeps a queue of pieces, and an idle thread **steals** from a busy one's queue, so uneven work balances itself with no tuning. `fold` gives each piece its own accumulator, and `reduce` combines them pairwise, so the combining operation must be associative (merging indexes is).

### Deadlocks

The compiler can't see these, and a deadlocked program just stops:

- Two threads lock mutexes A and B in opposite orders, and each waits for the other forever. Fix: always lock in one fixed order, or hold one lock at a time.
- A thread locks a `Mutex` it already holds (Rust's `Mutex` is not re-entrant).
- A loop over a `Receiver` while a `Sender` is still alive somewhere, even your own original.
- Holding a lock while blocking: sending into a full `sync_channel`, or `join()`ing a thread that needs that lock.

The tests run every version with a 60-second limit, so a deadlock fails with a hint instead of hanging CI.

### Measuring

Always benchmark with `--release`; debug builds are many times slower. Take the best of several rounds to filter noise. The serial part of a job limits the speedup (Amdahl's law): here that's merging, so merge whole indexes, not single words. More threads than cores rarely helps.

## Your tasks

1. Read `src/index.rs` and `src/lib.rs`, then run `cargo run --release` to see the serial time (the next version panics with `todo!`).
2. **Part 1** (`src/shared.rs`): `index_shared`, with `thread::spawn`, an atomic work counter and `Arc<Mutex<Index>>`. The comments walk you through it.
3. **Part 2** (`src/channels.rs`): `index_channels`, with `thread::scope`, one slice of documents per thread, and an `mpsc` channel.
4. **Part 3** (`src/with_rayon.rs`): `index_rayon`, with `par_iter`.
5. `cargo test`, then `cargo run --release` with different `--threads` values. Which version wins on your machine, and why?
6. Grade (`bash ../../tools/grade.sh 06-concurrency`), then commit and push.

## What the grader checks

- `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy` are clean; the tests, `lib.rs` and `main.rs` are unchanged.
- All tests pass: every version, with 0 to 64 threads, empty and uneven inputs, matches `index_serial`.
- Each part uses its tool (`thread::spawn` + `Arc` + `Mutex`; `thread::scope` + a channel; rayon's `par_iter`) and doesn't call `index_serial`.
- The release benchmark: no parallel version may be more than 25% slower than serial. That's a deliberately low bar for noisy shared CI machines; on 4 cores you should see 2 to 4 times faster.

## Hints

- `threads` can be 0 (treat it as 1) or larger than the number of documents (some threads get nothing, which must still work).
- `while let Some(doc) = docs.get(next.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed))` is a whole work queue in one line.
- With `docs.chunks(n)`, use `n = docs.len().div_ceil(threads)`, but never 0: `chunks(0)` panics.
- If a test times out, look for a `Sender` you didn't `drop`.

## Going further

- In `index_shared`, lock once per *line* instead of once per document and measure the difference. That's lock contention.
- Write a deliberate deadlock with two mutexes locked in opposite orders, watch it hang, then fix it.
- Replace the `mpsc` channel with a bounded `sync_channel(1)`. Does it still work if you receive *after* the scope ends? Why not?
- Implement a parallel merge sort with `rayon::join`.
- Profile with `perf` or `cargo flamegraph` (project 11) to see where the serial time goes.

pro.title: Async networking with Tokio
pro.summary: Write an async TCP server that handles many clients at once, shares state safely, and shuts down cleanly, tested with real connections.
pro.readme:
# 07 · Async networking with Tokio

A network server spends nearly all its time waiting: for a client to send something, for a slow client to read. A thread per connection works until you have ten thousand connections and ten thousand mostly idle threads. **Async** Rust lets a handful of threads juggle any number of connections: a task that would wait gives its thread back to the runtime instead. **Tokio** is the runtime most Rust services are built on (axum, tonic, the AWS SDK...).

You'll build a chat server: many clients at once, shared state, messages broadcast to everyone, and a clean shutdown. The tests start it in-process and talk to it over real TCP connections.

**You'll practice:** `async`/`.await`, `tokio::spawn` and `JoinSet`, `Arc<Mutex>` in async code, broadcast and watch channels, `select!`, graceful shutdown, and per-connection error handling.

## The protocol

One command per line. Replies and events are lines too.

| Client sends | Server sends |
|---|---|
| `NICK <name>` | `OK welcome <name>`, then every joined client (you too) gets `JOIN <name>`. Or `ERR invalid name` (1 to 16 letters, digits, `_` or `-`), `ERR name taken`, `ERR already joined` |
| `MSG <text>` | every joined client (you too) gets `MSG <name> <text>`. Or `ERR send NICK first`, `ERR empty message` |
| `WHO` | `USERS alice bob` (sorted; works before joining) |
| `QUIT` | `BYE`, then the server closes the connection |
| anything else | `ERR unknown command` |

- Clients receive JOIN, MSG and LEAVE events only after they have joined.
- When a joined client leaves (QUIT or disconnect), its name is freed and everyone else gets `LEAVE <name>`.
- A line longer than 1024 bytes (`MAX_LINE`) gets `ERR line too long` and the connection is closed.
- On shutdown, every client gets `SHUTDOWN` and its connection is closed.

Try it: `cargo run` in one terminal, then `nc 127.0.0.1 7878` in two more. The starter answers the first client only. The second gets nothing until the first leaves.

## Background

### Futures, tasks and the runtime

An `async fn` returns a **future**: a value that does nothing until it's awaited. `#[tokio::main]` starts the runtime, which polls futures; at each `.await` that can't finish yet, the task steps aside and the thread runs another one. That only works if tasks actually step aside, so **never block in async code**: no `std::thread::sleep`, blocking file or network calls, or long CPU loops. Use `tokio::time::sleep`, `tokio::fs`, or `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`.

`tokio::spawn(future)` starts a **task**: a few hundred bytes, not a thread, so a task per connection is normal. The future must be `Send + 'static` because it may move between worker threads, so share data through an `Arc`. A `JoinSet` holds many tasks and lets you wait for all of them.

### Shared state

A `std::sync::Mutex` inside an `Arc` is fine in async code as long as you **never hold the guard across an `.await`**: lock, update, unlock. Holding it across an await could block a worker thread, and makes the future non-`Send`, so `tokio::spawn` refuses it (clippy's `await_holding_lock` warns too). The alternative is an **actor**: one task owns the state, and the others send it requests over an `mpsc` channel.

### Tokio's channels

| Channel | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `mpsc` | many senders, one receiver: a work queue |
| `oneshot` | one value, once: "here's your reply", "stop now" |
| `broadcast` | every receiver gets every message: chat events. A receiver that falls behind gets `RecvError::Lagged(n)` |
| `watch` | only the latest value: "we are shutting down" |

### select!

```rust
loop {
    tokio::select! {
        line = lines.next_line() => { /* the client sent something */ }
        event = events.recv() => { /* someone else did something */ }
        _ = stop.changed() => { /* the server is shutting down */ }
    }
}
```

`select!` waits for several futures and runs the branch of the first one to finish. The others are **dropped**, so each must be *cancellation safe*: dropping it mid-way must not lose data. `TcpListener::accept`, `Lines::next_line` and `broadcast::Receiver::recv` are; the docs of every Tokio method say so. `read_line` into a buffer you clear each time is not.

### Graceful shutdown

Deployments stop services by sending a signal and waiting a little (Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, then kills after 30 s). A clean stop is: stop accepting, tell every connection, let each finish what it's doing, wait for all tasks, return.
