topics.title: Option in Rust: Some, None and handling missing values
topics.description: How Rust's Option<T> replaces null: Some and None, match and if let, unwrap_or, map, and_then, the ? operator, and when unwrap is OK.
topics.body:
Rust has no `null`. A value that might be missing has the type **`Option<T>`**, an enum from the standard library:

```rust
enum Option<T> {
    Some(T),
    None,
}
```

An `Option<u32>` is either `Some(5)` or `None`, and the type system **forces** you to handle `None` before you can use the number. The famous "billion-dollar mistake" of null pointer crashes simply can't happen by accident.

Many standard methods return an `Option`: `v.first()`, `v.get(i)`, `v.pop()`, `map.get(&key)`, `s.find('x')`, `iter.max()`, `s.chars().next()`, `text.parse().ok()`.

## Getting the value out

```rust
fn find_price(item: &str) -> Option<u32> {
    match item {
        "apple" => Some(3),
        "bread" => Some(5),
        _ => None,
    }
}

fn main() {
    match find_price("apple") {
        Some(p) => println!("apple costs {p}"),
        None => println!("no apples"),
    }
    if let Some(p) = find_price("bread") {
        println!("bread costs {p}");
    }
    println!("caviar costs {}", find_price("caviar").unwrap_or(0));
}
```

```text
apple costs 3
bread costs 5
caviar costs 0
```

## The methods worth knowing

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `unwrap_or(default)` | the value, or a default |
| `unwrap_or_default()` | the value, or `0` / `""` / empty |
| `unwrap_or_else(\|\| ...)` | the value, or compute a default (only when needed) |
| `map(\|v\| ...)` | transform the value if there is one |
| `and_then(\|v\| ...)` | chain another step that also returns an `Option` |
| `filter(\|v\| ...)` | turn `Some` into `None` if a test fails |
| `ok_or(err)` | turn it into a `Result` with an error for `None` |
| `is_some()`, `is_none()` | test without taking the value |
| `as_ref()`, `as_deref()` | borrow the contents: `Option<&T>`, `Option<&str>` |
| `copied()`, `cloned()` | `Option<&T>` to `Option<T>` |
| `take()` | move the value out, leaving `None` |

Inside a function that returns `Option`, the **`?` operator** returns `None` early: `let first = words.first()?;`.

## let else

To bail out when a value is missing and keep going with a plain value otherwise:

```rust
let Some(user) = find_user(id) else {
    return Err("no such user".to_string());
};
// `user` is a plain value from here on
```

## unwrap and expect

`unwrap()` returns the value or **panics** on `None` with "called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value". `expect("message")` panics with your message. They're fine in tests, quick scripts, and when `None` really is impossible (say why in the `expect` message). In code that handles user input or data from outside, handle `None` properly.

## Common mistakes

- **Using an `Option` as the value:** `let first: i32 = v.first();` is E0308, expected `i32`, found `Option<&i32>`.
- **Option of a reference.** `v.first()` gives `Option<&i32>`, not `Option<i32>`; call `.copied()` to get the number.
- **`if x.is_some() { x.unwrap() }`.** Use `if let Some(v) = x` instead: one check, no unwrap.
- **Using `Option` for errors.** If the caller needs to know *why* something failed, return a `Result`.

topics.title: Vec in Rust: creating, adding, removing and iterating
topics.description: A practical guide to Rust's Vec<T>: vec!, push and pop, get vs indexing, insert and remove, sort, retain, dedup, and with_capacity.
topics.body:
`Vec<T>` is Rust's growable array: a list of values of the same type, stored next to each other on the heap. It's the collection you'll use most.

## Creating

```rust
let mut scores: Vec<u32> = Vec::new();  // empty, type given
let names = vec!["Ferris", "Corro"];     // with values, type inferred
let zeros = vec![0; 10];                 // ten zeros
let mut buf = Vec::with_capacity(1000);  // room for 1000 before reallocating
```

## Reading

- `v[i]` returns the element, and **panics** if `i` is out of range: `index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 3`.
- `v.get(i)` returns an `Option<&T>`: `None` instead of a panic. Use it when the index comes from outside (user input, a file).
- `v.first()`, `v.last()`, `v.len()`, `v.is_empty()`, `v.contains(&x)`, `v.iter().position(|x| ...)`.

## Adding and removing

| Method | Does | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `push(x)` | add at the end | fast (amortized O(1)) |
| `pop()` | remove the last, returns `Option<T>` | fast |
| `insert(i, x)` | add at index `i`, shifting the rest right | O(n) |
| `remove(i)` | take out index `i`, shifting the rest left | O(n) |
| `swap_remove(i)` | take out index `i`, filling the gap with the last | fast, changes order |
| `truncate(n)`, `clear()` | drop elements past `n` / all of them | |
| `extend(other)` | append everything from an iterator | |
| `retain(\|x\| ...)` | keep only elements that pass a test | O(n) |
| `dedup()` | remove consecutive duplicates (sort first) | O(n) |

## Sorting

`sort()` for types with a natural order (integers, strings). `sort_by_key(|p| p.age)` to sort by a field, `sort_by(|a, b| b.score.cmp(&a.score))` for full control (this one sorts descending). `f64` has no total order, so `sort()` on floats doesn't compile; use `sort_by(|a, b| a.total_cmp(b))`. `sort_unstable*` variants are a bit faster when equal elements don't need to keep their order.

## Iterating

- `for x in &v`: borrow each element (`&T`); `v` is still usable afterwards.
- `for x in &mut v`: change elements in place (`*x += 1`).
- `for x in v`: consume the vector, taking each element by value.

## Capacity

A `Vec` has a **length** (elements in use) and a **capacity** (room reserved). When `push` exceeds the capacity, it allocates a bigger block (roughly double) and moves everything. That's why holding a reference into a `Vec` while pushing is forbidden (E0502), and why `with_capacity` helps when you know the size up front.

## Common mistakes

- **Indexing with the wrong integer type.** Indexes are `usize`:

```rust-error
fn main() {
    let v = vec![10, 20, 30];
    let i: i32 = 1;
    println!("{}", v[i]);
}
```

```compiler
error[E0277]: the type `[{integer}]` cannot be indexed by `i32`
```

Convert with `v[i as usize]` (if `i` can't be negative) or use `usize` for the variable.
- **`v.len() - 1` on an empty vector** panics (`attempt to subtract with overflow`). Use `v.last()`.
- **Moving out with an index:** `let s = names[0];` for a `Vec<String>` is E0507. Borrow (`&names[0]`) or `clone()`.
- **Removing while iterating:** use `retain` instead of a loop with `remove`.

index 9: None
popped Some(Item { name: "sword", qty: 2 }), 3 left
[-1.0, 2.25, 3.5, 9.0]

topics.title: HashMap in Rust: insert, get and the entry API
topics.description: How to use HashMap in Rust: insert, get, contains_key, remove, counting with entry().or_insert(), and printing keys in a stable order.
topics.body:
A **`HashMap<K, V>`** stores values by key, with average O(1) lookup. It isn't in the prelude, so import it: `use std::collections::HashMap;`.

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    let mut stock: HashMap<String, u32> = HashMap::new();
    stock.insert(String::from("apples"), 12);
    stock.insert(String::from("pears"), 4);

    println!("{:?}", stock.get("apples"));
    println!("{:?}", stock.get("kiwis"));
    println!("{}", stock.contains_key("pears"));

    let old = stock.insert(String::from("pears"), 9);
    println!("replaced {old:?}, now {}", stock["pears"]);
}
```

```text
Some(12)
None
true
replaced Some(4), now 9
```

- `insert` returns the **old** value as an `Option` (`None` if the key was new).
- `get` returns `Option<&V>`. A map with `String` keys can be searched with a `&str`.
- `map[&key]` panics if the key is missing. Prefer `get` unless absence is a bug.
- `remove(&key)` returns the removed value as an `Option`.

## The entry API

The most common map job is "update the value for this key, or start it with a default". The **entry API** does it with one lookup:

```rust
*counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1;
```

`entry(key)` finds the slot for the key. `or_insert(default)` inserts the default if it's empty and returns a `&mut V` either way; `*... += 1` updates it. Variants:

| Call | Use |
|---|---|
| `.or_insert(v)` | insert `v` if missing |
| `.or_default()` | insert `0`, `""`, empty `Vec`... |
| `.or_insert_with(\|\| ...)` | build the default only when needed |
| `.and_modify(\|v\| ...).or_insert(x)` | change an existing value, or insert `x` |

Grouping is the other classic: `groups.entry(dept).or_default().push(name)` builds a `HashMap<Dept, Vec<Name>>`.

## Iteration order is random

A `HashMap` iterates in an **unspecified order** that changes between runs (Rust seeds its hash function randomly to resist denial-of-service attacks). Never rely on it for output. When order matters:

- collect the entries into a `Vec` and sort it, or
- use a **`BTreeMap`**, which keeps keys sorted (O(log n) operations, same API).

## Keys

Keys must implement `Eq` and `Hash`. Strings, integers, `char`, `bool`, tuples of those, and your own types with `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]` all work. `f64` doesn't (NaN isn't equal to itself); store prices in cents as integers instead.

## Common mistakes

- **Printing a map directly in output that must be stable** (tests, reports): sort first.
- **`get` then `insert`** (two lookups, and a borrow conflict if you hold the `get` reference): use `entry`.
- **Moving keys in:** `map.insert(name, 1)` moves a `String` `name`; insert `name.clone()` if you still need it, or use `&str` keys when the strings outlive the map.
- **Holding a reference from `get` while inserting** is E0502: copy the value out first.

topics.title: Why you can't index a String in Rust (UTF-8, chars and bytes)
topics.description: Why s[0] doesn't compile for a Rust String, how UTF-8 works, and how to get characters with chars(), char_indices() and safe slicing.
topics.body:
Coming from Python or JavaScript, the first surprise is that this doesn't compile:

```rust-error
fn main() {
    let s = String::from("hello");
    let c = s[0];
    println!("{c}");
}
```

```compiler
error[E0277]: the type `str` cannot be indexed by `{integer}`
```

## Why: strings are UTF-8 bytes

A Rust `String` (and `&str`) stores text as **UTF-8**, where one character takes between 1 and 4 bytes. ASCII letters take 1 byte, `é` takes 2, `€` takes 3, and an emoji like 🦀 takes 4.

```rust
fn main() {
    for word in ["crab", "café", "🦀"] {
        println!("{word}: {} bytes, {} chars", word.len(), word.chars().count());
    }
}
```

```text
crab: 4 bytes, 4 chars
café: 5 bytes, 4 chars
🦀: 4 bytes, 1 chars
```

So `s[0]` would be ambiguous (the first byte? the first character?), and finding the n-th character requires scanning from the start, which isn't the O(1) that indexing promises. Rust makes you say what you mean.

## What to use instead

| You want | Write |
|---|---|
| the first character | `s.chars().next()` (an `Option<char>`) |
| the n-th character | `s.chars().nth(n)` (O(n)) |
| number of characters | `s.chars().count()` |
| number of bytes | `s.len()` |
| characters with byte positions | `s.char_indices()` |
| the raw bytes | `s.bytes()` or `s.as_bytes()` |
| a substring by byte range | `&s[start..end]`, at character boundaries |
| reverse | `s.chars().rev().collect::<String>()` |

If you do many position-based operations, convert once: `let chars: Vec<char> = s.chars().collect();` and then index `chars[i]` freely.

## Slicing is by bytes, and must hit boundaries

`&s[0..3]` takes **bytes** 0 to 2. If the range ends in the middle of a character, the program **panics**:

```rust
fn main() {
    let s = String::from("héllo");
    println!("{}", &s[0..1]);
    println!("{}", &s[0..2]);
}
```

```text
h
```

The panic message is `end byte index 2 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 1..3 of string)`. Get safe positions from `find`, `char_indices`, or `s.is_char_boundary(i)`, or use `s.get(0..2)`, which returns `None` instead of panicking.

## ASCII-only data

For data you know is ASCII (hex strings, simple identifiers, DNA sequences), working with bytes is fast and simple: `s.as_bytes()[0]` is a `u8`, and `b'a'` is a byte literal. Methods like `is_ascii_digit`, `to_ascii_uppercase` and `eq_ignore_ascii_case` exist for both `char` and `u8`.

## Characters vs what users see

A `char` is a Unicode **scalar value**, not always what a reader would call one character. "é" can be written as one `char` or as `e` plus a combining accent (two `char`s), and many emoji are several `char`s joined together. For user-facing text operations such as truncating names for display, use the `unicode-segmentation` crate's grapheme clusters.

topics.title: Closures in Rust and the Fn, FnMut and FnOnce traits
topics.description: How Rust closures capture variables, the difference between Fn, FnMut and FnOnce, the move keyword, and passing or returning closures.
topics.body:
A **closure** is an anonymous function you can store in a variable or pass to another function. Unlike a normal `fn`, it can use variables from the scope where it's created; this is called **capturing** them.

```rust
fn main() {
    let tax_rate = 0.2;
    let with_tax = |price: f64| price * (1.0 + tax_rate);
    println!("{:.2}", with_tax(10.0));

    let double = |x| x * 2;
    println!("{}", double(21));
}
```

```text
12.00
42
```

Parameters go between `|` bars; the body is an expression (use `{ }` for several statements). Types are usually inferred, but each closure gets **one** set of types: after `double(21)`, calling `double(1.5)` is E0308, mismatched types.

## How closures capture

The compiler picks the least powerful capture that works:

1. **By shared reference** if the closure only reads the variable.
2. **By mutable reference** if it changes it.
3. **By value (move)** if it consumes it (moves it somewhere, drops it).

The kind of capture decides which **Fn traits** the closure implements:

| Trait | The closure... | Can be called | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Fn` | only reads its captures | many times, even concurrently | `\|x\| x * factor` |
| `FnMut` | changes its captures | many times, needs `mut` | `\|\| count += 1` |
| `FnOnce` | consumes a capture | once | `\|\| drop(buffer)` |

Every `Fn` is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, so a function asking for `FnOnce` accepts anything; one asking for `Fn` accepts the fewest closures.

## The move keyword

`move |...| ...` forces the closure to take **ownership** of everything it captures, even if it only reads it. You need it when the closure outlives the current scope: threads (`thread::spawn(move || ...)`), async tasks, and closures you return. `move` doesn't change which Fn trait the closure implements; it changes where the data lives.

## Taking closures as parameters

```rust
fn apply<F: Fn(i32) -> i32>(f: F, x: i32) -> i32 { f(x) }
fn apply(f: impl Fn(i32) -> i32, x: i32) -> i32 { f(x) }      // same thing
fn retry<F: FnMut() -> bool>(mut attempt: F) { ... }           // stateful callback
```

Pick the most permissive bound that your function's use allows: `FnOnce` if you call it once, `FnMut` if you call it repeatedly, `Fn` only if you need to call it through a shared reference or from several threads.

## Returning closures

Each closure has its own unnamed type, so you return it as `impl Fn(...)`, or as `Box<dyn Fn(...)>` when different branches return different closures:

```rust
fn make_multiplier(n: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 {
    move |x| x * n
}
```

## Common mistakes

- **A mutating closure stored without `mut`:** E0596, "cannot borrow `bump` as mutable, as it is not declared as mutable". Write `let mut bump = || ...`.
- **Using a captured variable while the closure still holds a mutable borrow:** E0502 or E0499. Call the closure for the last time first.
- **Passing an `FnMut` closure where `Fn` is required:** E0596, "cannot borrow `log` as mutable, as it is a captured variable in a `Fn` closure". Change the bound to `FnMut`.
- **Moving out of a capture in an `Fn` closure:** E0507, "cannot move out of `name`, a captured variable in an `Fn` closure". Clone inside, or accept `FnOnce`.
- **Forgetting `move` for a thread:** E0373, "closure may outlive the current function".

Closures shine with iterator adapters and sorting: `v.sort_by_key(|p| p.age)`, `v.retain(|x| *x > 0)`, `items.iter().map(|i| i.price).sum()`.

topics.title: Iterators in Rust: map, filter, collect and other adapters
topics.description: How Rust iterators work: the Iterator trait, lazy adapters like map, filter and enumerate, consumers like collect, sum and fold, and writing your own.
topics.body:
An **iterator** produces a sequence of values, one at a time. Anything implementing the `Iterator` trait has a `next` method that returns `Some(item)` until it's done, then `None`. `for` loops call `next` for you.

```rust
fn main() {
    let orders = vec![120, 45, 300, 80, 15];
    let big_total: i32 = orders
        .iter()
        .filter(|&&amount| amount >= 50)
        .map(|amount| amount * 2)
        .sum();
    println!("{big_total}");

    let labels: Vec<String> = orders.iter().enumerate().map(|(i, a)| format!("#{}={a}", i + 1)).collect();
    println!("{labels:?}");
}
```

```text
1000
["#1=120", "#2=45", "#3=300", "#4=80", "#5=15"]
```

## Three ways to start

- `v.iter()` yields `&T` (borrows), `v.iter_mut()` yields `&mut T`, `v.into_iter()` yields `T` (consumes `v`).
- Ranges are iterators: `(1..=10)`, `(0..n).rev()`, `(0..100).step_by(5)`.
- Many methods return one: `s.chars()`, `s.lines()`, `s.split(',')`, `map.keys()`, `slice.windows(2)`.

## Adapters (lazy) and consumers (do the work)

**Adapters** take an iterator and return a new one. They're **lazy**: nothing runs until a **consumer** pulls values through. Calling `v.iter().map(|x| x * 2);` on its own does nothing, and rustc warns: "unused `Map` that must be used... iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed".

| Adapters | Consumers |
|---|---|
| `map`, `filter`, `filter_map` | `collect`, `sum`, `product`, `count` |
| `enumerate`, `zip`, `chain` | `min`, `max`, `min_by_key`, `max_by` |
| `take`, `skip`, `take_while`, `skip_while` | `fold`, `reduce` |
| `rev`, `step_by`, `peekable` | `any`, `all`, `find`, `position` |
| `flat_map`, `flatten`, `inspect` | `last`, `nth`, `for_each`, `partition` |
| `cloned`, `copied`, `windows`/`chunks` (on slices) | `join` (on `Vec<String>` after collect) |

## collect needs a target type

`collect` can build a `Vec`, `String`, `HashMap`, `HashSet`, `BTreeMap` and more, so tell it which: `let v: Vec<_> = ...collect();` or `.collect::<Vec<_>>()`. Without that you get E0283 or E0282, "type annotations needed". Two handy tricks:

- Collecting `(key, value)` pairs builds a map: `.collect::<HashMap<_, _>>()`.
- Collecting `Result`s into `Result<Vec<T>, E>` stops at the first error: `lines.map(|l| l.parse::<i32>()).collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>()?`.

## Zero-cost

Iterator chains compile down to the same machine code as a hand-written loop, often better, since bounds checks can be removed. Prefer them for clarity; there's no speed penalty in release builds.

## Writing your own

Implement `next`, and every adapter above comes for free:

```rust
impl Iterator for Countdown {
    type Item = u32;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u32> { ... }
}
```

## Common mistakes

- **Collecting references when you wanted values:** "a value of type `Vec<i32>` cannot be built from an iterator over elements of type `&i32`" (E0277). Add `.copied()` or `.cloned()`.
- **`filter` closures get a reference to the item**, so with `iter()` you see `&&i32`. Write `|&&x| x > 5` or `|x| **x > 5`, or use `.copied()` first.
- **Collecting just to iterate again.** `v.iter().map(...).collect::<Vec<_>>().iter().sum()` allocates for nothing; chain directly.
- **`sum()` without a type:** write `let total: i32 = ...sum();` or `.sum::<i32>()`.

topics.title: Modules and visibility in Rust: mod, pub and use
topics.description: How Rust modules work: mod blocks and files, private by default, pub and pub(crate), paths with crate:: and super::, use, and re-exports.
topics.body:
**Modules** organize code into named groups and control what's visible from outside. Every crate has a tree of modules rooted at `src/main.rs` (for a binary) or `src/lib.rs` (for a library).

## Private by default

```rust
mod bank {
    pub struct Account {
        pub owner: String,
        balance: u64,          // private field
    }

    impl Account {
        pub fn new(owner: &str) -> Self { ... }
        pub fn balance(&self) -> u64 { self.balance }
        fn audit(&self) { ... }  // private method
    }
}
```

Everything inside a module is **private** to that module (and its child modules) unless marked `pub`. That includes struct **fields**: a `pub struct` with private fields can only be created through the functions you provide, which is how you protect rules like "balance never goes negative".

Using private items from outside is a compile error:

- E0603, "function `audit` is private"
- E0616, "field `balance` of struct `Account` is private"
- E0451, "field `balance` of struct `Account` is private" when building the struct with `Account { ... }` from outside

| Visibility | Visible to |
|---|---|
| (nothing) | this module and its children |
| `pub` | everyone who can see the module |
| `pub(crate)` | anywhere in this crate, not to users of your library |
| `pub(super)` | the parent module |

## Paths and use

Refer to items with **paths**: `crate::bank::Account` (absolute, from the crate root), `super::helper` (the parent module), `self::inner` (this module). `use` brings a path into scope so you can write the short name:

```rust
use std::collections::{HashMap, HashSet};
use crate::bank::Account;
use std::io::Result as IoResult;   // rename to avoid a clash
```

Conventions: import types, traits and macros by name (`use std::collections::HashMap;`), but call functions through their module (`use std::fs;` then `fs::read_to_string(...)`), so readers can see where a function comes from.

## Modules in files

A `mod bank;` declaration (with a semicolon instead of a body) tells the compiler to load the module from a file:

```text
src/
├── main.rs        // mod bank;  mod report;
├── bank.rs        // the bank module; may declare `pub mod ledger;`
├── bank/
│   └── ledger.rs  // bank::ledger
└── report.rs
```

Files are never compiled unless some module declares them with `mod`. The older `bank/mod.rs` layout also works.

## Re-exports with pub use

`pub use` makes an item available at a different path. Libraries use it to offer a flat, stable API while keeping a deeper internal structure: `pub use crate::bank::ledger::Entry;` in `lib.rs` lets users write `mycrate::Entry`.

## Crates and packages

A **crate** is one compilation unit (a library or a binary). A **package** is what `Cargo.toml` describes: one or more crates. Dependencies from crates.io are added under `[dependencies]` and used with their crate name: `use serde::Deserialize;`.

## Common mistakes

- **Forgetting `pub` on the struct's fields or `new`** and then being unable to build it from `main`.
- **Creating `foo.rs` but never writing `mod foo;`**: the file is ignored and its items are "not found".
- **Writing `mod foo;` in several places**: declare each module once, in its parent; elsewhere, `use` it.
- **Making everything `pub`.** Start private and widen only what callers need. Private items can be changed freely without breaking anyone.

topics.title: Box, Rc and RefCell in Rust: smart pointers explained
topics.description: When to use Box<T>, Rc<T>, RefCell<T>, Rc<RefCell<T>> and Weak<T> in Rust, with the trade-offs and the runtime borrow panic to avoid.
topics.body:
A **smart pointer** is a type that acts like a reference but also owns and manages what it points to. You've already used two: `String` and `Vec<T>`. The standard library adds three you'll meet constantly.

| Type | Gives you | Cost | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Box<T>` | one owner, value on the heap | one allocation | recursive types, trait objects, large values |
| `Rc<T>` | several owners (single thread), read-only | allocation + reference count | shared data in trees and graphs, caches |
| `RefCell<T>` | mutation through a shared reference, checked at run time | a borrow flag | interior mutability |
| `Rc<RefCell<T>>` | several owners that can all mutate | both | shared mutable state in one thread |
| `Weak<T>` | a non-owning link to `Rc` data | a second count | parent pointers, breaking cycles |
| `Arc<T>`, `Mutex<T>` | the thread-safe versions of `Rc`, `RefCell` | atomic operations, locking | sharing across threads |

## Box<T>: single ownership on the heap

`Box::new(x)` moves `x` to the heap and gives you a pointer that owns it. The box frees the value when it's dropped. You need it for **recursive types** (a tree node containing nodes: without a box the type would have infinite size, error E0072) and for **trait objects** like `Box<dyn Error>` or `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>`.

## Rc<T>: shared ownership

**`Rc`** (reference counted) lets several parts of a program own the same value. `Rc::clone(&rc)` doesn't copy the data, it increments a counter; the value is freed when the last `Rc` is dropped. `Rc::strong_count(&rc)` shows the count. The data inside is **read-only**:

```rust-error
use std::rc::Rc;

fn main() {
    let shared = Rc::new(vec![1, 2]);
    shared.push(3);
}
```

```compiler
error[E0596]: cannot borrow data in an `Rc` as mutable
```

`Rc` is not thread-safe (its counter isn't atomic). The compiler stops you from sending it to another thread; use `Arc` there.

## RefCell<T>: borrow checking at run time

**`RefCell`** moves the borrowing rules from compile time to run time. `.borrow()` gives a shared borrow, `.borrow_mut()` a mutable one, both through a plain `&RefCell<T>`. This is **interior mutability**. The rules still apply: if you call `borrow_mut()` while another borrow is alive, the program **panics** with `RefCell already borrowed`. Keep borrows short (don't hold one across a call that might borrow again), or use `try_borrow_mut()` to get a `Result`.

For `Copy` values, **`Cell<T>`** is simpler: `get()` and `set()`, no borrows, no panics.

## Rc<RefCell<T>>: shared and mutable

Combine them when several owners must change the same data, such as observers sharing a log, or nodes in a graph. Each owner holds an `Rc`, and calls `.borrow_mut()` to change the value.

## Weak<T>: avoiding cycles

Two `Rc`s pointing at each other never reach a count of zero, so they **leak**. Make one direction **weak**: `Rc::downgrade(&rc)` gives a `Weak`, which doesn't keep the value alive; `weak.upgrade()` returns `Option<Rc<T>>`. Trees typically use `Rc` for children and `Weak` for the parent link.

## Advice at work

- Reach for plain ownership and references first. `Rc<RefCell<T>>` everywhere is often a sign the data structure should be redesigned (indices into a `Vec`, or an arena).
- Write `Rc::clone(&x)` rather than `x.clone()`, so readers see it's a cheap pointer copy.
- In multithreaded code the pair is `Arc<Mutex<T>>` (or `Arc<RwLock<T>>`).

topics.title: Unit testing in Rust: #[test], assert_eq! and cargo test
topics.description: How to write tests in Rust: #[test] functions, assert!, assert_eq! with messages, should_panic, tests returning Result, and unit vs integration tests.
topics.body:
Rust has testing built in: no framework to install. A **test** is a function marked `#[test]`; `cargo test` compiles your crate in test mode, runs every test, and reports which passed.

## Unit tests live next to the code

```rust
pub fn apply_discount(price_cents: u64, percent: u64) -> u64 {
    price_cents - price_cents * percent / 100
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn ten_percent_off() {
        assert_eq!(apply_discount(1000, 10), 900);
    }

    #[test]
    fn zero_percent_changes_nothing() {
        assert_eq!(apply_discount(1999, 0), 1999, "0% should keep the price");
    }
}
```

- `#[cfg(test)]` compiles the module only for `cargo test`, so tests add nothing to your real program.
- `use super::*;` brings the parent module's items into scope, **including private functions**: unit tests can test internals.

```text
$ cargo test
running 2 tests
test tests::ten_percent_off ... ok
test tests::zero_percent_changes_nothing ... ok

test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
```

`cargo test discount` runs only tests whose name contains "discount". Output from `println!` in passing tests is hidden; `cargo test -- --nocapture` shows it.

## The assertion macros

| Macro | Fails when |
|---|---|
| `assert!(cond)` | `cond` is false |
| `assert_eq!(left, right)` | they're not equal; prints both values |
| `assert_ne!(left, right)` | they're equal |

All accept a trailing message with format arguments: `assert_eq!(total, 30, "cart total for {items:?}")`. The values compared with `assert_eq!` must implement `PartialEq` and `Debug`, so derive both on your types. Floats rarely compare exactly; assert that the difference is small: `assert!((a - b).abs() < 1e-9)`.

## Testing failures

- `#[should_panic(expected = "divide by zero")]` passes only if the test panics with a message containing that text.
- A test can return `Result<(), E>` and use `?` inside; returning `Err` fails the test.
- For functions returning `Result`, assert on the error: `assert!(parse("x").is_err())` or `assert_eq!(parse("x"), Err(ParseError::Empty))`.

## Integration tests and doc tests

- Files in a top-level `tests/` directory are **integration tests**: each one is a separate crate that can only use your library's public API, the way real users would.
- Code blocks in `///` doc comments are compiled and run as **doc tests** by `cargo test`, so examples in your documentation can't go stale.

## Good tests at work

- Name tests as sentences describing behavior: `rejects_empty_username`, not `test1`.
- One behavior per test, with the edge cases: empty input, zero, negative numbers, unicode, the maximum value.
- Test through the public interface where possible; tests that poke at internals break on every refactor.
- Keep tests deterministic: no real clock, no network, no random numbers without a fixed seed.
- Run `cargo test` in CI on every pull request, alongside `cargo clippy` and `cargo fmt --check`.

## Common mistakes

- **Forgetting `use super::*;`**: "cannot find function `apply_discount` in this scope".
- **Comparing types without `PartialEq` or `Debug`** in `assert_eq!` (E0369 or E0277): derive them.
- **`#[should_panic]` without `expected`**: the test passes for *any* panic, including the wrong one.

topics.title: Ownership and moves in Rust
topics.description: Rust's ownership rules explained: one owner per value, moves on assignment and function calls, drop at end of scope, and how to fix use after move.
topics.body:
**Ownership** is how Rust manages memory without a garbage collector and without you calling `free`. The compiler checks three rules:

1. Every value has exactly one **owner**, the variable (or struct field, or collection) responsible for it.
2. There is only one owner at a time.
3. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is **dropped**: its memory (and any file, socket or lock it holds) is released.

Rule 3 means cleanup always happens, exactly once, at a place you can see in the code. Rules 1 and 2 are what make "exactly once" possible.

## Moves

A `String` is a small handle on the stack (pointer, length, capacity) pointing at text on the heap. If assigning one `String` to another simply copied the handle, two variables would point at the same text and both would try to free it: a **double free**. Rust prevents that by **moving** instead:

```rust-error
fn main() {
    let s1 = String::from("crab");
    let s2 = s1;
    println!("{s1} {s2}");
}
```

```compiler
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s1`
```

After `let s2 = s1;`, `s2` owns the text and `s1` is no longer usable. Nothing on the heap was copied; the move is as cheap as copying three numbers. The compiler simply stops you from using the old name.

The same happens when you pass a value to a function: the parameter becomes the owner, and the value is dropped when the function ends, unless the function gives it back by returning it.

```rust
fn shout(mut msg: String) -> String {
    msg.push('!');
    msg
}

fn main() {
    let msg = String::from("hello");
    let msg = shout(msg);
    println!("{msg}");
}
```

```text
hello!
```

## What moves and what copies

Simple values that live entirely on the stack (`i32`, `f64`, `bool`, `char`, and tuples or arrays of them) are **`Copy`**: assigning them duplicates the bits, and both variables stay usable. Types that own heap memory or other resources (`String`, `Vec<T>`, `Box<T>`, `HashMap`, files) **move**.

## Dropping

When a value's owner goes out of scope, Rust calls its **drop** code automatically. Values are dropped in the reverse order they were created. You can run it early with `drop(value)`. This pattern (resource tied to an owner's scope) is called **RAII**, and it's why Rust code doesn't need `finally` blocks or manual `close()` calls.

## How to fix "use after move"

- **Borrow instead of moving.** If a function only reads the value, make it take `&String` (better, `&str`) or `&Vec<T>` (better, `&[T]`), and call it with `&value`. This is the usual answer.
- **Clone** when you really need two independent copies: `let backup = report.clone();`. It copies the heap data, so it costs time and memory.
- **Return the value** from the function (as `shout` does above), or restructure so the last use is the move.

## Best practices at work

- Take ownership (`String`, `Vec<T>`) in a function or constructor when you're going to **store** the value; borrow when you only need to look at it.
- Don't sprinkle `.clone()` until it compiles. Each clone is an allocation, and code reviewers will ask why. Borrowing is usually the right fix.
- Moving is cheap. Returning a big `Vec` from a function doesn't copy its elements.

topics.title: Copy vs Clone in Rust
topics.description: The difference between Copy and Clone in Rust: implicit bitwise copies vs explicit .clone(), which types are Copy, and when to derive each.
topics.body:
Both `Copy` and `Clone` produce a duplicate of a value, but they work very differently.

| | `Copy` | `Clone` |
|---|---|---|
| How it happens | implicitly, on every assignment or call | explicitly, when you write `.clone()` |
| What it does | copies the bits on the stack | whatever the type's `clone` method does (often a deep copy) |
| Cost | always cheap | can be expensive (allocates, copies heap data) |
| Old value afterwards | still usable | still usable |
| Examples | `i32`, `f64`, `bool`, `char`, `&T`, `(i32, i32)`, `[u8; 4]` | `String`, `Vec<T>`, `HashMap`, `Box<T>`, plus every `Copy` type |

## Copy: values that are just bits

A type can be **`Copy`** only if duplicating its bytes produces a correct, independent value. An `i32` qualifies: two copies of the number 5 never interfere. A `String` doesn't: its bytes are a pointer to heap memory, so a bitwise copy would give two owners of the same text, and a double free when both are dropped. That's why `String` **moves** instead.

Shared references `&T` are `Copy` (many readers are allowed), but `&mut T` is not (only one writer at a time).

## Clone: an explicit, possibly expensive duplicate

`.clone()` asks a type to make a full, independent copy. For a `String` it allocates new heap memory and copies the text. Because it's explicit, you can see every place your code pays for a copy.

## Deriving them for your own types

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}
```

`Copy` requires `Clone` (it's a **supertrait**), so you always derive both. You can only derive `Copy` if every field is `Copy`:

```rust-error
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Player {
    name: String,
    score: u32,
}

fn main() {}
```

```compiler
error[E0204]: the trait `Copy` cannot be implemented for this type
 --> src/main.rs:2:8
  |
1 | #[derive(Clone, Copy)]
  |                 ---- in this derive macro expansion
2 | struct Player {
  |        ^^^^^^
3 |     name: String,
  |     ------------ this field does not implement `Copy`
```

Derive only `Clone` for such types. A type that implements `Drop` can't be `Copy` either.

## When to derive Copy

Derive `Copy` for small **value types**: coordinates, colors, ids, money amounts, small enums like `Direction`. Code using them reads naturally (`let p2 = p1;`) and there's no performance cost.

Think twice before making a type `Copy` if it might later gain a `String` or `Vec` field: removing `Copy` then is a breaking change for every user of the type. For large structs, `Copy` can also hide expensive memcpys.

## Common mistakes

- **Cloning to silence the borrow checker.** It compiles, but each clone of a `Vec<String>` copies every string. First ask whether a reference (`&`) would do.
- **Calling `.clone()` on a `Copy` value.** It works but is noise; clippy says `clone_on_copy` ("using `clone` on type `Point` which implements the `Copy` trait").
- **Expecting a clone to stay in sync.** A clone is independent: changing it doesn't change the original. For shared data, use a reference or `Rc`/`Arc`.
- **`Rc::clone` is cheap.** Cloning an `Rc` or `Arc` copies a pointer and bumps a counter; it does not copy the data. Writing `Rc::clone(&x)` instead of `x.clone()` makes that obvious to readers.

topics.title: Borrowing and references in Rust (&T and &mut T)
topics.description: How borrowing works in Rust: shared references &T, mutable references &mut T, the one writer or many readers rule, and dereferencing with *.
topics.body:
Moving a value into every function that needs to look at it would be painful. **Borrowing** lets code use a value without taking ownership: you hand out a **reference**, and the owner keeps the value.

- `&value` creates a **shared reference** (`&T`): read-only access.
- `&mut value` creates a **mutable reference** (`&mut T`): read and write access. The variable itself must be declared `mut`.

```rust
fn count_words(text: &str) -> usize {
    text.split_whitespace().count()
}

fn add_signature(text: &mut String) {
    text.push_str(" -- Ferris");
}

fn main() {
    let mut note = String::from("ship it on friday");
    println!("{} words", count_words(&note));
    add_signature(&mut note);
    println!("{note}");
}
```

```text
4 words
ship it on friday -- Ferris
```

`note` is never moved, so `main` can keep using it.

## The borrowing rules

At any moment, a value can have **either**:

- any number of shared references `&T`, **or**
- exactly one mutable reference `&mut T`,

but not both. And a reference can never outlive the value it points to.

This "many readers or one writer" rule is checked at compile time by the **borrow checker**. It's what prevents a whole family of bugs:

- **Iterator invalidation:** pushing to a `Vec` can move its elements to a new heap block. Any reference into the old block would dangle. The rule stops you from pushing while a reference into the `Vec` is alive.
- **Data races:** two threads writing the same memory at once can't happen if only one `&mut` exists.
- **Dangling pointers:** references to freed memory are rejected.

## Borrows end at their last use

A borrow lasts from where it's created to the **last place it's used**, not to the end of the block (this is called **non-lexical lifetimes**). This compiles, because `first` isn't used after the `push`:

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut scores = vec![10, 20];
    let first = &scores[0];
    println!("first {first}");
    scores.push(30);
    println!("{scores:?}");
}
```

```text
first 10
[10, 20, 30]
```

Move the `println!` of `first` below the `push` and you get error E0502.

## Dereferencing with `*`

To read or change the value behind a reference, use `*`: `*count += 1`. Method calls and field access dereference automatically (`text.len()`, `player.score`), and so does `println!`, so you mostly need `*` for assignment and arithmetic on numbers.

## The errors you'll meet

| Error | Meaning |
|---|---|
| E0502 | mutable borrow while a shared borrow is still in use (or the reverse) |
| E0499 | two mutable borrows alive at once |
| E0596 | `&mut` of something not declared `mut`, or behind a `&` |
| E0597 | the value is dropped while a reference to it is still used |
| E0506 | assigning to a value while it's borrowed |
| E0515 | returning a reference to a local variable |

Each one is the compiler finding a real bug pattern, not being pedantic.

## Best practices

- Accept `&str` and `&[T]` in functions that only read; accept `&mut T` when you modify the caller's value; take ownership only to store or consume.
- Keep borrows short: copy small values out (`let first = v[0];`) instead of holding a reference across a mutation.
- When the borrow checker fights you, the usual fixes are reordering statements, splitting a function in two, or using indices instead of references, not `.clone()` everywhere.

topics.title: Slices in Rust: &str, &[T] and ranges
topics.description: What slices are in Rust, how to take &s[a..b] and &v[a..b], why &str and &[T] make better parameters, and the panics to avoid.
topics.body:
A **slice** is a reference to a contiguous part of a collection: a view into some elements, without owning them. It's stored as a pointer plus a length (a **fat pointer**), so taking a slice never copies data.

- `&str` is a slice of UTF-8 text, from a `String` or a literal.
- `&[T]` is a slice of elements, from an array, a `Vec<T>`, or another slice.
- `&mut [T]` is a mutable slice: you can change elements, but not add or remove them.

## Range syntax

| Range | Means |
|---|---|
| `&v[1..4]` | indexes 1, 2, 3 (end is excluded) |
| `&v[1..=4]` | indexes 1 to 4 inclusive |
| `&v[..3]` | from the start to index 2 |
| `&v[2..]` | from index 2 to the end |
| `&v[..]` | everything |

```rust
fn main() {
    let temps = [18, 21, 25, 23, 19];
    let weekend = &temps[3..];
    println!("{weekend:?} has {} days", weekend.len());

    let line = String::from("WARN low disk");
    let level = &line[..4];
    println!("level={level}");
}
```

```text
[23, 19] has 2 days
level=WARN
```

## Slices make better parameters

A function taking `&[T]` accepts arrays, vectors and parts of either; one taking `&str` accepts literals, `String`s and substrings. `&Vec<T>` or `&String` would accept only the owned type, so prefer slices for anything you only read. (Clippy warns about `&Vec<T>` and `&String` parameters with `ptr_arg`.) A `&Vec<T>` or `&String` converts to a slice automatically when you pass it.

```rust
fn average(values: &[f64]) -> f64 { ... }

average(&readings);        // a whole Vec
average(&readings[..7]);   // the first week
average(&[1.0, 2.0]);      // an array
```

Because slices borrow, the borrowing rules apply: while a slice of a `Vec` is in use, you can't push to the `Vec` (error E0502). That's exactly what keeps the slice from dangling when the `Vec` reallocates.

## Useful slice methods

`len`, `is_empty`, `first`, `last`, `get(i)` (returns an `Option`), `contains`, `iter`, `split_at(mid)`, `chunks(n)`, `windows(n)`, `sort` and `reverse` (on `&mut [T]`), `binary_search`, `starts_with`. For strings: `find`, `split`, `trim`, `starts_with`, `lines`.

## Common mistakes

- **Out-of-range slices panic.** `&v[2..10]` on a 3-element array panics with `range end index 10 out of range for slice of length 3`. Use `v.get(2..10)`, which returns `None` instead.
- **Slicing text in the middle of a character.** String ranges are in **bytes**, and many characters take more than one byte in UTF-8. `&"héllo"[0..2]` panics: `end byte index 2 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 1..3 of string)`. Use `char_indices()`, `find`, or `chars()` to get safe positions.
- **Returning a slice of a local `String`.** The `String` is freed at the end of the function, so the compiler refuses (E0515 or E0106). Return a `String`, or return a slice of the *input* parameter, like `first_word` below.

topics.title: Stack vs heap in Rust
topics.description: Where Rust stores your data: the stack for fixed-size values, the heap for String, Vec and Box, how ownership frees heap memory, and the costs.
topics.body:
A running program keeps data in two regions of memory, and knowing which one a value uses explains most of Rust's ownership rules.

## The stack

Each function call gets a **stack frame** holding its local variables. When the function returns, the frame is discarded in one step. Allocation is just moving a pointer, so it's extremely fast, and the memory is right next to other recently used data (good for the CPU cache).

The rule: every value on the stack must have a **size known at compile time**. `i32` (4 bytes), `f64` (8), `[u8; 100]` (100), a struct of those, a tuple of those.

## The heap

Data whose size is only known at run time, or that grows, goes on the **heap**: a large pool where the program **allocates** blocks of any size while it runs. Allocating means asking the allocator for space (slower than the stack), and every block must later be **freed** exactly once.

In Rust, heap data always has an owner on the stack:

| Type | On the stack | On the heap |
|---|---|---|
| `i32`, `f64`, `bool`, `char` | the value | nothing |
| `[i32; 4]`, tuples, plain structs | all of it | nothing |
| `String` | pointer, length, capacity (24 bytes) | the text |
| `Vec<T>` | pointer, length, capacity (24 bytes) | the elements |
| `Box<T>` | a pointer (8 bytes) | the `T` |
| `&str`, `&[T]` | pointer and length (16 bytes) | nothing of its own: it borrows |

(Sizes are for a 64-bit machine.) When the owner goes out of scope, Rust's generated **drop** code frees the heap block. That's ownership: the compiler knows statically where each heap block is freed, so there's no garbage collector and no manual `free`.

## Why moves exist

Copying a `String` handle would leave two handles pointing at the same heap text, and both would free it. So assigning a `String` **moves** it (the old variable becomes unusable) instead of copying. Stack-only types like `i32` have nothing to double-free, so they are simply **copied**.

## Box: putting a value on the heap on purpose

`Box::new(value)` moves a value to the heap and keeps a pointer to it. You need it for **recursive types**, whose size would otherwise be infinite:

```rust-error
enum List {
    Node(i32, List),
    Empty,
}

fn main() {}
```

```compiler
error[E0072]: recursive type `List` has infinite size
```

`Node(i32, Box<List>)` fixes it: a `Box` is always one pointer wide. `Box` is also used for trait objects (`Box<dyn Trait>`) and to move very large values off the stack.

## Performance notes

- Allocation isn't free. In hot loops, reuse buffers (`buf.clear()` keeps the capacity) and pre-size collections with `Vec::with_capacity(n)` or `String::with_capacity(n)`.
- The stack is small: the main thread typically gets 8 MB on Linux (1 MB on Windows), and spawned threads get 2 MB by default. Huge local arrays or very deep recursion end with `thread 'main' has overflowed its stack`. Use a `Vec` for big buffers.
- Moving a `String` or `Vec` copies only the 24-byte handle, never the heap data.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Structs live on the heap."** No: a struct lives wherever you put it. A local struct is on the stack; its `String` fields point to the heap.
- **"String literals are on the heap."** `"hello"` is stored in the program binary. `String::from("hello")` copies it into a new heap block.

topics.title: Rust error E0106: missing lifetime specifier
topics.description: How to fix Rust's E0106 missing lifetime specifier: adding <'a> to functions and structs, the elision rules, and when to return owned data.
topics.body:
**E0106** appears when a function returns a reference, or a struct holds one, and the compiler can't tell **which data the reference borrows from**. It needs that to check that the reference never outlives the data. You answer with a **lifetime parameter** (a name like `'a`), or by not returning a reference at all.

## Case 1: two reference parameters, one returned reference

```rust-error
fn longest(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str {
    if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", longest("arena", "crab"));
}
```

```compiler
error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
 --> src/main.rs:1:33
  |
1 | fn longest(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str {
  |               ----     ----     ^ expected named lifetime parameter
  |
  = help: this function's return type contains a borrowed value, but the signature does not say whether it is borrowed from `a` or `b`
help: consider introducing a named lifetime parameter
  |
1 | fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
  |           ++++     ++          ++          ++
```

The suggested fix is right: `fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str` says "the result borrows from `a` or `b`, so it's only valid while both are". Annotations don't change how long anything lives; they describe the relationship so the compiler can check every caller.

## Case 2: a struct that holds a reference

```rust-error
struct Excerpt {
    text: &str,
}

fn main() {
    let e = Excerpt { text: "call me Ferris" };
    println!("{}", e.text);
}
```

```compiler
error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
```

Write `struct Excerpt<'a> { text: &'a str }`: an `Excerpt` can't outlive the text it points into. But first ask whether the struct should just own its data (`text: String`). For most structs (config, records, API types) owning is simpler. Reference-holding structs make sense for short-lived views: parsers, iterators, borrowed wrappers.

## Case 3: returning a reference with nothing to borrow from

`fn default_name() -> &str` fails because there's no input to borrow from. rustc offers two fixes: `&'static str` if you return a string literal (literals live for the whole program), or, as it says, "instead, you are more likely to want to return an owned value": `-> String`.

## When you don't need annotations: elision

Most functions with references need no lifetimes because of three **elision rules**:

1. Each reference parameter gets its own lifetime.
2. If there's exactly one reference parameter, the output gets its lifetime. So `fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str` is fine.
3. In methods with `&self` or `&mut self`, the output gets `self`'s lifetime. So `fn name(&self) -> &str` is fine.

E0106 means none of the rules applied, and you must say which input the output comes from.

## Choosing the fix

- The result really points into one of the inputs: add `<'a>` and tie the output to that input only (`fn pick<'a>(a: &'a str, _b: &str) -> &'a str`).
- The function creates new data: return `String`, `Vec<T>` or another owned type.
- Adding `'static` everywhere to silence the error is almost always wrong: it forces callers to pass literals or leaked data.

topics.title: Rust error E0507: cannot move out of borrowed content (behind a reference)
topics.description: Fix Rust's E0507 cannot move out of index, behind a shared reference: borrow, clone, as_ref, take or mem::replace.
topics.body:
**E0507** means you tried to **move** a value out of something you only **borrowed**. Older compilers said "cannot move out of borrowed content"; today's messages are more specific: "cannot move out of index of `Vec<String>`" or "cannot move out of `self.name` which is behind a shared reference".

Moving out would leave a hole: the owner (the vector, the struct) would still think it holds a valid `String`, and would drop it again later. So you can only **look** through a borrow, or replace what you take.

## Case 1: taking an element out of a Vec by index

```rust-error
fn main() {
    let names = vec![String::from("Ferris"), String::from("Corro")];
    let first = names[0];
    println!("{first}");
}
```

```compiler
error[E0507]: cannot move out of index of `Vec<String>`
 --> src/main.rs:3:17
  |
3 |     let first = names[0];
  |                 ^^^^^^^^ move occurs because value has type `String`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
  |
help: consider borrowing here
  |
3 |     let first = &names[0];
  |                 +
```

Fixes, depending on what you want:

- Just read it: `let first = &names[0];`
- Your own copy: `let first = names[0].clone();`
- Really take it out of the vector: `names.remove(0)` (shifts the rest), `names.swap_remove(0)` (fast, changes order), `names.pop()`, or `std::mem::take(&mut names[0])` (leaves an empty `String` behind).

(With `Vec<i32>`, `let x = v[0];` works fine: `i32` is `Copy`, so it's copied rather than moved.)

## Case 2: returning a field from a `&self` method

```rust-error
struct User {
    name: String,
}

impl User {
    fn name(&self) -> String {
        self.name
    }
}

fn main() {
    let u = User { name: String::from("Ferris") };
    println!("{}", u.name());
}
```

```compiler
error[E0507]: cannot move out of `self.name` which is behind a shared reference
```

Usually the right getter returns a reference: `fn name(&self) -> &str { &self.name }`. Return `self.name.clone()` if the caller needs ownership, or write `fn into_name(self) -> String` to consume the whole struct.

## Case 3: `unwrap()` on an `Option` field

`self.result.unwrap()` inside a `&self` method fails the same way, because `unwrap` takes the `Option` by value. rustc suggests the fixes:

- `self.result.as_ref().unwrap()` or `self.result.as_deref()`: borrow the contents (`Option<&String>` / `Option<&str>`).
- `self.result.take()` in a `&mut self` method: move the value out and leave `None` behind.
- `self.result.clone().unwrap()` when you need an owned copy.

## Case 4: dereferencing a reference into an owned value

`let owned: String = *r;` where `r: &String` tries to move the `String` out from behind `r`. Use `r.clone()`, or keep it as a reference.

## The general toolbox

| You want to... | Use |
|---|---|
| look at it | `&x`, `as_ref()`, `as_deref()`, `iter()` |
| a copy | `.clone()` |
| take it, leave a default | `std::mem::take(&mut x)` |
| take it, leave something specific | `std::mem::replace(&mut x, new)` |
| take it out of an `Option` | `opt.take()` |
| take it out of a `Vec` | `remove`, `swap_remove`, `pop`, `drain` |
| consume the whole container | iterate with `into_iter()`, or a method taking `self` |

topics.title: Serde JSON in Rust: serialize and deserialize structs
topics.description: How to convert Rust structs to and from JSON with serde and serde_json: derive, to_string, from_str, rename, Option fields, defaults and errors.
topics.body:
**serde** (SERialize/DEserialize) is the standard Rust framework for converting data to and from formats like JSON, TOML and YAML. You describe your data as normal structs and enums, **derive** two traits, and a format crate such as `serde_json` does the rest.

```toml
[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1"
```

## Struct to JSON and back

```rust
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Player {
    name: String,
    level: u32,
    tags: Vec<String>,
}

fn main() {
    let p = Player { name: "Ferris".into(), level: 7, tags: vec!["crab".into()] };
    let json = serde_json::to_string(&p).unwrap();
    println!("{json}");

    let back: Player = serde_json::from_str(r#"{"name":"Corro","level":3,"tags":[]}"#).unwrap();
    println!("{back:?}");
}
```

```text
{"name":"Ferris","level":7,"tags":["crab"]}
Player { name: "Corro", level: 3, tags: [] }
```

- `serde_json::to_string(&value)` produces compact JSON; `to_string_pretty` adds indentation.
- `serde_json::from_str::<T>(text)` parses. It needs the target type, from an annotation or turbofish.
- Both return a `Result`: serialization rarely fails, but parsing outside data fails all the time.

`r#"..."#` is a **raw string**: quotes inside don't need escaping, which is handy for JSON in code.

## Shaping the JSON with attributes

| Attribute | Effect |
|---|---|
| `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` on the struct | `user_id` becomes `"userId"` |
| `#[serde(rename = "type")]` on a field | use a JSON name that's a Rust keyword |
| `Option<T>` field | `null` or a missing key becomes `None` |
| `#[serde(default)]` | missing key uses `Default::default()` |
| `#[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]` | leave out `None` fields when writing |
| `#[serde(skip)]` | never read or write this field |
| `#[serde(tag = "type")]` on an enum | internally tagged: `{"type": "Click", "x": 1}` |
| `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` | reject keys you didn't expect |

By default, unknown JSON keys are **ignored**, and a missing non-`Option` field is an error.

## Handling errors

`serde_json::Error` says what went wrong and where:

- ``missing field `level` at line 1 column 17``
- `invalid type: string "seven", expected u32 at line 1 column 15`
- `expected value at line 1 column 1` (not JSON at all)

Match on the `Result`, or propagate with `?` into your error type (with `anyhow`, add context: `.context("parsing config.json")`).

## Untyped JSON: Value and json!

When the shape isn't known in advance, parse into `serde_json::Value` and index it: `v["user"]["name"].as_str()`. The `json!` macro builds a `Value` with JSON-like syntax. Prefer typed structs for anything you'll use more than once: the compiler then checks every field access.

## Common mistakes

- **Forgetting the derive feature:** ``cannot find derive macro `Serialize` in this scope``. Enable `features = ["derive"]` on `serde`.
- **Field names not matching** the JSON's naming style: use `rename_all` instead of renaming every Rust field.
- **`unwrap()` on `from_str` with user data.** One bad request crashes the server. Return the error.
- **Floats for money.** `19.99` in JSON parses into an `f64` with rounding error; use integer cents or a decimal crate.
- **Expecting map key order** from a `HashMap` field. Use `BTreeMap` for stable output.

topics.title: anyhow vs thiserror in Rust: which should you use?
topics.description: The difference between anyhow and thiserror for Rust error handling, when to use each, with context(), bail!, #[error] and #[from] examples.
topics.body:
Two crates dominate Rust error handling, and they solve different problems. The short version: **thiserror for libraries, anyhow for applications**, and many projects use both.

| | `thiserror` | `anyhow` |
|---|---|---|
| What it gives you | a derive that writes `Display`, `Error` and `From` for **your own** error enum | one catch-all error type, `anyhow::Error` |
| Callers can match on the error | yes, it's a normal enum | not easily (only by downcasting) |
| Adding context | add fields to variants | `.context("...")` on any `Result` |
| Best for | libraries, modules with errors callers handle differently | binaries, CLIs, `main`, glue code, tests |

## thiserror: typed errors without boilerplate

```rust
use thiserror::Error;

#[derive(Debug, Error)]
pub enum StoreError {
    #[error("item `{0}` not found")]
    NotFound(String),
    #[error("only {available} left, asked for {requested}")]
    OutOfStock { requested: u32, available: u32 },
    #[error("invalid quantity")]
    BadQuantity(#[from] std::num::ParseIntError),
}
```

- `#[error("...")]` writes the `Display` message, with fields in braces.
- `#[from]` writes `impl From<ParseIntError> for StoreError`, so `?` converts automatically, and records it as the `source()`.
- The result is an ordinary enum: callers can `match` and retry on `OutOfStock`, show a 404 on `NotFound`, and so on. thiserror doesn't appear in your public API; it only generates code.

## anyhow: one error type for the whole application

```rust
use anyhow::{bail, Context, Result};

fn load_config(path: &str) -> Result<Config> {
    let text = std::fs::read_to_string(path)
        .with_context(|| format!("reading {path}"))?;
    let config: Config = toml::from_str(&text).context("parsing config")?;
    if config.workers == 0 {
        bail!("workers must be at least 1");
    }
    Ok(config)
}
```

- `anyhow::Result<T>` is `Result<T, anyhow::Error>`, and `?` accepts **any** error type.
- `.context(...)` / `.with_context(|| ...)` wrap the error with a message describing what you were doing. Needs `use anyhow::Context;`.
- `bail!("...")` returns an error immediately; `ensure!(cond, "...")` bails if the condition is false; `anyhow!("...")` builds an error value.
- `main` can return `anyhow::Result<()>`; on error it prints the whole chain:

```text
Error: reading /etc/arena.toml

Caused by:
    No such file or directory (os error 2)
```

Print a chain yourself with `{:#}` (one line, causes joined with `: `) or `{:?}` (the multi-line report).

## How they fit together

A typical service: each module (database, payments, parsing) defines a `thiserror` enum that callers inside the codebase can match on. Request handlers and `main` use `anyhow::Result` and `.context()`, converting module errors with `?`, and log the full chain at the top. When code really needs to inspect an `anyhow::Error`, `err.downcast_ref::<StoreError>()` recovers the typed error.

## Common mistakes

- **anyhow in a library's public API.** Callers lose the ability to handle specific failures. Expose a typed error.
- **Forgetting `use anyhow::Context;`**: then `.context()` is "no method named `context` found".
- **Context that repeats the cause.** Say what you were trying to do ("loading user 42"), not what failed ("file not found"); the cause is already in the chain.
- **Formatting with `{}` and losing causes.** `{}` prints only the outermost message; use `{:#}` in logs.

topics.title: Cargo.toml explained: dependencies, versions and features
topics.description: A practical guide to Cargo.toml: package metadata, dependency version requirements (semver), features, dev-dependencies, profiles and Cargo.lock.
topics.body:
Every Rust project is described by a `Cargo.toml` file at its root, written in **TOML** (a simple `key = value` format with `[sections]`). Here's a realistic one for a small web service:

```toml
[package]
name = "arena-api"
version = "0.3.1"
edition = "2024"
rust-version = "1.85"

[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1"
tokio = { version = "1.40", features = ["rt-multi-thread", "macros"] }
anyhow = "1"
regex = { version = "1", optional = true }

[dev-dependencies]
pretty_assertions = "1"

[features]
default = ["search"]
search = ["dep:regex"]

[profile.release]
lto = true
```

## [package]

`name` and `version` identify the crate; `edition` selects the language edition (2024 is current; editions are opt-in language updates, and crates of different editions work together). `rust-version` declares the oldest compiler you support.

## Version requirements are semver ranges

`serde = "1.0.200"` does **not** mean exactly 1.0.200. It's a **caret requirement**: any version compatible with it under **semantic versioning**, here `>=1.0.200, <2.0.0`. Cargo picks the newest matching version. The rules:

| Requirement | Allows |
|---|---|
| `"1.4.2"` (same as `"^1.4.2"`) | `>=1.4.2, <2.0.0` |
| `"0.4.2"` | `>=0.4.2, <0.5.0` (for 0.x, the minor number is the breaking one) |
| `"~1.4.2"` | `>=1.4.2, <1.5.0` |
| `"=1.4.2"` | exactly 1.4.2 |
| `"*"` | anything (not allowed on crates.io) |

`cargo add serde --features derive` edits the file for you; `cargo update` moves to the newest allowed versions; `cargo tree` shows the full dependency graph.

## Cargo.lock

`Cargo.lock` records the **exact** version of every dependency that was resolved, so every build (yours, CI's, a colleague's) uses the same code. Commit it. (Older advice said not to commit it for libraries; current guidance is to commit it for all projects.)

## Features

**Features** are named switches that turn on optional code or optional dependencies. Using a crate's feature: `tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }`. Defining your own: the `[features]` table above makes `regex` an **optional dependency** pulled in only by the `search` feature, and `default` lists features enabled unless a user opts out with `default-features = false`. In code, `#[cfg(feature = "search")]` includes an item only when the feature is on.

Features must be **additive**: enabling one may add functionality but must never break code that doesn't use it, because Cargo unifies features across the whole dependency graph.

## Other sections

- `[dev-dependencies]`: only for tests, examples and benchmarks.
- `[build-dependencies]`: for `build.rs` scripts.
- `[profile.release]` / `[profile.dev]`: optimization settings (`opt-level`, `lto`, `codegen-units`, `debug`, `overflow-checks`, `panic = "abort"`).
- `[workspace]`: several crates in one repository sharing one `Cargo.lock` and `target/` directory.
- `[lints]`: set rustc and clippy lint levels for the whole package.

## Common mistakes

- Pinning exact versions (`=1.2.3`) everywhere, which blocks bug fixes and causes conflicts. Use caret requirements and rely on `Cargo.lock`.
- Forgetting a feature a crate needs (`serde` without `derive`, `tokio` without `macros` for `#[tokio::main]`): the error is a missing macro or item.
- Treating `0.x` minor bumps as safe: `0.4` to `0.5` is a breaking change.

topics.title: Clippy and rustfmt: linting and formatting Rust code
topics.description: How to use cargo clippy and cargo fmt: the most common clippy suggestions with before and after code, lint levels, configuration, and running both in CI.
topics.body:
Two tools come with every Rust installation and are used on virtually every professional Rust project:

- **rustfmt** (`cargo fmt`) formats code in the community style: indentation, line breaks, spacing. Nobody argues about style in code review because nobody formats by hand.
- **clippy** (`cargo clippy`) is a **linter** with hundreds of checks for bugs, slow code, and non-idiomatic patterns, each with an explanation and usually a suggested fix.

## rustfmt

```text
$ cargo fmt            # format the whole project
$ cargo fmt --check    # CI: fail if anything isn't formatted
```

Configure it (rarely) with a `rustfmt.toml`, for example `max_width = 120`. Most teams keep the defaults. Set your editor to format on save; rust-analyzer does it for you in VS Code.

## clippy's most common suggestions

| Lint | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `needless_return` | `return x;` as the last line | `x` |
| `len_zero` | `if v.len() == 0` | `if v.is_empty()` |
| `needless_range_loop` | `for i in 0..v.len() { v[i] ... }` | `for x in &v` or `.iter().enumerate()` |
| `ptr_arg` | `fn f(s: &String)`, `fn g(v: &Vec<i32>)` | `fn f(s: &str)`, `fn g(v: &[i32])` |
| `bool_comparison` | `if done == true` | `if done` |
| `clone_on_copy` | `x.clone()` on an `i32` | `x` |
| `manual_map` | `match opt { Some(x) => Some(f(x)), None => None }` | `opt.map(f)` |
| `collapsible_if` | `if a { if b { ... } }` | `if a && b { ... }` |
| `single_match` | a `match` with one arm and `_ => {}` | `if let` |
| `useless_format` | `format!("{}", s)` | `s.to_string()` |
| `unwrap_or_default` | `.unwrap_or(Vec::new())` | `.unwrap_or_default()` |
| `map_entry` | `if !m.contains_key(k) { m.insert(k, v) }` | `m.entry(k).or_insert(v)` |

A clippy warning looks like a compiler warning, with a link to the lint's documentation:

```text
warning: length comparison to zero
 --> src/main.rs:4:8
  |
4 |     if names.len() == 0 {
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ help: using `is_empty` is clearer and more explicit: `names.is_empty()`
```

## Lint groups and levels

Lints are grouped: `clippy::correctness` (likely bugs, **deny** by default), `suspicious`, `style`, `complexity` and `perf` (warn by default), plus opt-in `pedantic`, `nursery` and `restriction`. Adjust them:

- In code: `#[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]` on an item, or better `#[expect(clippy::lint_name, reason = "...")]`, which warns you when the exception is no longer needed.
- Project-wide in `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[lints.clippy]
pedantic = { level = "warn", priority = -1 }
unwrap_used = "warn"
module_name_repetitions = "allow"
```

## In CI

```text
cargo fmt --check
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
cargo test
```

`-D warnings` turns every warning into an error, so the main branch stays clean. `cargo clippy --fix` applies machine-applicable suggestions automatically.

## Advice

- Fix clippy warnings as you go; they're cheap when the code is fresh.
- Read the lint's explanation before silencing it. Most suggestions also make code faster or clearer.
- Don't enable all of `pedantic` on an existing codebase in one go; pick the lints your team agrees on.

topics.title: macro_rules! in Rust: writing your own macros
topics.description: How to write declarative macros in Rust with macro_rules!: matchers, fragment specifiers like expr and ident, repetition with $(...),*, and when to use them.
topics.body:
You've been calling macros since your first program: `println!`, `vec!`, `format!`, `assert_eq!`. A **macro** is code that writes code at compile time. `macro_rules!` lets you write your own **declarative macros**: you describe input patterns, and what each one expands to.

## A first macro

```rust
macro_rules! square {
    ($x:expr) => {
        $x * $x
    };
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", square!(7));
    println!("{}", square!(2 + 3));
}
```

```text
49
25
```

- Each **rule** is `(matcher) => { expansion };`. Rules are tried top to bottom; the first that matches is used.
- `$x:expr` matches any expression and names it `$x`. `square!(2 + 3)` gives 25, not 11: macros work on syntax trees, not text, so `$x` stays one expression. (Unlike C's `#define`.)

## Fragment specifiers

| Specifier | Matches |
|---|---|
| `expr` | an expression: `1 + 2`, `foo(x)`, `vec![1]` |
| `ident` | an identifier: `count`, `Player` |
| `ty` | a type: `u32`, `Vec<String>` |
| `literal` | a literal: `42`, `"hi"`, `true` |
| `pat` | a pattern: `Some(x)`, `1..=5` |
| `block` | a `{ ... }` block |
| `tt` | a single token tree (the most flexible) |

## Repetition

`$( ... ),*` matches zero or more comma-separated items; `+` means one or more; `?` means optional. Repeat the same group in the expansion to emit code per item:

```rust
macro_rules! hashmap {
    ($($key:expr => $value:expr),* $(,)?) => {{
        let mut map = std::collections::HashMap::new();
        $( map.insert($key, $value); )*
        map
    }};
}

let ages = hashmap! { "Ferris" => 7, "Corro" => 3 };
```

`$(,)?` accepts an optional trailing comma. The double braces `{{ ... }}` make the expansion a block expression, so the macro can be used where a value is expected.

## Hygiene

Variables created inside a macro (like `map` above) can't clash with the caller's variables of the same name: `macro_rules!` is **hygienic** for local variables. Items (functions, types) are not, so refer to them with full paths (`$crate::helper`, `::std::collections::HashMap`) in macros you export.

## When to write a macro

Reach for a function or a generic first: they're easier to read, type-check and debug. Macros earn their place when you need something functions can't do:

- a variable number of arguments (`vec!`, `println!`),
- generating repetitive items (`impl` blocks for many types, enum variants with matching methods),
- small domain-specific syntax (`hashmap!{ k => v }`, test tables),
- code that needs the caller's tokens, like `stringify!(expr)` for assertion messages.

`#[macro_export]` makes a macro available to other crates. `cargo expand` (an installable tool) shows what macros expand to, which is the best way to debug them.

## Errors

Calling a macro with input no rule matches gives errors like ``no rules expected `,` `` or `unexpected end of macro invocation`. Errors inside the expansion point into the macro's body.

## Procedural macros

`#[derive(Serialize)]`, `#[tokio::main]` and `#[test]`-like attributes are **procedural macros**: Rust functions, in a separate crate, that receive a token stream and return a new one. They're far more powerful (and more work) than `macro_rules!`; most developers use them every day but rarely write one.

topics.title: Unsafe Rust: what it allows and when to use it
topics.description: What the unsafe keyword actually permits in Rust, raw pointers, unsafe functions, FFI, writing safe abstractions with SAFETY comments, and when it's justified.
topics.body:
Safe Rust guarantees no dangling pointers, no data races and no use-after-free. Some correct programs can't be proven safe by the compiler, though: talking to C libraries, writing a new data structure, using special CPU instructions. **`unsafe`** marks code where **you** take responsibility for upholding those guarantees.

## What unsafe allows (and only this)

Inside an `unsafe { }` block you may:

1. dereference a **raw pointer** (`*const T`, `*mut T`),
2. call an **`unsafe fn`** (including C functions via FFI),
3. read or write a **`static mut`**,
4. implement an **`unsafe trait`** (like `Send` or `Sync`),
5. access fields of a **`union`**.

That's the complete list. `unsafe` does **not** turn off the borrow checker, type checking or bounds checks on normal code. Creating a raw pointer is safe; only using it needs `unsafe`:

```rust-error
fn main() {
    let x = 5;
    let p = &x as *const i32;
    println!("{}", *p);
}
```

```compiler
error[E0133]: dereference of raw pointer is unsafe and requires unsafe block
```

## Undefined behavior

If unsafe code breaks Rust's rules (a dangling or misaligned pointer, two `&mut` to the same data, an invalid `bool` or `char` value, a data race), the program has **undefined behavior**: the compiler's optimizations assume it can't happen, and anything may result, including bugs that appear far away and only in release builds.

## Safe abstractions

The idiomatic use of `unsafe` is a small block inside a function with a **safe** signature, where the function's own checks guarantee the unsafe operations are valid. The standard library is full of these: `Vec`, `String` and `split_at_mut` are built on unsafe code that you call safely.

Every unsafe block should have a `// SAFETY:` comment explaining why it's sound, and every `unsafe fn` a `# Safety` doc section listing what callers must guarantee. Clippy can require these (`undocumented_unsafe_blocks`).

## FFI: calling C

Functions from other languages are declared in an `extern` block. In the 2024 edition the block itself is written `unsafe extern "C"`, because declaring a foreign signature wrongly is itself unsound. Calls to the functions need an `unsafe` block, since the compiler can't check C code. Libraries usually wrap these calls in safe Rust functions (the `-sys` crate plus a safe wrapper crate pattern).

## When unsafe is justified at work

- **FFI**: calling C libraries or the OS, or exposing Rust to other languages.
- **Performance**, only after profiling shows a real need, and after trying safe options (iterators, `chunks_exact`, slices instead of indexing) that remove bounds checks anyway.
- **Low-level data structures** that need raw pointers (intrusive lists, lock-free queues, custom allocators).

Otherwise, prefer existing well-reviewed crates. Many companies require extra review for any new `unsafe`, and `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` at the crate root lets a project ban it outright.

## Tools

**Miri** (`cargo +nightly miri test`) runs your tests in an interpreter that detects many kinds of undefined behavior. Sanitizers (AddressSanitizer, ThreadSanitizer) help with FFI-heavy code.

## Common mistakes

- **`static mut` for global state.** Use atomics, `Mutex`, or `OnceLock`/`LazyLock`; the 2024 edition rejects references to `static mut` by default (`static_mut_refs`).
- **Large unsafe blocks.** Keep them to the exact operations that need it, so reviewers know where to look.
- **"It works in my test" as proof.** Undefined behavior can pass every test. Reason about the rules, and run Miri.

topics.title: Rust performance tips: release builds, allocations and iterators
topics.description: Practical ways to make Rust code faster: build with --release, measure first, avoid needless clones and allocations, pre-size collections, buffer output.
topics.body:
Rust is fast by default, but a few habits make a big difference, and a few mistakes are common enough to check first.

## 1. Build in release mode

`cargo run` and `cargo build` produce **debug** builds: no optimizations, overflow checks on. They can be 10 to 100 times slower than **release** builds. Before measuring or comparing anything:

```text
cargo run --release
cargo build --release   # binary in target/release/
```

For a little more speed, `[profile.release]` in `Cargo.toml` can set `lto = true` (link-time optimization across crates) and `codegen-units = 1`, at the cost of compile time.

## 2. Measure before optimizing

Guessing where time goes is usually wrong. Use real tools:

- **criterion** (a crate) for reliable micro-benchmarks with statistics, run with `cargo bench` (the built-in `#[bench]` attribute is nightly-only).
- **perf** (Linux), **Instruments** (macOS), or **cargo flamegraph** to see which functions use the CPU.
- `std::time::Instant` for quick, rough timings of whole phases.

## 3. Fix the algorithm first

Replacing an O(n²) nested loop with a `HashMap` lookup or a sort plus binary search beats any micro-optimization. Check that membership tests in big collections use a `HashSet`, not `Vec::contains`.

## 4. Avoid needless allocations

Each `String`, `Vec`, `Box` or `.clone()` allocates on the heap. In hot code:

- **Borrow instead of cloning.** Take `&str` and `&[T]` parameters; return references when the data already exists.
- **Pre-size collections:** `Vec::with_capacity(n)`, `String::with_capacity(n)`, `HashMap::with_capacity(n)`.
- **Reuse buffers:** `buf.clear()` keeps the capacity, so a loop that reads lines into one `String` allocates once.
- **Don't `collect` in the middle of a chain** just to iterate again.
- **`Cow<str>`** returns borrowed data when nothing changed and allocates only when it must.

## 5. Use iterators

Iterator chains (`iter().filter().map().sum()`) compile to tight loops, frequently without bounds checks, and the optimizer can vectorize them. They're at least as fast as index loops, and clearer.

## 6. Buffer I/O

`println!` locks stdout and may flush on each line. For lots of output, lock once and wrap it in a `BufWriter`; use `BufReader` (or `read_to_string`) for input. This alone can speed up a text-processing program many times over.

## 7. Choose the right collection

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| push/pop at the end, index | `Vec` |
| push/pop at both ends (queue) | `VecDeque` |
| key lookup | `HashMap` (or `BTreeMap` if you need ordering or ranges) |
| always take the smallest/largest | `BinaryHeap` |
| membership tests | `HashSet` |

## 8. Smaller wins

- `sort_unstable` is faster than `sort` when equal elements' order doesn't matter.
- Prefer generics (static dispatch) to `Box<dyn Trait>` in very hot loops.
- Parallelize CPU-bound work over large data with `rayon` (`par_iter()`).
- `#[inline]` rarely helps inside one crate; the optimizer already decides well.

## Common mistakes

- Benchmarking a debug build.
- Cloning to satisfy the borrow checker inside a loop.
- Calling `to_string()` or `format!` just to compare or look up keys (compare `&str` directly).
- `v.contains(&x)` on a big `Vec` inside a loop: O(n²) overall.
